Indigenous participation will ensure that students are exposed to Indigenous methodologies, as well as conventional Western approaches.
learning_outcomes: Produce a variety of fieldwork outputs to an acceptable professional standard
Evaluate the diverse techniques and methods used by archaeologists and Indigenous people in recording Indigenous artefacts, sites, places and landscapes
Accurately and appropriately assess Indigenous artefacts, sites, places and landscapes at an advanced level
Plan research with Indigenous communities in an ethical and culturally appropriate manner
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPSM-Graduate Diploma in Screen and Media Production 1a Admission into GCARCH-Graduate Certificate in Archaeology 1b Admission into GDPAHM-Graduate Diploma in Archaeology and Heritage Management 1c Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management 1d Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] 1e Admission into MSMA-Master of Screen and Media Production [1 year] Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e))

title: Historical Archaeology Field School
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop recording, oral history and analytical skills associated with the practice of historical archaeology in Australia Develop historical documentary research skills associated with the practice of historical archaeology Improve understanding of the relationship between local communities, heritage and historical archaeology Further develop students' understanding of ethical practice in Australian archaeology

This topic provides experience in historical archaeological field methods. The topic contains some lecture and workshop content, but will mostly be directed towards teaching students in-depth practical recording, excavation and assessment skills necessary for historical archaeological research.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the range of recording processes necessary on a historical archaeological project
Produce a variety of fieldwork outputs to an acceptable professional standard
Integrate evidence from primary and secondary historical sources with material evidence provided by archaeology
Accurately and appropriately assess historical archaeological sites, artefacts and landscapes at an advanced level
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPSM-Graduate Diploma in Screen and Media Production 1a Admission into GCARCH-Graduate Certificate in Archaeology 1b Admission into GDPAHM-Graduate Diploma in Archaeology and Heritage Management 1c Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] 1d Admission into MSMA-Master of Screen and Media Production [1 year] 1e Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e))

title: Advanced Archaeology Field School
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop advanced skills associated with the professional practice of archaeology and heritage management in Australia and internationally Further develop students' knowledge of what constitutes ethical practice in archaeology and heritage management Advance students' familiarity with theoretical, methodological and political issues in archaeology and heritage research

This topic builds upon students' previous knowledge to provide training in a range of advanced field and/or laboratory methods. The topic will contain some lecture and workshop content, but will mostly be directed towards teaching students hands-on technical skills.
learning_outcomes: Assess sites, artefacts and landscapes at an advanced level
Produce a variety of archaeological and heritage management outputs to an acceptable professional standard
Appraise research with communities and other professionals in an ethical and culturally appropriate manner
Evaluate the diverse techniques used in archaeological and heritage site and artefact recording, as well as heritage management
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCARCH-Graduate Certificate in Archaeology 1a Admission into GDPSM-Graduate Diploma in Screen and Media Production 1b Admission into GDPAHM-Graduate Diploma in Archaeology and Heritage Management 1c Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management 1d Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] 1e Admission into MSMA-Master of Screen and Media Production [1 year] Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e))

title: Community Archaeology Field School GE
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Consolidate for students the practical and personal skills necessary to conducting field research with community members Broaden students awareness of the political and ethical dimensions of community archaeology Give students extended practical experience in working with community members Help students to develop recording skills used in community archaeology fieldwork, such as site recording, rock art recording, site and artefact recording, archival research, collecting oral histories and creating plans, maps and other records

This topic will develop students' abilities to participate in community archaeology work, including those who have previously undertaken ethnoarchaeology. Students will be required to employ skills to an advanced level, which may include those related to site recording and artefact recording, collecting oral histories, and ethical interactions with community members, including Indigenous groups, as appropriate to the community archaeology context. Student will enhance skills in communicating effectively with a range of community members.
learning_outcomes: Plan research with communities in an ethical and culturally appropriate manner
Determine the range of recording processes necessary on an archaeological field project
Integrate a broad range of community understandings and perspectives into fieldwork and interpretation
Produce a variety of fieldwork outputs to an acceptable professional standard
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCARCH-Graduate Certificate in Archaeology 1a Admission into GDPAHM-Graduate Diploma in Archaeology and Heritage Management 1b Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management 1c Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Introductory Archaeological Geophysics
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with a theoretical introduction to geophysical techniques that might be employed in archaeological contexts Introduce students to a range of archaeological case studies within which geophysical techniques have been applied Provide students with the opportunity to gain hands-on experience with a range of different geophysical techniques, including but not necessarily limited to ground penetrating radar, magnetometer and electromagnetic induction Provide students with an understanding of geophysical data editing, processing and interpretation procedures Provide students with an understanding of standard geophysical reports

This topic is aimed at graduates in archaeology or an earth sciences background who wish to gain experience in archaeological geophysics. The topic will provide you with an understanding of the scientific principles behind a range of techniques used in shallow archaeological prospection, the basic field operation of such techniques, data processing, data interpretation and geophysical reporting. Techniques covered may include magnetometry, electromagnetic induction, direct current resistivity, seismic techniques and ground penetrating radar. The topic will be delivered through a series of lectures, demonstrations, practical hands-on sessions and computer based labs.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and produce simple maps of geophysical information
Appraise the major geophysical techniques that might be applied in an archaeological context
Critique a range of literature concerning the geophysical techniques covered during the topic
Set up basic field operation of a range of different geophysical techniques, including but not limited to ground penetrating radar, magnetometer and electromagnetic induction
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCARCH-Graduate Certificate in Archaeology 1a Admission into GDPSM-Graduate Diploma in Screen and Media Production 1b Admission into GDPMA-Graduate Diploma in Maritime Archaeology 1c Admission into MMARCH-Master of Maritime Archaeology 1d Admission into GDPAHM-Graduate Diploma in Archaeology and Heritage Management 1e Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management 1f Admission into MSMA-Master of Screen and Media Production [1 year] 1g Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g))

title: Thesis Research Project (9/18 units)
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop advanced independent research skills in one area of archaeological theory or practice Enable students to generate particular skills/knowledge relating to an area of archaeological theory or practice Improve students' research skills and their ability to evaluate literature critically Develop students' skills in justifying and interpreting theoretical positions, and the ability to construct, test and defend an argument

This topic is an in depth independent study into any facet of maritime archaeology, either applied or theoretical. The topic consists of a thesi to be written under the supervision of a staff member. The thesis should give evidence of the student's abilities in collecting and evaluating information, constructing, testing or defending an argument or thesis, and examining critically the available literature in their chosen area of enquiry. The area of study must be developed in consultation with the supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of theoretical, practical and/or political approaches to archaeology
Construct, test and defend an argument
Carry out research in a specialised area, including the analysis of complex ideas and/or data
Assess literature relating to archaeological theory and practice critically
Apply theoretical propositions to an appropriate research methodology, as part of an extended research project
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MMARCH-Master of Maritime Archaeology 1a Admission into MMARCHA-Master of Maritime Archaeology [1.5 years] 1b Admission into MAHM-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management 1c Admission into MAHMA-Master of Archaeology and Heritage Management [1.5 years] Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))
incompatibilities: 1 of ARCH8520, ARCH8520A, ARCH8520B, ARCH8520C, ARCH9001A

faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire the appropriate research skills and training to enable them to work independently and complete a body of research at the level of a Masters by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Master's degree by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Masters by Research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Master's degree by research.
learning_outcomes: Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work
Explain their understanding of chosen methodological practices
Demonstrate their capacity to formulate a significant problem and synthesise a complex body of knowledge
Validate research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Demonstrate their review and application of the literature in writing and orally (where appropriate)

Construct, test and defend an argument

title: Higher Degree Thesis (PhD)
faculty: History, Archaeology, Indigenous Studies and Geography
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire high-level research skills and training, to enable them to work independently and complete a body of original research at the level of a Doctorate by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Doctorate by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Doctorate by research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Doctorate by research.
learning_outcomes: Independently assess evidence of an original investigation or testing of ideas and competence in independent research or experimentation
Demonstrate their review and application of the literature in writing and orally (where appropriate)
Validate the originality of their research topic in relation to a broader framework of knowledge
Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work
Explain their mastery of appropriate conceptual and methodological skills
Assess research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works

title: Truth and Knowledge in a Changing World
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the skills and knowledge to: Understand the different definitions and uses of knowledge in historical and contemporary contexts Engage with debates on the value of different forms of knowledge as they relate to social issues Become critical and creative producers and consumers of knowledge, to aid them in their undergraduate study and future professional contexts

How do we know what we know? Why do we invest in certain truths over others? This topic introduces students to different ways of knowing the world, with a particular focus on diverse knowledge systems, including Indigenous knowledge, that challenge dominant ways of knowing. We encourage students to explore the often-contested role of knowledge in constructing and responding to real world problems historically and in contemporary times, and across national and global contexts. We will consider the relationship between truth and knowledge and our current methods for evaluating knowledge in Humanities and Social Sciences disciplines. This topic explores current debates on the ethics of knowledge ownership and sharing.
learning_outcomes: Compare knowledge claims about key social issues
Explain the implications of diverse knowledge claims
Communicate knowledge across different media
Evaluate the value and utility of different types and sources of information

title: Education, Work, and Identity
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with conceptual and personal knowledge about work and employment, specifically as it is facilitated through studying a Bachelor of Arts. It aims to assist students to develop knowledge, skills and language that will empower them to proceed more confidently in imagining, planning and implementing future careers.

This topic engages students to develop their relationship to education, work, skills and employability. We will focus on contemporary debates relating to pathways into work, the meaning and significance of work and the role of education, specifically the Bachelor of Arts, in shaping work futures. These are explored as 'big ideas' and as individual orientations and aspirations. This topic includes collaboration with Flinders Careers and Employability.
learning_outcomes: Build professional documents (CV, LinkedIn etc) and career plans.
Develop your relationship to education and work contextualised in social, cultural and disciplinary issues.
Integrate concepts, personal understanding and disciplinary knowledge to discuss work and education in contemporary society.

title: Professional and Academic Futures
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to synthesise and ethically apply the knowledge and skills they have acquired throughout their BA degree in new professional or education contexts.

In this topic, students will have the opportunity to synthesise the knowledge and skills that they have acquired from their BA and will have the chance to ethically apply their university study to either real-world experiences and contexts, or as preparation for future studies. In ARTS3001, students can choose one of two pathways: professional, or further studies. In the professional pathway students will complete a placement of 60 hours in a field related to their major. In the further studies pathway students will work with an academic supervisor on an agreed project or aspect of a research project related to their own major.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional behaviours in work or educational contexts
Reflect on and measure your own learning, skill development, and employability
Critically evaluate institutions and work practices
Appraise connections between your university study and opportunities to perform as informed and engaged citizens in local and global contexts

title: Audiology 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge and proficiency in the evidence based clinical principles and practices of audiology, as introduced through the Enquiry Based Learning cases and theory content.

The topic aims to provide students with knowledge of: the anatomy, physiology and typical development of the human auditory system, basic pathology with particular reference to the auditory system, and the genetics of hearing loss at an introductory level. The epidemiology and major causes of hearing loss will be explored, as will the acoustic, psychological, developmental and statistical principles underlying audiological assessment in children and adults. Finally, the topic will provide an overview of acoustic, linguistic and other characteristics of human communication, as well as an introduction to typical development in children.
learning_outcomes: Explain the rationale for clinical hearing assessments within the context of auditory physiology, and relevant acoustic, psychoacoustic, psychological and developmental principles
Discuss the genetic basis of hearing loss at an introductory level in relation to various clinical cases
Describe the structure, function and typical development of the human auditory system across the lifespan
Identify the linguistic characteristics of human communication across the lifespan
Demonstrate effective teamwork, professional communication, and critical reflection on learning and group processes
Analyse the acoustic, psychoacoustic, linguistic, and statistical principles underlying various audiological assessments
Explain basic pathologies and their effect on the auditory system with reference to pathophysiology and assessment results
Interpret case history information and the results of audiological assessments, for a range of paediatric and adult cases
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Foundational Sciences for Audiological Practice
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the foundational knowledge pertaining to the peripheral hearing and its physiology from the pinnae to the cochlea, required for application to clinical scenarios presented in EBL1.

This topic provides the fundamentals of the auditory system, its related physiology, and mechanisms.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the acoustic, psychoacoustic, and linguistic principles underlying various audiological assessments
Integrate knowledge of auditory physiology, acoustics, and psychoacoustics to explain audiological results
Describe the structure and function of the peripheral human auditory system

title: Audiology 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to apply knowledge and practical skills in the scientific and clinical principles and practices of audiology with particular emphasis on the basic hearing aid selection and fitting, communication-based rehabilitation, and diagnostic assessment.

This topic continues to focus on developing and applying knowledge of the aetiology, natural history, and prognosis of otological conditions. In addition, the effects of congenital or acquired hearing loss upon children and adults will be explored, including early intervention and rehabilitation. The topic will also develop skills in test selection with routine and special populations; test result interpretation; formulating audiological diagnosis and basic management plans, the acoustic characteristics of hearing aids and other amplification devices.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the human vestibular and central auditory system
Discuss the causes of congenital or acquired hearing and balance disorders and their associated linguistic, psychosocial, and developmental effects across the lifespan
Discuss diagnostic tests of hearing and balance, how they are conducted, and their interpretation
Examine the acoustic, psychoacoustic, linguistic, and statistical principles underlying audiological assessments and rehabilitative processes
Apply the principles of early intervention and patient centred care in the development of management and intervention plans
Demonstrate effective teamwork, professional communication and critical reflection on learning and group processes
Distinguish pathologies and their effect on the auditory system considering both pathophysiology and clinical assessment results
Analyse factors influencing candidacy and the process of the selection, fitting and outcome evaluation of hearing aids and other auditory devices
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Enquiry Based Learning in Audiology 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge and proficiency in the evidence based clinical principles and practices of audiology through clinically focused cases. The cases target fundamental and introductory knowledge and skills in foundation sciences, clinical sciences, client management skills and other areas that may arise in a case. A set of learning objectives is associated with each case that together will comprise the main teaching/learning nexus of this topic within the program.

Enquiry based learning previously referred to as Problem-based learning, is a strategy that uses real world scenarios that enable the students to explore their ideas through research, discussion, and reflection. This marks a unique course structure as the topic does not offer single-content topics (e.g., general audiology, acoustics or hearing aids).
learning_outcomes: Explore the historial context and social factors influencing health in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
Recognise the importance of teamwork, communication, and critical reflection in group learning
Explain basic pathologies and their effect on the auditory system with reference to pathophysiology and assessment results
Examine the reasoning behind clinical hearing assessments using knowledge of auditory physiology, psychoacoustic principles, and client factors.

title: Evidence Based Practice and Research Methods
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to develop students’ skills in research methods, evidence-based practice, critical thinking, database searching, reviewing of literature, scientific writing as well as presenting research to non-scientific audiences.

The Master of Audiology aims to produce graduates who can apply research findings to their clinical practice and build an evidence-base themselves through research. This topic introduces students to research-based principles and practices in audiology applicable throughout the course. Sessions include evidence-based practice, literature searches and reviews, critical thinking and writing. The topic is designed both for students with prior research experience to refresh their skills as well as for those without students research experience.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate audiological literature to inform evidence-based practice
Evaluate research methodologies and their applications in hearing research in clinical settings
Formulate a research question, proposal, and search protocol to address a topic related to clinical audiology
Communicate effectively with stakeholders of various backgrounds to promote mutual understanding and evidence-based practice

title: Clinical Audiological Skills 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to prepare the students to acquire the fundamental skills of hearing assessments and apply the theoretical knowledge to understand the applications within the clinical setting.

The clinical program within the Master of Audiology runs concurrently with the academic program. The level of student engagement and participation depends on the level of knowledge, and the timing within the course of a particular clinical experience. As soon as a topic has been lectured on and covered in practical classes, students are expected to attempt these skills under supervision in their clinical placements, with increasing independence over time.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate client centred informational counselling skills for common clinical conditions
Perform reliable and efficient administration of basic audiological tests in older children and adults
Use critical reflection on skills in test administration and interpretation to inform own professional development
Interpret and integrate case history information and basic audiological test results to develop appropriate clinical hypotheses

title: Enquiry Based Learning in Audiology 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge and proficiency in the evidence based clinical principles and practices of audiology through clinically focused cases. The cases chosen in the topic strengthen the fundamental knowledge and skills acquired in semester 1 and introduce new diagnostic and client management skills pertaining to children. A set of learning objectives is associated with each case that together will comprise the main teaching/learning nexus of this topic within the program.

EBL (previously referred to as Problem-based learning), similar to EBL 1, uses real world scenarios to enable the students to explore their ideas through research, discussion, and reflection.
learning_outcomes: Analyse factors influencing candidacy and the process of the selection, fitting and outcome evaluation of hearing aids and other auditory devices
Synthesise clinical data and research literature to inform clinical practice
Demonstrate teamwork, communication, and critical reflection in group learning
Evaluate diagnostic tests of hearing and balance, how they are conducted, and their interpretation
prerequisites: 2 of AUDI9121, AUDI9122

title: Clinical Audiological Skills 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to prepare the students to acquire the fundamental skills of hearing assessments and management especially of paediatric population and apply the theoretical knowledge within the clinical setting.

The clinical program within the Master of Audiology runs concurrently with the academic program. The level of student engagement and participation depends on the level of knowledge, and the timing within the course of a particular clinical experience. As soon as a topic has been lectured on and covered in practical classes, students are expected to attempt these skills under supervision in their clinical placements, with increasing independence over time.
learning_outcomes: Conduct basic verification measurements and troubleshooting of hearing aids and other assistive listening devices
Integrate client and clinical information to inform selection of hearing aids and other assistive listening devices to provide family centered care
Interpret and reframe clinical information in written and oral formats as appropriate to the intended audience
Articulate communication results and subsequent recommendations to clients, their carers, and other health professionals using a patient-centred care approach
prerequisites: AUDI9124

title: Paediatric Audiology
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to address knowledge and skills pertaining to hearing assessments in paediatric population. The topic aims to provide knowledge of common paediatric diseases and disorders and skills to understand the necessary adjustments required when assessing paediatric population.

This topic examines the development of audition in children, including paediatric auditory anatomy and physiology. It addresses hearing assessment, common paediatric auditory disorders, and principles of early identification, intervention and management in paediatric audiological care.
learning_outcomes: Advocate for access pathways to family-centred paediatric audiological care by identifying and facilitating access to education, resources and services that promote ethical service delivery.

Critically analyse the personal, family, and cultural implications of having a child with a significant hearing loss to support families in making informed decisions about their child’s audiological care by sharing relevant information using inclusive language
Create and justify valid hearing assessments in paediatric settings, recognising barriers that prevent access to services and elements influencing cultural safety and inclusion

Apply principles of early intervention and family-centred care to develop culturally responsive management and intervention plans for diverse clients, including Deaf community, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and those from other cultural and linguistically diverse backgrounds
prerequisites: AUDI9122

title: Foundational Sciences for Advanced Audiological Practice
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop students’ skills in the use of objective techniques to evaluate hearing with minimal participation from the client and in the analysis, interpretation, and integration of results to make diagnoses and plan management.

Babies, young infants or populations with neurological difficulties often are difficult-to-test as they are unable to actively participate in hearing assessments, therefore audiologists require tools that are objective and do not require responses from a client.
learning_outcomes: Integrate the findings from the objective assessments to determine audiological diagnosis and provide appropriate referral pathway
Demonstrate the use of and ability to modify objective audiological test battery used for site-of-lesion assessments
Critique current literature to inform the selection and use of relevant objective audiological and vestibular assessments in diagnosis of various hearing related disorders
prerequisites: AUDI9122

title: Research Project
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims for students to: undertake a research project involving the collection and analysis of data, interpretation of findings, and manuscript preparation.

This topic is a continuation of Research Methods. Students will conduct and write up a research project. Students will meet regularly in their groups and with their supervisor(s) through the semester. Each group will work on this project and present their progress in both oral and written formats.
learning_outcomes: Disseminate research outcomes in written and oral formats
Collaborate with research team members and reflect on the group process
Analyse and demonstrate an integrated knowledge of research data
Conduct a study which generates a substantial contribution to knowledge by appropriately addressing a research question through suitable research methods and principles
prerequisites: 1 AUDI9204 - Research Methods 1a AUDI9404 - Research Methods Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a))

title: Paediatric Audiology
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop student knowledge and skills in assessment, diagnosis and intervention of paediatric auditory disorders Introduce students to aspects of paediatric health services and their management in order to co-ordinate the topic with the paediatric clinical topic AUDI9217

This topic uses PBL cases to develop students' knowledge and skills in diagnosing and managing paediatric clients with auditory disorders, including peripheral hearing loss and auditory processing disorders, as well as intervention techniques such as hearing aid fitting, cochlear implantation, and auditory habilitation techniques. Lectures and seminars address relevant foundation sciences, and specialist topics in paediatric audiology and related medical, health and educational issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and proficiency with regard to the scientific and clinical principles and practices of paediatric audiology as introduced through the Problem Based Learning cases

title: Paediatric Clinical Audiology
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The main aim of the topic is to introduce students to the practice of paediatric audiology across a variety of clinical settings and populations. The objectives incorporated into this aim are for students to acquire and/or demonstrate: The ability to select and undertake age appropriate assessment tasks The ability to evaluate and respond to the child's auditory development The ability to interpret test results The ability to provide information and advice to parents and others about the outcomes of testing The ability to plan and undertake audiological intervention relevant to the child- the ability to plan longer term management of the child's hearing and associated needs

This topic offers students two to three regular weekly sessions of direct clinical experience in paediatric audiology in FU/FMC clinics and in other clinics in metropolitan Adelaide. These sessions are supported by the opportunity to practice clinical techniques via weekly practical skills sessions. Practical skills classes introduce students to clinical techniques associated with paediatric assessment, diagnosis and intervention.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a range of competencies in basic paediatric audiological skills focusing on the range of testing techniques for the assessment of peripheral hearing loss, and related skills in children under four years of age, as well as in case history taking and providing post-assessment information

title: Complex Audiological Case Management
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
In this topic, students will learn about diagnosing and managing complex disorders such as Tinnitus, Auditory Processing Disorders amongst others that require understanding of the client, within their context. The students will learn to apply the ICF framework provided by WHO,to the various disorders when planning their diagnostic routine and management plan.

Disorders such as Tinnitus, ANSD, Auditory Processing Disorder and Hidden Hearing Loss are challenging as the diagnoses and management often require multidisciplinary approaches. The disorders require strategies that go beyond the conventional audiological test battery. Similarly, management may need a wholistic approach with considerations of WHO's International Classification, Functioning and Health framework.
learning_outcomes: Describe the features and presentation of a range of complex hearing and balance disorders based on available literature
Evaluate interprofessional assessment and management strategies in the context of family-centred care for clients with complex needs
Weigh up case-based factors and research evidence to design evidence-based assessment and management protocols
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MAUD 2 Completion of 36 units of study in the MAUD Must satisfy: ((1 and 2))

title: Application of Evidence in Audiology Practice
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to extend the students' knowledge on how to explore quality of research, find evidence about different clinically relevant topics in Audiology and aim to plan their clinical approach based on evidence-based practice.

The students will extend their knowledge regarding quality of research, and find evidence about various audiological disorders.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise the current research findings related to management of complex hearing and balance disorders to develop evidence based practice
Design their clinical approach based on principles of evidence based practice considering interdisciplinary strategies
Create content to support effective and respectful communication with stakeholders of various cultural and professional backgrounds
prerequisites: 36 units of AUDI topics

title: Enquiry Based Learning in Audiology 3
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge and proficiency in the evidence based clinical principles and practices of audiology through clinically focused cases. The topic aims to use complex audiological cases to consolidate the knowledge and skills that the students acquired in year 1 and introduce new knowledge and skills when assessing and managing complex audiology cases.

This topic continues to build on previous Enquiry Based Learning Topics (EBL1 and 2) where students will continue to build their ideas through research, discussion, and reflection.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate audiological management approaches in the context of client-centered care
Explain complex pathologies and their effect on the auditory and balance systems with reference to pathophysiology and assessment results
Demonstrate effective teamwork, professional communication and critical reflection on group learning processes
Appraise audiological assessment results to diagnose and manage complex auditory disorders
prerequisites: 1 36 units of AUDI topics 2 ^AUDI9223 Must satisfy: ((1 and 2)) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

title: Clinical Audiological Skills 3
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to prepare the students to acquire the fundamental skills of hearing device evaluation and fitting and management as well as to apply the theoretical knowledge within the clinical setting.

The clinical program within the Master of Audiology runs concurrently with the academic program. Simulations provide the students opportunity to learn, practice and establish new skills. The students are required to apply newly acquired skills of hearing assessments and management under supervision in their clinical placements, with increasing independence over time.
learning_outcomes: Use critical reflection to appraise own performance and set goals for future clinical interactions
Integrate case history and assessment results to explain valid audiological diagnoses and basic management recommendations
Select, fit, and program appropriate hearing devices based on client and family requirements
Conduct case history and standard adult audiological assessment using a family-centered approach
prerequisites: 36 units of AUDI topics

title: Enquiry Based Learning in Audiology 4
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to ensure that students are aware of and understand that complex cases require critical thinking and principles of evidence-based practice for diagnosis and management. The cases are selected to consolidate the knowledge and skills that the students have already acquired and to apply critical thinking and evidence-based practice when planning the diagnose and management of the complex cases.

This is the final EBL Topic in the program. It continues to build on the students abilities to build and convey ideas based on discussions and reflections.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate diagnostic tests of hearing and balance, how they are conducted, and their interpretation
Demonstrate teamwork, communication, and critical reflection in group learning
Analyse factors influencing candidacy and the process of the selection, fitting and outcome evaluation of hearing aids and other auditory devices
Synthesise clinical data and research literature to inform clinical practice
prerequisites: AUDI9221

title: Clinical Audiological Skills 4
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to prepare the students to acquire the fundamental skills of hearing assessments and management across all ages and cases and apply the theoretical knowledge within the clinical setting.

The clinical program within the Master of Audiology runs concurrently with the academic program. This is the last clinical placment Topic and has a large workload dedicated for students to apply their hearing assessment and management skills on real clients, under supervision, with increasing independence over time.
learning_outcomes: Conduct case history and routine adult and paediatric audiological assessments meeting Audiology Australia professional standards
Perform safe and appropriate hearing device selection, fittings and related tasks including evaluation of client outcomes
Appraise own clinical performance and professional behaviour and reflect on areas for future development
Integrate case history and assessment results to explain valid audiological diagnoses and make individualised management recommendations
prerequisites: AUDI9224

title: Audiology Research Project
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to advance the students' research skills encompassing problem solving, critical and creative thinking, and scientific writing.

This topic builds on students' knowledge and skills to provide them with opportunities to work with experts in research, industry and service providers.
learning_outcomes: Disseminate research outcomes in written and oral formats
Analyse and demonstrate an integrated knowledge of research data
Conduct a study which generates a substantial contribution to knowledge by appropriately addressing a research question through suitable research methods and principles
prerequisites: AUDI9222

title: Transition to Practice in Audiology
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
To develop students' capacity to critically evaluate and apply public health principles, quality and safety frameworks, and evidence-based practice to the delivery of audiological services across diverse clinical contexts. To prepare students to work responsibly and responsively with populations who face systemic barriers to hearing health services, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, people living with dementia, and those with dual sensory loss. To equip students with the research and analytical skills to critically appraise literature and policy, and formulate evidence-based recommendations for the improvement of audiological practice and hearing health services. To foster the professional and flexible skills required to navigate the intern-to-practitioner transition, including self-directed learning, reflective practice, and effective collaboration within healthcare teams. To support students to integrate quality improvement principles into audiological service delivery, enabling them to identify service gaps and contribute to the ongoing development of the audiology profession.

This topic prepares students for the transition from audiology student to audiology intern by developing the advanced knowledge, professional judgment, and flexible skills required for contemporary audiological practice. Drawing on public health principles, quality and safety frameworks, culturally responsive approaches, and evidence-based practice, students engage with the complex and dynamic contexts in which audiologists work across diverse healthcare settings. The topic integrates online and in-person learning experiences to develop graduates who are equipped to practise with autonomy, ethical responsibility, and a commitment to continuous professional improvement, consistent with the expectations of Audiology Australia accreditation standards and the Australian Qualifications Framework Level 9.
learning_outcomes: Integrate quality and safety principles with professional behaviours, to support client and clinician well-being in audiology practice.
Critically evaluate public health principles to improve access, client experience and shared decision-making within audiological practice.
Critically appraise literature on vulnerable population groups commonly accessing audiology services and formulate evidence-based recommendations for enhancement of the profession.
Design culturally responsive approaches to audiological service delivery.

title: Professional Studies 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to ensure students can: Identify and understand core considerations in professional practice and demonstrate personal development related to interpersonal skills, clinical communication and observation Confidently communicate with clients in a simulated environment and understand the principles of client focused practice Demonstrate the principles of evidence-based practice and how it relates to the role of the Audiologist

This topic introduces students to generic aspects of clinical practice as a health professional as well as areas more specific to audiology. This introductory topic (1 of 2) will provide conceptual foundations and develop skills such as clinical interviewing and giving information. Core elements include: Evidence based practice, oral and written communication/interpersonal skills, and fundamentals of client focused practice. The topic links directly to other concurrent topics.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a simulated patient interview using client centered practices
Use critical reflection to appraise the professional role of the Audiologist and how this relates to their personal learning journey
Discuss the principles of client-centred practice in clinical settings
Critically evaluate health literature to inform evidence-based practice within the scope of an Audiologist
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Clinical Audiology 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to introduce students to a range of basic audiological skills focusing on the standard test battery for the assessment of peripheral hearing loss. The emphasis at this stage will be on the acquisition of skills in obtaining information from clients, examination of the ear and basic testing of hearing. Skills in observation, description and results interpretation will also be developed.

This topic concentrates on the development of clinical skills. Weekly practical sessions introduce students to clinical assessment skills and provide hands-on experience in preparation for clinical placements. The students will be rostered for clinical placements with audiologists in the Adelaide metropolitan area. These will include hospital and community settings, including private practices. The student will work under supervision with clients of different ages.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate client centred informational counselling skills for common clinical conditions
Interpret and integrate basic audiological test results and develop sound clinical hypotheses
Perform reliable and efficient administration of basic audiological tests across the lifespan
Use critical reflection on skills in test administration and interpretation to inform own professional development
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Professional Studies 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to demonstrate application of knowledge and skills in core areas of professional practice and personal development related to interpersonal skills, observation, and aspects of written and oral clinical communications. There is a particular focus on the integration of general principles in paediatric and educational audiology.

This topic introduces students to generic aspects of clinical practice as a health professional as well as areas more specific to audiology. This topic (2 of 2) will provide conceptual foundations and develop skills, in areas such as ethics, cultural awareness, communication skills, specialist considerations in paediatrics and work readiness. The topic links directly to all concurrent clinical topics. Students will continue to develop skills in observing, recording and reflecting on clinical activity. Personal development in relation to professional practice will be fostered.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise clinical data and research literature to inform clinical practice
Critically reflect on clinical processes, the roles played by all participants in clinical settings, and elements influencing cultural safety and inclusion
Create accurate clinical reports for varied audiences that include suitable recommendations
Theorise the personal and family implications of having a child with a significant hearing loss
Interpret and reframe clinical information in written and oral formats as appropriate to the intended audience
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Clinical Audiology 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an opportunity to demonstrate application of knowledge and skills with regard to competencies in clinical audiology across a range of client types, rehabilitation and assessment methods.

Students will be rostered for clinical placements with audiologists in the Adelaide metropolitan area. The emphasis will be on the consolidation of clinical skills and interacting with clients. Clinical activities will be undertaken in hearing aid fitting and diagnostic audiology and include the integration of clinical information and the development of management plans.
learning_outcomes: Integrate client and clinical information to make clinical judgements on hearing aids and other assistive listening devices
Critically reflect on clinical placement experiences, including skills performance, key learnings, and interactions with clients and other health professionals
Conduct basic audiometry and other routinely used audiological tests in clinical simulations and placements
Conduct basic verification measurements and trouble shooting of hearing aids and other assistive listening devices
Articulate audiological results and subsequent recommendations to clients, their carers, and other health professionals using a patient-centred care approach
prerequisites: Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology

title: Audiology 3
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge regarding advanced and specialised areas of audiological practice as introduced in the enquiry--based learning cases and associated sessions in this semester.

This topic develops students' knowledge and skills in diagnosing and managing clients with complex needs and auditory disorders. Focus is on the development of clinical theory and method in adult hearing aid fitting and diagnostic audiology.
learning_outcomes: Generate critical reflection on professional behaviours and communication, including teamwork and collaboration with peers
Describe the features and presentation of a range of complex hearing and balance disorders
Appraise audiological assessment results to diagnose auditory disorders and devise management plans for clients with complex hearing and balance needs
Explain the function and benefits of a range of hearing aid technology features
prerequisites: 1 36 unit(s) of AUDI9% 2 Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Clinical Audiology 3
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Create opportunity for clinical interaction and assessment competency and the application of knowledge and evidence to the practice of clinical audiology Foster basic understanding of management issues related to the practice of audiology, including aspects of health service delivery, the administrative requirements, funding arrangements and clinical governance.

The main component will be the first of two clinical block placements. The placements in metropolitan, regional and remote audiology services provide students with the opportunity to apply knowledge and develop clinical competence and confidence under the guidance of qualified clinicians. Practical workshops in the first weeks of Semester 1 are designed to assist students to develop skills in giving client feedback and in hearing aid selection and fitting.
learning_outcomes: Conduct case history and standard adult audiological assessment using a client centered approach
Conduct appropriate hearing aid selection, fittings and fine-tuning using hearing devices and software from different manufacturers
Use critical reflection to appraise own performance and set goals for future clinical interactions
Integrate case history and assessment results to explain valid audiological diagnoses and basic management recommendations
prerequisites: 1 36 unit(s) of AUDI9% 2 Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Research Methods
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the principles and practices of research in allied health and related disciplines Provide students with understanding and skills in the evaluation of scientific literature, determination of research methodology and analysis Provide students with skills and experience in scientific writing, and the dissemination of research findings Provide students with experience working in research teams

This topic introduces basic principles and practices of research in allied health and related disciplines. Students will be assigned to small groups and allocated a research project. Each group will work on this project throughout the semester and present their progress in both oral and written formats.
learning_outcomes: Explain different experimental and non-experimental research designs
Explain the relationship between evidence-based practice, study design and research quality
Formulate a research question, proposal and search protocol to address a topic related to audiology
Critique research methodologies and outcomes within the context of a research project
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology 2 36 unit(s) of AUDI% Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Clinical Audiology 4
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to build on the clinical skills developed in Clinical Audiology 3. Students will become confident with; clinical interaction, audiological assessment and intervention competency and the application of knowledge and evidence to the practice of clinical audiology understanding of management issues related to the practice of audiology

The main component will be the second of two clinical block placements of 4 days per week for 5 weeks. The placements in metropolitan, regional and remote audiology services will be organised by staff.
learning_outcomes: Integrate case history and assessment results to explain valid audiological diagnoses and make individualised management recommendations
Perform safe and appropriate hearing device selection, fittings and related tasks including evaluation of client outcomes
Appraise own clinical performance and professional behaviour and reflect on areas for future development
Conduct case history and routine adult and paediatric audiological assessments, meeting Audiology Australia professional standards
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology 2 36 unit(s) of AUDI9% Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Introduction to Biodiversity and Conservation
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: An understanding of the extent of the world's biodiversity An appreciation of the threat to biodiversity posed by human activities, including an understanding of the nature and levels of current rates of extinction An understanding of the scientific bases of biological conservation An appreciation of the nature of the scientific method and of its strengths and limitations An ability to assess critically current and future developments relevant to the conservation of biological diversity An appreciation of the societal and ethical contexts of conservation biology, of human impacts on biodiversity and of the professional practice of biologists An appreciation of First Nations Peoples connections to biodiversity An ability to work effectively and cooperatively as a member of small teams An ability to communicate effectively using a variety of media

During the topic lectures will be delivered on the following:- What is biodiversity? How many living species are there? What is the distribution of global biodiversity? How is biodiversity measured? The role of systematics in assessing biodiversity. The role of ecology in understanding species interactions. Loss of biodiversity - rates of extinction. Loss of biodiversity - human impacts. The values of biodiversity - economic, social etc. Bioprospecting. Biological conservation - what are we trying to preserve and how can we achieve this? Weekly tutorials will be held to assist students in the design and execution of their practical projects and to address any questions arising from the lecture material. On the field trip and during practicals students will work in teams of approximately 5 students and will conduct a project over the semester on assessing biodiversity within a particular habitat.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to conduct biodiversity surveys, summarise numerical data and evaluate its relevance to evidence-based conservation
Express the values of biodiversity and conservation, including their societal and cultural significance in an Australian context.
Recognise different characterisations of biodiversity and describe the major threatening process leading to biodiversity loss and species extinctions.
Review major threats to species of conservation significance and apply knowledge of conservation and restoration practices to develop a species recovery plan

title: Audiology 4
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with knowledge of advanced and specialised areas of evidence-based audiological practice as introduced in the enquiry-based learning cases and associated sessions in this semester.

This topic further develops students' knowledge and skills in diagnosing and managing adult and paediatric clients with complex needs and auditory disorders. Focus is on the development of clinical theory and method in diagnostic audiology, aural rehabilitation and hearing aid fitting.
learning_outcomes: Appraise audiological assessment results to diagnose auditory disorders, devise management plans for clients with complex hearing and balance needs, and evaluate client outcomes
Evaluate audiological literature and create evidence-based resources to communicate findings
Critically reflect on professional behaviours and communication, including teamwork and collaboration with peers
Describe the features and presentation of a range of complex hearing and balance disorders
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MAUD-Master of Audiology 2 36 unit(s) of AUDI9% Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Introduction to Plant Science
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic will provide a platform to understand the foundations of plant science. Students will learn about a range of plant biological patterns and processes through the lenses of physiology, cell biology, genetics and ecology. They will be provided an appreciation of the evolutionary history of plants and their varied uses and threats in modern society.

In this introductory topic, you will learn about the origin, diversity, structure, and internal processes of plants and how plants form the basis of ecosystems and human societies. You will gain an appreciation of the critical role the plants have in supporting life on earth and to human societies and therefore how fundamental plants are to the natural history of our planet and the evolution humankind.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge to classify the roles, issues, and opportunities that plants have in society
Apply problem solving, critical thinking and written communication to addressing scientific scenarios related to plant science
Develop a sound knowledge of fundamental plant science concepts

title: Human Impacts and Biodiversity
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop: An understanding of the nature, significance and role of major components of the Australian native biota An understanding of the major conservation issues regarding the major components of the Australian native biota An appreciation of the biological, cultural, economic and social issues involved in conservation of endangered species An understanding of the methodologies of monitoring and conserving endangered species An understanding of the changing nature of ecosystems and biological communities, particularly in the Australian context An understanding of the impact of human activities on biodiversity in Australia A knowledge of current examples of ecosystem conservation and restoration following disturbances of varying severities and types, focussing on Australian case histories

This topic includes: Field trips during an intensive, which will illustrate principles of conservation biology in an Australian context Studies on the evolutionary history, relationships and ecological roles of major groups of Australian native plants and animals Analyses of human impacts on, and conservation biology of, major components of the Australian native biota Relevant skills in critical analysis in the area of biodiversity and conservation
learning_outcomes: Determine the values and appropriateness of genetic, behavioral, community and ecosystem-based approaches to conservation and restoration programs
Evaluate and communicate key issues in biodiversity and conservation and develop solutions independently and in small groups
Apply skills in monitoring and identifying organisms to evaluate human impacts
Utilize modern analytical software packages to analyse biodiversity data and evaluate the information for use in the conservation of taxa.
Assess anthropogenic drivers of ecosystem change and species decline and understand the nature of drivers that lead to the loss of biodiversity
prerequisites: 1 of BIOL2711, BIOD2701

title: Biodiversity and Conservation
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: An understanding of the impact of habitat change on species persistence A knowledge of the processes leading to population extinction An appreciation of the issues involved in conservation of endangered species An appreciation of the changing nature of ecosystems An appreciation of the contribution of ecology and genetics towards our understanding of the interactions among species within ecosystems An understanding of evolutionary phylogeny and its relationship to conservation issues

The topic will focus on conservation biology, including setting the priorities for conservation, identifying causes of extinction, and assessing vulnerability to extinction. Lectures and workshops will cover landscape ecology, including fire ecology, and systematic and evolutionary biology, including studies on the origin and evolution of biodiversity, description and classification of biota, and conservation genetics. Case studies from Australian ecosystems will be explored. On a 5-day fieldtrip to Brookfield Conservation Park, students will work in groups to conduct biodiversity surveys of conservation significance.
learning_outcomes: Apply practical skills involved in biodiversity studies
Analyse biological and other processes leading to the generation and loss of biodiversity
Argue effectively in spoken and written media
Interpret the scientific bases of biological conservation
Critically review practical methods available for conserving rare and endangered species
prerequisites: 1 of BIOL1101, BIOD1102

title: Evolution of Biological Diversity
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a basic understanding of: The evolution of life on Earth The classification of living organisms Nutrition and reproduction How organisms adapt to changes in their environment within their own lifetimes How organisms adapt to changes in their environment over many generations How organisms interact with one another

This topic focuses on the diversity of animals, plants and microorganisms. Emphasis is placed on biological diversity, evolution, the relationship between structure and function in selected groups of organisms, how organisms are adapted to their environment and how organisms interact with one another. This topic is designed for all biology students.
learning_outcomes: Apply generic scientific and critical thinking skills to solve practical problems individually and collaboratively as part of a team
Apply basic skills to search, retrieve and interpret articles published in scientific journals
Apply basic laboratory skills including technical skills, design and interpret the results of experiments, maintain a laboratory notebook and to communicate scientific information
Have a basic understanding of areas covered by the topic description

title: Molecular Basis of Life
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Following the completion of this topic, students should have a basic understanding of the following: The cellular nature of life and the function of intracellular organelles The genetic systems of prokaryotes and eukaryotes The nature of genetic information and how it is replicated, how it is expressed and how the expression is regulated How a multicellular organisms can develop from a single cell and how cells communicate in multicellular organisms How the intracellular environment is regulated and metabolic energy derived and utilised How the needs of organisms are met from their environment

This topic discusses how plants, animals and microbes control their internal activities at the biochemical, genetic and physiological level. Emphasis will be placed on the similarities between the different groups and on how they can be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Describe the microscopic structure of cells and how the needs of organisms are met from their environment.
Analyse how cellular processes are regulated.
Explain how complex organisms develop from a single cell.
Develop, apply and communicate laboratory skills including technical skills, experimental design, data recording and interpretation of results.
Develop and apply skills to search, retrieve and communicate information published in scientific journals and identify directions for future research.
Examine the nature and flow of genetic information and predict simple Mendelian inheritance.

title: Human Evolution
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to: Gain understanding of the evolutionary history of our species and its relatives Gain an appreciation of the evolutionary and cultural drivers that have led to the pre-eminence of modern humans Develop skills in identifying and assessing differences in elements of the human skeleton Gain an understanding of the anatomy and function of the skeleton of hominins Use information in the fossil and archaeological records to identify and interpret major factors in the development of Homo sapiens

This topic will give students an understanding of how our species fits into a wider evolutionary framework. We will discuss the origins and early evolutionary history of hominids, explore their spread throughout the world and identify the key evolutionary and cultural drivers that have underpinned the success of Homo sapiens as a species. Students will examine the morphological and behavioural characteristics of hominins in order to gain a better understanding of how we move, feed and reproduce. They will learn how we can use the fossil record to better understand the diversification of hominins, the position of our species in this evolutionary framework and the reasons we're the only hominin species on the planet today.
learning_outcomes: Have a good understanding of the factors influencing the evolution of hominids
Understand the ecological impacts of the global spread of humans
Distinguish between the various bones comprising the human skeleton
Have an appreciation of the ways in which we can extract information from the fossil record

title: Fundamentals of Molecular Biology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to ensure that students have a basic understanding of the following: The cellular nature of life and the function of intracellular organelles The genetic systems of prokaryotes and eukaryotes The nature of genetic information and how it is replicated, how it is expressed and how the expression is regulated How DNA technology can be applied to research How a multicellular organisms can develop from a single cell and how cells communicate in multicellular organisms How the intracellular environment is regulated and metabolic energy derived and utilised

This topic discusses how animals and microbes control their internal activities at the molecular, biochemical and genetic level. Emphasis will be placed on the similarities between the different groups and on how they can be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Develop scientific skills including experimental design and data interpretation
Explain how complex organisms develop from a single cell
Examine the nature and flow of genetic information
Analyse how cellular processes are regulated
Describe how DNA technology can be applied to research
Develop and apply research skills to search, retrieve and interpret articles published in scientific journals
Describe the microscopic structure of cells
Predict outcomes of simple Mendelian inheritance
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BNE-Bachelor of Nutrition and Exercise 1a Admission into DIPHS-Diploma in Health Sciences 1b Admission into BHSHM-Bachelor of Health Sciences (Health Management) 1c Admission into BHSHP-Bachelor of Health Sciences (Health Promotion) 1d Admission into BHSDH-Bachelor of Health Sciences (Digital Health) 1e Admission into BHSAG-Bachelor of Health Sciences (Ageing) 1f Admission into BHSPS-Bachelor of Health Sciences (Psychology) Must satisfy: (1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f)

title: Molecular Basis of Life PW
school: Flinders University Academy
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to ensure that students have a basic understanding of the following: The cellular nature of life and the function of intracellular organelles The genetic systems of prokaryotes and eukaryotes The nature of genetic information and how it is replicated, how it is expressed and how the expression is regulated How a multicellular organisms can develop from a single cell and how cells communicate in multicellular organisms How the intracellular environment is regulated and metabolic energy derived and utilised How the needs of organisms are met from their environment

This topic discusses how plants, animals and microbes control their internal activities at the biochemical, genetic and physiological level. Emphasis will be placed on the similarities between the different groups and on how they can be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Describe how cellular processes are regulated
Describe how complex organisms develop from a single cell
Predict outcomes of simple Mendelian inheritance
Understand the microscopic structure of cells
Develop basic laboratory skills including technical skills, experimental design and data interpretation
Describe the needs of organisms and how these are met from their environment
Understand the nature and flow of genetic information
Develop basic skills to search, retrieve and interpret articles published in scientific journals
prerequisites: 1 Admission into DIPHLTH-Diploma in Health 1a Admission into DIPHLTHE-Diploma in Health - Extended 1b Admission into DIPIT-Diploma in Information Technology 1c Admission into DIPITE-Diploma in Information Technology - Extended Must satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Introduction to Marine Biology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a supportive and stimulating environment in which students: Develop an understanding of the foundations of marine biology and related sciences Appreciate the breadth of marine biology and related sciences Develop analytical and research skills Develop awareness of the societal contexts in which marine biologists work Develop effective oral, written and interpersonal communication skills

This topic introduces students to the field of marine biology and related sciences. It includes an introduction to the science of marine biology, an overview of marine organisms, an introduction to marine ecosystems and major resources from the sea, basic knowledge about aquaculture practices, and principles of marine conservation and management. The workshops and practicals develop generic skills in research, analysis and communication as applied to topical issues in marine biology and aquaculture. The field trips provide students with first hands on experience with marine organisms and sampling techniques. Both workshops and practicals develop students' communication and written skills in the context of marine biology.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and in teams in marine biology related projects
Investigate scientific evidence and analyse scientific issues in marine biology and related sciences
Use basic marine biology and aquaculture techniques

Communicate information in the field of marine biology and related sciences by participating in presentations during workshops and practical sessions and by submitting online presentations and a written report
Understand the fundamentals of marine biology and related sciences, including marine organisms, environments, resources, aquaculture, and marine conservation management

title: Plants in Action
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop students' broad understanding of plant structure, physiology and development and expand knowledge of how plants interact with their environment. Students will study techniques available for investigating plant metabolism, physiology and interactions and apply this knowledge to find solution to real world problems related to crops and ecosystems.

In this topic, you will study plants from molecular, cellular, physiological and ecological perspectives and develop an understanding of plant development and reproduction, as well as genetic, ecological and physiological studies that aim to elucidate how plants interact with their environments. In addition, you will study the abundance and diversity of plant species and vegetation communities and how these have evolved, using molecular tools and field studies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how plants interact with the environment at the organism, organ, tissue and cellular level and how this enables plant response to the environment
Communicate effectively using a range of formats relevant to professional scientists
Understand some of the practical methods and techniques available for studying plants
Demonstrate a broad understanding of plant anatomy, physiology and development
Understand the patterns and processes of plants in nature
prerequisites: 1 of BIOL1001, BIOL1101, BIOL1102, BIOD1102

title: Introduction to Animal Behaviour
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
After completing this topic, students will have an understanding of the evolutionary forces that shape animal behaviour. Students will explore critical issues for the study of animal behaviour such as captive versus field studies, and the role of animal welfare and ethics for research. In-class analysis of video and audio data will train students in data collection techniques including instantaneous sampling, one-zero sampling, and continuous recording. Students will gain practical experience from a field excursion to observe and subsequently analyse animal behaviour. Students will gain understanding about the evolutionary framework to interpret major behaviour patterns across a range of organisms.

This topic introduces students to key ideas that have underpinned the study of animal behaviour. Students will gain practical experience in data collection by observing and recording animal behaviour from video and audio recordings in class and in the field. The topic addresses major patterns of animal behaviour including courtship, parental care, aggression, foraging, and communication. Students will explore critical issues for the study of animal behaviour such as captive versus field studies, and the role of animal welfare and ethics for research. Lectures convey the theory of animal behaviour and an overview of techniques to record and analyse animal behaviour, with a one day excursion to observe, collect, and analyse data on animal behaviour in follow-up independent research.
learning_outcomes: Observe and collect data on animal behaviour
Understand the evolutionary framework for animal behaviour theory
Formulate hypotheses to test observations about animal behaviour
Analyse data for animal behaviour at an introductory level (basic statistics and graphs)

title: Scientific Illustration
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the basic skills necessary to accurately draw an object in order to create an illustration suitable for scientific publication.
