prerequisites: 1 108 units of topics 2 Admission into BSCHAB-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Animal Behaviour) 2a Admission into BSCHAQ-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Aquaculture) 2b Admission into BSCHBD-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Biodiversity and Conservation) 2c Admission into BSCHMN-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Marine Biology) 2d Admission into BSCHMNAQ-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Marine Biology and Aquaculture) 2e Admission into BSCHFS-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Forensic and Analytical Science) 2f Admission into BSCH-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Enhanced Program for High Achievers) 2g Admission into BSCHBT-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Biotechnology) 2h Admission into BSCHPL-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Palaeontology) 2i Admission into BSCHPSC-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Plant Science) 2j Admission into BSCHEN-Bachelor of Science (Honours)(Environmental Science) 2k Admission into BSCHLS-Bachelor of Science (Honours)(Life Sciences) 3 Admission into HBSC-Bachelor of Science (Honours) 3a Admission into HBA-Bachelor of Arts (Honours) 3b Admission into HBBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Honours) 3c Admission into HBAGIS-Bachelor of Applied Geographical Information Systems (Honours) 3d Admission into HBGIS-Bachelor of Geospatial Information Systems (Honours) 3e Admission into HBEM-Bachelor of Environmental Management (Honours) 4 A GPA of at least 5 in 36 units of study in the MSCES-Master of Science (Environmental Science) 5 A GPA of at least 5 in 36 units of study in the MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) Must satisfy: ((1) and (2 or 2a or 2b or 2c or 2d or 2e or 2f or 2g or 2h or 2i or 2j or 2k)) or (3 or 3a or 3b or 3c or 3d or 3e) or (4) or (5))

title: New Colombo Plan - Offshore Placement
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Allow the students to gain a deeper understanding of their host country and its culture Further develop a student's practical and theoretical knowledge in an area related to their degree program Provide students with the opportunity to develop ongoing international relationships

In this topic, students will undertake an individual structured program of study in an overseas university or research organisation. On completion of the placement the students will complete a written report and oral presentation summarising their activities. This topic is designed to meet the requirements of mobility grants awarded under schemes such as the Australian government's New Colombo Plan. Placements will be dependent on the availability of suitable international hosts and mobility schemes and need to be arranged with the topic coordinator prior to enrolment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to operate effectively in an international workplace

Articulate how commercial, economic, social, cultural, political, legal, industrial and/or environmental issues affect the way in which professionals would operate overseas or with overseas organisations
Demonstrate enhancement of their practical and theoretical knowledge in the area of their degree
Demonstrate awareness of major social and political issues relating to the country visited
prerequisites: 27 units of topics

title: DNA to Genome GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Familiarise students with recombinant DNA technology and how it is applied to gene discovery and understanding more about the function of genes and proteins. A particular emphasis will be placed on the Human genome project and how in recent years we have moved to study genes and gene interactions on more global scale and how bioinformatics had aided this Further develop students' scientific skills for work in a molecular biology laboratory Further develop students' generic skills in the areas of accurate record keeping (attention to detail), creativity and problem-solving, independence, using online resources, communication to scientific and non-scientific audiences and critical thinking

In this topic students will learn fundamental concepts about genes and genomics that form the core of current molecular approaches that are now used to study biological processes. Students will review the central dogma of molecular biology DNA to RNA to protein and then go on to explore in more detail how gene expression is controlled. In addition students will learn more about basic tools of recombinant DNA and how these are applied to solve interesting biological problems in human medicine, forensic science and the biotechnology industry. Finally students will learn the fundamentals of whole genome sequencing, how the human genome was sequenced and will also review bioinformatics and experimental approaches to make use of sequence data. Students will also have the opportunity to apply their knowledge in practical laboratory exercises.
learning_outcomes: Advance your understanding of the inherent challenges in working with DNA and RNA in the laboratory and increase your awareness of the importance of using appropriate controls
Demonstrate practical and numerical skills required for the preparation of laboratory reagents, interpretating DNA and RNA experiments and conducting independent laboratory work
Understand advanced concepts in molecular biology regarding the synthesis and regulation of DNA, RNA and proteins

Articulate and address different critical issues in genomic and DNA based research and to present and communicate these issues, DNA based data and scientific ideas to both scientific and non-scientific audiences
Deeply appreciate how essential bioinformatics and information technology are to genomics research

Advance your knowledge of how DNA and genomics techniques of the past and the present including those used for sequencing are used to diagnose and understand the pathology of human, animal and plant diseases; develop new disease treatments; underpin approaches to personalised medicine and in numerous ways to benefit society
Further your awareness and ability to use bioinformatic programs including online and stand-alone software to enable database searches for DNA and protein sequences and construct sequence alignments
Maintain a laboratory notebook such that others can reproduce your work and present your experimental results in tables and figures in a format suitable for a thesis or scientific journal

title: Protein to Proteome GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Give students an understanding of the processes that regulate and control the function of cellular proteins with a particular emphasis on how protein structure relates to function Familiarise students with laboratory and bioinformatic techniques that are used to identify and characterise both individual proteins and entire proteomes Further develop students' scientific skills for work in a biochemistry or molecular biology laboratory Further develop students' generic skills in the areas of accurate record keeping, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, independence, teamwork, and good written and oral communication

In this topic students will learn about the functions of cellular proteins and contemporary approaches that are used for the study and characterisation of proteins. Students will review the process of protein translation, and then examine the post-translational events that affect the structure, function and cellular location of proteins. Traditional techniques for the study of proteins such as protein purification, electrophoresis, Western-blotting and enzyme kinetics will be contrasted with more contemporary techniques such as mass spectrometry for identification of entire proteomes and computer based approaches for evaluating protein structure and function. Students will also have the opportunity to apply their knowledge in practical laboratory exercises.
learning_outcomes: Design experimental strategies to answer research questions about protein structure, function and regulation
Write scientific text
Manage experimental data, calculations and record-keeping
Combine theoretical and practical skills in a laboratory setting
Communicate scientific information in a variety of formats
Draw conclusions from scientific data
Examine protein structure, localisation, interaction, regulation, signalling and turnover
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1b Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology 1c Admission into MFS-Master of Forensic Science 1d Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d))

title: Biochemistry GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop students' knowledge and understanding of food and energy metabolism and to provide them with opportunities to apply their knowledge and understanding to the solution of 'real-world' problems related to enzyme function, nutritional deficiencies and metabolic disorders.

Biochemistry is the study of chemical processes occurring within and related to living cells and plays an essential role in Medicine, Pharmacy, Agriculture, Environment, Nutrition and Engineering. In this topic students will focus on understanding the chemical basis underpinning biological molecules and processes and their regulation in living cells. Students will gain an in depth understanding of the most important enzymes, transport proteins, metabolic pathways and regulatory mechanisms and understand the implications of perturbations of important pathways and processes. This topic will provide students the opportunity to be a part of next generation of biochemists who will provide solutions to complex biological problems that we currently see.
learning_outcomes: Integrate, evaluate and analyse the regulation of biochemical pathways required for food and energy metabolism.
Demonstrate competence in experimental design, performing experiments, data recording, data analysis, and interpretation of scientific results.
Analyse, interpret and effectively communicate experimental data and conclusions of scientific research.
Integrate and communicate the knowledge gained from metabolic pathways to problem solve real world case studies collaboratively.

title: Foundations in Microbiology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to provide students with an increased awareness and understanding of the fundamental importance of microbiological processes in the world around them. Students will gain an understanding of the impacts microbial processes have on diverse areas such as human health, food, drinking water quality, the environment etc. The topic aims to enhance students' learning of laboratory skills and practices. The specific aims and objectives of this topic are to: Develop bacteriological techniques, such that students can conduct laboratory work with bacteria with confidence and safety Examine the diversity of form and fundamental biological activity found amongst bacteria Learn strategies for isolating and enumerating microbes from environmental samples Learn methods for confirming the identity of specific bacteria Study bacteria which have a direct impact on human welfare Develop techniques for recording observations accurately in a notebook which is then available as a definitive long-term record of experimental work Develop numerical skills relevant to practical microbiology Develop skills in communicating (oral and written) for a general and expert scientific audience

This topic is designed to give students knowledge of the fundamental aspects of the actions of microorganisms as well as laboratory skills in isolating, handling, enumerating and identifying microorganisms. The aim is to promote understanding and awareness in these students of the important roles microorganisms have in major areas such as human health and the environment. Assessment will be made on the basis of assignments, oral and written examination and also performance in the laboratory.
learning_outcomes: Understand the principles governing the function, organisation and manipulation of micro-organism and relevance to human health and the environment.
Clearly and effectively communicate (oral and written) for a general and expert scientific audience
Lead a range of laboratory and theoretical studies to master analytical and critical thinking capabilities.
Apply the technical skills to handle and comprehensively analyse microorganisms, as well as to work safely in a laboratory.

title: Advanced Microbiology: Microbial Ecology and Infectious Disease GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The theory component will present information to prepare students for further study in specific areas of molecular biosciences that include a microbiological aspect, such as; biology, biotechnology, forensics, infectious disease and ecology. The laboratory-based experimental section of the topic will provide students with practical experience in the handling, isolation and identification of microbes and will provide them with opportunities to work independently and as part of a team. The specific aims and objectives of this topic are to: Consolidate bacteriological techniques, such that students can conduct work with bacteria with confidence and safety Examine the diversity of form and biological activity found amongst bacteria Learn strategies for isolating and enumerating specific bacterial species Learn methods for confirming the identity of specific bacteria Study bacteria which have a direct impact on human welfare Develop techniques for recording observations accurately in a notebook which is then available as a definitive long-term record of experimental work Learn analytical skills relevant to practical microbiology Mastering skills in communicating (oral and written) for a general and expert scientific audience

This topic is designed to give students a broad understanding of major elements of microbiology including bacteriology, microbial genomics, the role of microbes in disease and microbial ecology, expanding on the material covered in Foundations of Microbiology. The practical work is designed to extend skills in handling bacteria, to apply these skills to the study of microbes in particular environments, preparing you for diverse future employment opportunities. The theme of this topic is life from the micro-organisms' perspective, with a focus on the traits of both harmful and beneficial micro-organisms and how this impacts on microbial habitats and environments (from waterways to human skin). Included are hands-on training in areas of microbiology, such as isolation, enumeration and identification of bacteria by traditional and new techniques, microbial physiology, microbial structure, microbial ecology, medical microbiology and pathogenesis, and immunology. Assessment will be made on the basis of assignments, oral and written examination and also performance in the laboratory.
learning_outcomes: Communicate (oral and written) for a general and expert scientific audience
Understand key processes in microbiology, including microbial cell biology, microbial genetics, microbial interactions and impacts on humans and the environment
Assimilate, formulate and interpret information in microbiology, all of which can be applied to other fields
Possess the technical mastery required to handle microorganisms as well as the confidence to work safely and independently in a laboratory
prerequisites: 1 of BIOL3761, BIOL8008

title: Restoration Ecology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic will critique the theoretical and technical scientific basis and practice of restoration ecology. Students will analyse a range of ecological processes underlying ecosystem degradation and ecosystem restoration. They will evaluate current practices of ecosystem restoration to recover degraded ecosystems (e.g. mining rehabilitation, post-agricultural restoration, marine/aquatic ecosystem restoration), as well as find solutions to unresolved issues and technical challenges in the practice of ecosystem restoration (e.g. climate change, novel ecosystems). Students will also examine the values provided by biodiversity in supplying ecosystem services and ecosystem functions, and how restoration can be used to return these valuable ecosystem components.

The world has billions of hectares of degraded ecosystems and faces a biodiversity crisis. In response, the UN has just initiated the Decade on Ecosystem Restoration this year and the global community has set aspirational targets to restore 350 million hectares by 2030 under The Bonn Challenge. Restoration ecology is a young discipline. The science of restoration is by no means settled and emerging technologies are pushing the boundaries of the very identity of what restoration is. Great debates and punctuated shifts in norms have resulted. In this topic, students will investigate why and how to restore today’s ecosystems and biodiversity. This topic will provide students the opportunity to be part of the next generation of restoration ecologists, who will ultimately be responsible for turning the global environmental tide from decline and degradation to repair and restoration.
learning_outcomes: Develop solutions to unresolved issues and technical challenges in the practice of ecosystem restoration
Analyse a range of ecological processes underlying ecosystem degradation and ecosystem restoration
Apply skills gained in problem solving, critical thinking, and in the development of written and oral presentations
Examine the value of biodiversity in supplying ecosystem services and ecosystem functions
Critique the theoretical and technical scientific basis of restoration ecology
Evaluate current practices of ecosystem restoration to recover degraded ecosystems

title: Genetics and Evolution GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Cover how genetic information flow from generation to generation, and in the formation of population and species structure Cover current biodiversity and how this has been shaped by the forces of evolution Vertically integrate principles of genetics and evolutionary theory so to provide an understanding of how events and processes at a cellular level, and that of the gene, effect and influence what happens at the level of an organism, a population and an ecosystem (and vice versa) Combine theory and practice to emphasise this vertical structure by following a single gene sequence from a variety of organisms to build a phylogenetic tree. The practical class provides the opportunity to introduce generic practical skills in laboratory-based biology

This topic covers advanced knowledge of the flow of genetic information from cell to cell and from parent to offspring, how the forces of selection impact on gene flow and ultimately how these processes shape the characteristics of species and biodiversity. It represents core and advanced information required by all Biology students. The practical component of the topic will cover modern molecular techniques that enable students to study gene flow, how populations are genetically structured, and how the Tree of Life can be reconstructed from genetic data. The practical classes will also assess students to generic skills of laboratory techniques and how this can be used in combination with field-based observations.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise the broad principles and theories of speciation
Critique research in the discipline
Apply phylogenetics to evaluate evolution and evolutionary relationships
Apply the principles of Mendelian genetics, epigenetics, and population genetics to solve complex problems
Collect laboratory data and synthesise results in a scientific manuscript for publication

title: Vertebrate Palaeontology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop an understanding of the concepts and methods used by palaeontologists to reconstruct the history of life on earth and in the process provide students with an overview of the evolution and radiation of the Australian vertebrate fauna.

Students will learn about the half-billion-year history of vertebrates as deduced from the fossil record. The topic begins by focusing on key palaeontological principles such as taphonomy, stratigraphy and palaeoecology. It then reviews the major patterns of vertebrate evolution and processes that have shaped them, particularly in Australia. It also includes a one-week field trip (in the mid-semester break) where students will get on-site experience in fossil excavation and processing, logging a geological section, dating methods and field trip logistics.
learning_outcomes: Locate, excavate, consolidate and retrieve vertebrate fossils
Synthesise data extracted from analysis of a fossil deposit in order to determine the ways in which past fauna have responded to changes in climate and habitat
Apply taphonomic, stratigraphic and palaeoecological principles to interpretation of a fossil deposit
Construct and analyse patterns within a phylogenetic tree based on morphological characters
Demonstrate understanding of key evolutionary transitions in vertebrates, including the transition to life on land and mammal diversification
Summarise and critically analyse the literature in a specific area of palaeontology
prerequisites: 1 1 of BIOL2706, BIOL8706 2 18 Units in ARCH, BIOL, CHEM, EASC or ENVS topics Must Satisfy: ((1) or (2))

title: Ecology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide an introduction to the fundamental ideas and practices of the science of ecology.

This topic explores the dynamics of natural populations of animals and plants. It focuses on the description of population demography through life table analysis and population growth models, the regulation of population size, and different life history strategies as adaptations for population persistence. It further explores the major interactions between species in ecological communities. These include adverse interactions such as competition between species within trophic levels, and predator-prey, parasite host, plant herbivore interactions across trophic levels. Finally we will discuss how we represent communities, food webs as flows of energy and nutrients. Examples from Australian ecosystems will be considered.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the range of factors that can influence the regulation of population size in natural and managed conditions
Explain the key concepts of interactions among species within an ecological community and the flow of energy within a community
Understand and operate basic mathematical formulae which model population growth, and derive basic parameters describing life history characters of a population
Understand theoretical models that explain the dynamics of population interactions and discuss the main issues involved in the evolution of life history strategies in a population
Have the practical skills to undertake basic ecological studies
Explain the key concepts of population dynamics and understand issues involved with conservation, management or control of populations
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) Must satisfy: (1 or 1a)

title: Functional Plant Science GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with a broad understanding of plant functional responses to negative impact of various climatic and soil factors in the environment. The students will gain insights into molecular mechanisms that govern plant functional responses. Student will be introduced to major plant groups and their characteristics, ecology and human uses and gain an understanding of the nature and diversity of vegetation ecosystems and their function. They will study ecological processes that underlie how communities assemble and breakdown.

In this topic, you will learn about the state-of-the-art knowledge of plant functional responses to diverse abiotic stresses. This knowledge is critical for understanding the way plants adapt to their environment, both under natural and agricultural conditions. You will gain an understanding of key physiological, biochemical pathways with molecular and whole plant approaches to gain a holistic view of plant functions that affect growth, development, and productivity.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critically interpret experimental data and effectively communicate scientific results
Analyse a range of ecological processes underlying vegetation assembly and degradation
Critically reflect on the latest developments into plant responses to water, light, salinity and nutrient stress
Evaluate scientific research critically and communicate critique with professional scientists
Analyse what constitutes plant stress and strategies plants employ to overcome stress
Examine the value of vegetation ecosystems in supplying ecosystem services and ecosystem functions
Construct and present logical arguments in an oral debate or discussion on a scientific topic
Apply key techniques in modern plant physiology and how these are being used to improve plant growth and productivity and what are their limitations
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into MEMG-Master of Environmental Management 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) 1c Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) 1d Admission into MEMS-Master of Environmental Management and Sustainability Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d))

title: Aquaculture Systems and Technology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Students completing this topic should be able to demonstrate advanced skills in designing systems of containment structures (tanks, ponds, cages etc.) and treatment systems for the maintenance and production of aquatic animals. Students will: Understand the importance of maintaining water quality to suit the species in culture, and how to achieve optimal water quality Have an advanced understanding of the various components of aquatic animal containment/ production systems and how these are applied in the culture of the different life stages of aquacultured species Be highly skilled at maintaining the nutritional well-being of animals in aquatic culture Be able to critically analyse research and other literature associated with aquaculture engineering and farming technology The topic will also develop students' abilities in: Laboratory practical skills Laboratory report writing skills Independent learning skills from current literature through writing a research report

The topic will provide students with an advanced theoretical and practical capacity to design construct and maintain systems for culturing aquatic animals. Students will become familiar with the requirements of aquatic animals in culture systems, the systems themselves, management of water quality within these systems, feeding practices within the aquaculture industry and industry placement. At the completion of this topic, students will be expected to demonstrate their ability in the areas of understanding design and management of aquatic animal production systems, know where to search for suppliers of equipment and stock, and be able to critically analyse peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed literature in this area.
learning_outcomes: Show advanced reporting skills for managing aquaculture systems
Manage commercial-scale systems for aquacultured organisms
Demonstrate advanced ability and understanding in systems management in aquaculture operations
Understand and apply relevant scientific principles and work effectively, cooperatively and productively within a team
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Vertebrate Form and Function GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an understanding of the diversity of the vertebrate body plan, and how the anatomy of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals relates to ecology and evolution. The topic provides students with an opportunity to: Become familiar with key defining features of the major vertebrate groups, especially of the skeletal and muscular systems Link form with function, especially in relation to diet, locomotory capabilities, body size and posture Apply observational, recording and analytical skills introduced during previous topics Conduct independent but guided research relating form to function in living and/or extinct vertebrates

Students will learn about the evolution of vertebrates and distinctive adaptive features of each major group. Content includes comparative anatomy, systematics and functional morphology, with an emphasis on the musculoskeletal system.
learning_outcomes: Visually and orally communicate project planning, approach and outcomes to stakeholders
Apply basic biomechanical principles to make deductions about the habits and locomotion of vertebrate animals
Evaluate and distinguish different vertebrate groups based on dental and skeletal attributes
Apply general principles to the identification and classification of different Australian vertebrate groups

title: Biostatistics 2 GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The educational aims of the topic are for the students to get an in depth understanding of the importance of collecting and analysing data when doing research in Biological Sciences.

Many investigations in aquaculture, biochemistry, botany, zoology, microbiology, molecular biology, genetics and ecology are quantitative, with observations and experiments consisting of numerical facts called data. As biological entities have to be counted and measured, some objective methods are necessary to aid the investigator in presenting and analysing research data. Before data can be analysed, they must be collected and often statistical considerations help in the design of experiments and hypotheses to be tested. Still too many biologists attempt the analysis of their data only to find out that too few data points were collected to enable reliable conclusions to be drawn. Alternatively, it may appear that some effort might have been put in collecting data that cannot be used in the analysis of the experiment. Hence, the knowledge of statistical principles and procedures is critical even before an experiment begins. This topic aims to introduce advanced concepts of sampling methods and statistical analysis that can be applied to any field of research in biology.
learning_outcomes: Design experiments and sampling regime for a specific scientific project
Communicate a scientific report using both written and oral communication skills
Apply appropriate advanced statistical tests to analyse data
Analyse and graph data using Excel and SPSS
Collect in depth data in the field or laboratory
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) 1c Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) 1d Admission into MSCES-Master of Science (Environmental Science) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d))

title: Disease and Immunology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: An advanced understanding of the animal, environment and pathogen concept An introduction to the major types of pathogens responsible for infectious disease and the process of pathogenesis Understanding of the stress response in animals An introduction to the natural defence mechanisms in animals (including humans) and the evolution of the immune system Skills in disease diagnosis Experience in writing up experiments in scientific paper format Skills in critical analysis and communication of the current literature in the field of human and/or animal health

The topic will provide an advanced understanding of the "animal, environment and pathogen" concept. Students will be familiarized with the major causes of disease, including both non-infectious and infectious disease. The topic will also introduce the major types of pathogens responsible for infectious disease and the process of pathogenesis. The topic also aims to introduce the natural defences mechanism in animals (including humans) and the evolution of the immune system. The importance of animal welfare, hygiene and quarantine control for preventing the spread of animal disease will be explained, along with artificial mechanisms for controlling disease in human medicine, aquaculture and agriculture. Hands-on practicals will facilitate the development of skills in disease diagnosis through examination of enteric parasites in scat samples, histological sections and blood pathology. Practicals will also expose students to the analysis of cell mediated immunity via laboratory assays.
learning_outcomes: Be skilled in identifying the major causes of infectious and non-infectious diseases in animals
Understand the importance of animal welfare, biosecurity and procedures for quarantine control of animals
Be familiar with the different types of pathogenic organisms and some of the disease symptoms associated with these infections
Understand how the environment, host and pathogens all interact to enable the manifestation of infectious disease
Be aware of animal health resources available on the World Wide Web and have the ability to critically analyse research and other literature associated with animal health and immunology
Understand the major components of the immune system and how it is affected by stress
Gain experience with some of the tools, techniques and reporting used in disease management
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Aquaculture Nutrition and Water Quality GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) Apply skills and comprehensive knowledge in global aquaculture Use the knowledge in aquaculture nutrition and water quality for the management of global aquaculture operations Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) Use key knowledge in aquaculture nutrition and water quality for the management of global aquaculture operations

The topic covers advanced knowledge in the biology and culture of live food organisms including algae, rotifers, cladocerans, copepods, Artemia that are used for aquaculture. The theory and practice of nutritional requirements (protein, lipid, carbohydrate, vitamins and minerals), aquaculture feed formulation and manufacture for a variety of aquatic species will be included. This topic teaches the fundamental impacts of the biological processes of aquatic organisms (photosynthesis, respiration, excretion of metabolites and biota/substratum interaction) upon water quality. It also covers advanced technologies and approaches (aeration, buffering) to minimise the deleterious effects of these processes in various aquaculture systems. The topic extends to pond management through nutrient fertilisation and liming. Completion of this topic will enable students to gain advanced understanding in the theoretical and applied aspects of green water culture, feed preparation, and feeding practices and water quality management in the culture of a variety of fish, mollusc and crustacean species.
learning_outcomes: Manage water quality in intensive and extensive aquaculture systems for commercial enterprises at advanced levels
Identify and solve practical issues with the advanced knowledge from literature
Demonstrate advanced ability and understanding in feeding management in any aquaculture operations
Manage live feed production and feed formulation for aquacultured organisms at an advanced level
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Fisheries Biology, Science and Management GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an advanced understanding of how small- and large-scale fisheries are managed nationally and internationally, and what are the critical life history parameters needed to enable stock assessments and fisheries modelling. After completing this topic, students will have a fundamental understanding of the methods and techniques used to undertake stock assessments as well as the related mathematical models. Through this topic, students will gain advanced cognitive, technical and communication skills through the additional assessment, which will require the ability to critically analyse data, solve a complex sustainability issue, and to generate a written report to transmit the solution to the complex problem presented. Finally, thanks to the contribution of guest speakers from various background, agencies and organisations, this topic also exposes the students to different scientists, managers, modellers, and industry representatives providing the students with an introduction to the type of agencies they could work for following their degree.

This topic will provide students with advanced theoretical and technical knowledge and skills in fish biology, fisheries management, and the critical parameters used by fisheries scientists to assess stock levels and manage populations of marine organisms. Students will gain a fundamental understanding of the scientific principles, conflicts, and methodologies relating to the use and management of fisheries resources, which will be outlined using South Australian and international examples. This will include various fisheries from crustaceans and cephalopods to large predators such as sharks. Students will also be taught some of the ideas and assumptions underlying the models used in various fisheries management as well as their application. Finally, the topic also addresses environmental impacts of fisheries and the sustainable management and protection of fisheries resources.
learning_outcomes: Efficiently communicate (orally and in writing) the results of fisheries models, and transmit knowledge, skills and ideas to others

Have an advanced understanding of the biological parameters required to undertake stock assessments and population modelling, and ability to use and apply these parameters to assess stock sustainability
Understand the principles behind fisheries management and the various conflicts between stakeholders to assess stock status and determine most suited management regulations
Undertake stock assessment and population models to assess stock dynamics and sustainability
Identify and solve practical issues with the advanced knowledge from literature
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) 1c Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Bioinformatics GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Provide students with a structured, progressive introduction to the conceptual and practical foundations of modern bioinformatics, spanning genomics, transcriptomics, metagenomics, and pathway and network biology. Expose students to the tools and analytical workflows that are actively used in contemporary research, clinical, and environmental biology contexts. Develop students' capacity to work with real biological datasets, building the analytical judgement needed to interpret findings and evaluate their significance. Build scientific communication skills through a structured written research proposal and an oral pitch that simulates the experience of presenting a project to a research supervisor or funding panel. Equip students with the integrative computational skill set needed to independently design, build, and critically evaluate a bioinformatic tool or analytical pipeline.

Bioinformatics sits at the intersection of biology, computer science, and data analysis, and has become an indispensable skill set for modern biological research. This topic provides students with hands-on competency in the core tools and analytical frameworks used across genomic, transcriptomic, metagenomic, and pathway-level biology. Structured across three progressive phases, students first build foundational skills, learning how genomic and other -omic data are generated, stored, and queried. The middle phase moves into applied bioinformatic analysis - students interrogate real biological datasets using pathway and network biology tools, while developing conceptual understanding of transcriptomic and metagenomic approaches. In the final phase, students bring these skills together through scripted, reproducible analysis using programming languages common to the field, reflecting the computational workflows expected in contemporary research and clinical settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the theoretical foundations of genomics, transcriptomics, and metagenomics, evaluating how bioinformatic approaches are selected and applied to address complex questions across biological and clinical contexts

Critically evaluate the outputs of multiple bioinformatic analyses by synthesising findings across complementary approaches, assessing their biological significance, and proposing evidence-based directions for further investigation informed by identified methodological limitations

Construct a reproducible bioinformatic tool or analytical pipeline using R, Python, or AI-assisted development approaches, demonstrating independent judgement in methodological decision-making and documenting methods to a standard appropriate for peer-reviewed publication

Communicate bioinformatic findings and research proposals with the authority and precision expected of an independent researcher, in written form structured as a scientific document and through oral presentation to a specialist audience

Evaluate bioinformatic tools and analytical approaches, including sequence analysis, pathway analysis, and network biology, to interrogate complex biological datasets, critically interpreting results and justifying analytical decisions
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology 1b Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Aquaculture Reproduction GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with an advanced understanding of the physiological and environmental factors affecting broodstock conditioning, spawning, hatching and larval rearing in aquaculture species Apply advanced management practices to monitor and control breeding of species under captivity Understand the impact of genetic factors on aquaculture-relevant outcomes at a high level Apply advanced genetic tools in characterising, managing and enhancing the genetic basis of commercially important stocks of aquatic species Foster advanced skills in laboratory practicals, writing reports and ability to critically analyse aquaculture literature

The topic deals with advanced reproductive biology and applied genetics of fish and other aquacultured species such as molluscs and crustaceans. Students will gain a fundamental understanding of the complex interplay of environmental, physiological and genetic factors that influence reproductive development in a variety of aquacultured species. This topic delivers advanced knowledge of the genetic characterisation of wild and domesticated fish stocks and the applications of population genetics techniques. The topic will also cover the cut-edge techniques and technologies used by aquaculturists to manage and manipulate broodstock, gametes, embryonic and larval stages to maximise productivity.
learning_outcomes: Identify and solve practical issues with the advanced knowledge from literature by writing a hatchery management plan with specific questions. The students need to use literature to support their claims
Demonstrate an advanced ability to apply genetic knowledge to the management of wild and cultured stocks of aquatic organisms
Manage hatchery operations including hatchery planning, spawning, hatching and larval rearing at an advanced level
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Aquaculture Health and Product Quality GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with an advanced understanding of the causes (and associated preventative measures) of a range of aquatic animal diseases and the principles and techniques of disease diagnosis, management and treatment in fish, mollusc and crustacean species Provide students with an advanced understanding of how product quality is affected and how it can be manipulated Foster high level skills in laboratory practicals, writing reports and ability to critically analyse aquaculture literature

This topic will cover the advanced theoretical background and practical skills related primarily to aquatic animal health management and product quality. Students will be expected to understand the general pathology, life history, diagnosis, management and treatment of pathogenic organisms in both hatchery and production systems. Students will be expected to develop an advanced knowledge of product quality, and how this can be manipulated both prior to and post-harvest.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a high level ability to apply knowledge for the manipulation of product quality
Demonstrate advanced skills in necroscopy procedures and the sampling procedures required for working with aquatic animals
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCSCAQ-Graduate Certificate in Science (Aquaculture) 1a Admission into GDPSCAQ-Graduate Diploma in Science (Aquaculture) 1b Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Aquaculture Practicum
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Each Student is expected to: Gain first-hand experience to understand the primary issues and constraints in the aquaculture industry Learn skills and knowledge in practical aspects of aquaculture operations to complement and contextualise the information they have received in lectures, practicals and from their readings Develop relationships with practising aquaculturists who will be valuable contacts and/or referees for the student Identify critical biological, water quality, technological and business issues that constrain or enhance production Develop skills in critical thinking and communication

The topic will provide students with a practical opportunity to apply learned knowledge, concept and theory to commercial aquaculture industry. Students will be familiar with the requirements of commercial farms in operational management, water quality management, feeding, handling and harvesting practices within the aquaculture industry placement. At the completion of this topic, students will be expected to demonstrate their ability in managing the biological and business aspects of industry operation. This topic comprises five weeks of work experience at an approved industry sector and one week of report writing and oral presentation at the end. The work plan must be approved by the academic supervisor before placement.
learning_outcomes: Understand the overall manner in which an aquaculture venture is practised and managed
Apply skills and knowledge already acquired into a practical situation associated with the planning, design, construction, testing, evaluation, operation or maintenance of systems
Further develop their own professional attitudes and communication skills with professionals

Participate as a member of a team, and understand the roles and value of all members of that team, including professional scientists, engineers and other professionals involved in the business, and technical and support staff at work placement
prerequisites: ENGR3750

title: Integrating Molecular Biosciences GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Improve the students ability to develop a hypothesis and experimental approaches to solve problems encountered by molecular bioscience researchers Build on students ability to critically analyse scientific literature, experimental design and data analysis Improve students understanding of the OH&S and other regulatory requirements that are associated with conducting molecular bioscience research Further develop students understanding of the role molecular bioscience takes in the community and the associated ethical issues Further develop and advance group work and presentation skills

In this graduate entry topic students will apply their existing knowledge in molecular bioscience to develop strategies, hypothesis, and experimental approaches to solve research problems faced by those working in a molecular bioscience laboratory. This will be achieved by a combination of facilitated group discussion and independent research. Students will also be exposed to and critique cutting edge research, through attending research seminars and reading research articles. They will also gain an appreciation of how molecular bioscience research can both support our society and raise ethical dilemmas by investigating the popular media. This topic will also cover current OH&S, biosafety, and animal ethics regulations which molecular bio scientists are required to meet.
learning_outcomes: Examine the role of molecular bioscience in the community and the possible ethical dilemmas that may arise from molecular bioscience research
Investigate and provide solutions to research problems via designing experiments utilising molecular methods, which include the appropriate use of controls and statistics
Comply with the regulatory requirements that would be required of a professional molecular bioscientist, in the areas such as WH&S, biosafety and animal ethics
Critically analyse scientific papers in the area of molecular bioscience, and reflect on potential pitfalls in experimental design and data interpretation
Work and communicate effectively as a member of a group in a professional setting
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MSCB-Master of Science (Biology) 1b Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1c Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology 2 ^ BIOL8005 3 BIOL8004 Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c) and (2 and 3)) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

school: College of Science and Engineering

The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire the appropriate research skills and training to enable them to work independently and complete a body of research at the level of a Masters by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Master's degree by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Masters by Research award. learning_outcomes: Validate research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Explain their understanding of chosen methodological practices

They will acquire high-level research skills and training, to enable them to work independently and complete a body of original research at the level of a Doctorate by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Doctorate by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Doctorate by research award. title: Introduction to Biotechnology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop an understanding of biotechnology through examples Give students an appreciation for the breadth of biotechnology Prepare students to be effective oral, written and interpersonal communicators to a wide range of audiences and using a variety of media Develop awareness of the social impact of biotechnology Develop an understanding of potential career paths in biotechnology and self-reflective practice in skills development

Biotechnology is the use of biological systems to solve practical problems for social and economic benefit. This topic introduces Biotechnology through examples drawn from each of the main areas: Environmental, Food, Plant Science, Medical, Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology. In the process, students learn about the science that underlies Biotechnology and develop the skills required of a Biotechnologist. This topic also develops an understanding of potential career paths for Biotechnologists.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of biotechnology methods Search for, retrieve and analyse scientific literature
Explain what biotechnology is and provide examples of its application
Research and explain biotechnology methods
Work individually and in groups to produce a piece of work adhering to the principles of academic integrity

title: Medical Biotechnology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Convey the breadth of interacting disciplines that comprise Medical Biotechnology Describe in-depth examples and illustrative case-studies representative of key areas of Medical Biotechnology Explain how core scientific concepts and practical techniques are applied in Medical Biotechnology Develop problem-solving and team work skills that incorporate culturally inclusive practices, especially as regards Indigenous groups and other stakeholders

Medical Biotechnology is the use of biological systems, living organisms or their derivates to address health issues. Medical Biotechnologists develop innovative solutions in areas such as diagnostics, medical products (e.g. drug discovery) and medical procedures. This topic exposes students to a range of cutting-edge Medical Biotechnology practices and areas of research. The topic also involves students in the process of applying their scientific, cultural and commercial knowledge to solve a medical problem and deliver a health product.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise information and communicate effectively, succinctly and sensitively with the scientific community, clients, the broad public and particular cultural and Indigenous communities about medical biotechnology products

Transfer and apply core concepts drawn from cellular biology, molecular biology, microbiology, chemistry and biochemistry to develop innovative solutions to address health issues including diagnostics, medical products and medical procedures

Demonstrate competence in experimental design, performing experiments, data recording, data analysis, and interpretation of scientific results, as well as the ability to analyze, interpret, and effectively communicate experimental data and conclusions of scientific research
Describe and discuss the breadth of interacting disciplines that comprise Medical Biotechnology and present examples of how they can be harnessed to improve health
prerequisites: 2 of BIOL2771, BIOL2772

title: Legal, Ethical and Social Aspects of Bioscience
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with an outline of the principal regulatory regimes that operate to regulate bioscience research both nationally and internationally Raise their awareness of the interface between bioscience and society Allow them to understand the sources of diversity in ethical stand points, such as religion and culture and personal experience

The purpose of this topic is to provide appreciation of the impact of new developments in Bioscience technology upon the law, ethics, society and the environment. The topic will consider the national and international regulatory aspects and the ethical and social aspects of: control of genetically modified organisms; cloning and reproductive technologies; stem cell therapy; clinical trials; genetic testing and protection of the environment. Through case study analysis the topic will also explore what it means to be an ethical bioscience professional.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the factors that drive a diversity of ethical opinions
Adopt ethical reasoning to assume and defend a coherent position in relation to an ethical issue
Demonstrate enhancement of their group work and oral presentation skills
Appreciate the role of bioscience in the community
Identify all the major national regulatory regimes relevant to bioscience research and commercialisation and how these contrast with those in other countries
prerequisites: 1 of BIOL1102, BIOL1203

title: Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Equip students with the knowledge and skills required for entry-level biotechnologists to perform in the Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology industry Develop the understanding and basic skills required to take an industrial and pharmaceutical product or process from discovery to commercialisation Expose students to key areas of industrial and pharmaceutical biotechnology using real-world case studies delivered by guest lecturers from industry Develop problem-solving, project management and teamwork skills in the context of integrating and applying fundamental knowledge into practical applications in large-scale industrial and pharmaceutical processes Develop understanding of indigenous biological resources and their potential application in industrial and pharmaceutical biotechnology by engaging Indigenous people and other stakeholders

Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology is the application of biotechnology and engineering in the exploitation of living organisms (mostly cells) and their subcomponents for sustainable, large-scale production of industrial biochemicals, biomaterials and pharmaceutical products. Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology has the potential to address the environmental sustainability of industry through the development of innovative technological solutions using renewable biomass as feedstock, rather than fossil materials, thereby having a significant impact on the existing chemical and pharmaceutical industry. This topic teaches students the biological and bioengineering principles that underpin the development of Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology processes and products. This topic trains the students in the development, scale-up, integration and commercialisation of bioprocesses, to be qualified as entry-level industrial biotechnologists, capable of performing best industry practice globally.
learning_outcomes: Display effective skills in self-directed learning, peer-learning, critical literature analysis, communication, and team work skills with the cultural diversity and social inclusiveness awareness required for global practice
Develop and apply skills to search, retrieve and interpret articles published in scientific journals
Develop and apply laboratory skills including technical skills, experimental design and data interpretation
Integrate and synthesise core concepts and information from other interacting disciplines to propose innovative solutions for the Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology industry

Apply knowledge and skills to the development and design of large-scale bioprocesses, for the production of Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology products at the technical level of a beginning practitioner and in accordance with best industry practice
Incorporate knowledge of regulatory requirements and pathways to commercialisation into the development of an Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology product
Describe the biomolecular and engineering concepts used in Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology processes and awareness of frontier areas of research and development
prerequisites: 2 of BIOL2771, BIOL2772

title: Molecular Biotechnology
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students the opportunity to learn the fundamentals of molecular biology needed to understand molecular biotechnology Prepare students for further study of biotechnology processes and products involving molecular biology Include activities which facilitate students working in a group environment in workshops and practicals as well as encourage self-directed learning through preparation of individual assignments

This topic provides information on the basis of molecular biology as needed for an understanding of molecular biotechnology. Information covered includes the basics of DNA replication and DNA transcription and the translation of genetic material into protein. This topic is also to develop the knowledge and understanding of DNA based techniques of the past and present including those used for DNA sequencing and emerging methods.
learning_outcomes: Exemplify a high level of laboratory recording skills such that other can reproduce their work
Visually exemplify the results from a data collection activity, present research data and scientific ideas in writing, using scientific language as appropriate
Devise and implement experimental designs lead it to independent and team work skills in a laboratory settings

Evaluate and identify the appropriate DNA based techniques of the past and present including those used for DNA sequencing and emerging methods used to study gene and protein functions in cells and organisms
Acquire skills in critical analysis, evaluate, thinking and self-reflection to academic and practical situations
Exhibit a detailed understanding of principles involved in the production of genetically modified organisms, their practical applications and ethical consideration
Identify the appropriate deployment of molecular biology and biotechnology tools within the biomedical, industrial, forensic, and environmental settings
Gain valuable experience in the application of molecular and biotechnology tools across a range of settings

title: BioBusiness
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
The aim of the topic is to give students experience and knowledge related to the commercialisation of biotechnology products or processes. This involves a basic knowledge of the scientific basis of the product/process, production and manufacture, marketing, sales, financial analysis, personnel and resource management, regulatory affairs, assessment of commercial viability, quality control and assurance. Students work in management teams with assigned tasks and work together to produce a pitch, a complete business plan, and then take part in an individual interview to relate content from the business plan to what they have learnt throughout the Semester. Workshops and tutorials are presented by industry-based experts including in financial management, patenting and intellectual property and marketing.

This topic provides an overview of the financial, business and management principles which would enhance understanding of business enterprise for the R&D-intensive bioscience industries. Students will work in management teams to prepare a Business Plan and will cover: an overview of Australia's science and technology policy, in particular how it relates to start-up research based industries; intellectual property management; team work and leadership skills; market research; commercial viability assessments; sales and marketing; strategic, financial and managerial processes which are applicable to the Bioscience industries.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the development of biotechnology products from first discovery through to market
Assess market and investment opportunities, personnel and resource management needs of the biotechnology industry
Demonstrate critical literature analysis, communication, self-directed learning, peer-learning, and teamwork skills
Communicate results using appropriate language and terminology using a range of formats
Evaluate the regulation of biotechnology industries and mechanisms for protecting Intellectual Property
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology 1a Admission into HBSC-Bachelor of Science (Honours) 1b Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1c Admission into MBA-Master of Business Administration 1d Admission into MSCAQ-Master of Science (Aquaculture) 1e Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1f Admission into GDPEG-Graduate Diploma in Entrepreneurial Growth 2 Admission into BSCBT-Bachelor of Science (Biotechnology) 2a Admission into BSC-Bachelor of Science 2b Admission into BSCHBT-Bachelor of Science (Honours) (Biotechnology) 3 72 Units of topics Must Satisfy: (((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f)) or ((2 or 2a or 2b) and 3))

school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Identify the outline systems of work, legal aspects, general duties, overview of safety responsibilities, resolution of safety issues, incident, accident reporting, chemical safety and biological safety. Recognize the outline of the principal regulatory regimes that operate to regulate bioscience research both nationally and internationally Raise their awareness of the interface between bioscience and society Discuss the sources of diversity in ethical stand points, such as religion and culture and personal experience

This graduate entry topic is designed to provide appreciation of the impact of new developments in Bioscience technology upon the law, ethics, society and the environment. The topic will consider the national and international regulatory aspects and the ethical and social aspects of: control of genetically modified organisms; cloning and reproductive technologies; stem cell therapy; clinical trials; genetic testing and protection of the environment. Through case study analysis the topic will also explore what it means to be an ethical bioscience professional.
learning_outcomes: Adopt ethical reasoning to assume and defend a coherent position in relation to an ethical issue
Develop teamwork, written and communication skills

Develop knowledge of skills at Australian and major international intellectual property law regimes, biotechnology regulation relevant to biotechnology research, development and commercialization, and societal issues relating to biotechnology
Identify the major national regulatory regimes relevant to bioscience research and commercialisation and how these contrast with those in other countries
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1b Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Human Molecular Genetics GE
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with a broad knowledge of contemporary issues in human genetics, including a detailed understanding of the applications of genetic techniques to human disease.

The topic will give an introduction to human genetics, modes of inheritance, and an overview of human chromosomes at the cytogenetic and molecular levels. The human genome will be discussed at the molecular level and biological mechanisms that modify human inheritance will be studied. An introduction to molecular genetic techniques used in diagnosis of human genetic disease will be presented in the context of specific diseases. The topic will be taught with Team Based Learning (TBL), an interactive, small group method of self-directed teaching and learning which is utilised in numerous universities and medical schools, including Flinders University Doctor of Medicine degree.
learning_outcomes: Understand how human genetics plays a key role in all areas of medicine and medical research
Discuss the ethical considerations regarding human genetics
Apply knowledge of human genetics to problem solving, clinical scenarios, and critical analysis of genetic research
Comprehend and critically examine principles that apply in human molecular genetics and human disease
Develop teamwork and communication skills

title: Advanced BioTechniques
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Equip students with the knowledge of techniques important to the biotechnology industry. Develop students’ ability to apply their knowledge of techniques to design experiments and analyse data. Expose students to broad areas of biotechnology where these techniques are used. Students to develop problem-solving, project management and teamwork skills and applying fundamental knowledge into practical applications in biotechnology industry Develop students communication skills, including writing and presenting.

In the dynamic field of biotechnology, the field is constantly advancing with the development of ground-breaking techniques and research platforms. This topic is designed to equip students with a foundational understanding of pivotal technologies shaping the future of biotechnology careers. Topics covered will include genome editing (CRISPR), genomics (next generation sequencing), flow cytometry, antibody engineering amongst others. Each of these has vast applications across the sector, and this will help students' understanding, and prepare them for innovation and discovery across the biotechnological landscape. The topic will be broken into module explain key concepts behind each technique and then analyse case studies and examples of where these technologies are applied in biotechnology. Lectures will be supplemented with workshops analysing data and designing experiments using these techniques.
learning_outcomes: Communicate results using appropriate language and terminology using a range of formats
Critique key technologies in biotechnology research and development
Appraise these technologies to solve real world problems
Evaluate experimental results from the biotechnology scientific literature
Demonstrate critical literature analysis, communication, self-directed learning, peer-learning, and teamwork skills; with cultural diversity and social inclusiveness awareness
prerequisites: Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology

title: Professional Skills for Biotechnology
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Equip students with the ability to analyse and interpret data using statistical methods, enabling them to make informed decisions in biotechnology. Teach students how to critically review scientific literature and utilize the latest published research to plan and conduct their own research projects, ensuring they can assess the quality and relevance of research findings while fostering a deeper understanding and application of current scientific knowledge Gain insight into potential career paths in biotechnology and identify the skills needed to pursue and develop these. Enhance students' effectiveness as oral, written and interpersonal communicators to the range of audiences with whom they will interact as practicing biotechnologists.

This topic provides students with the essential skills needed for a successful career in Biotechnology. Students will identify and develop the necessary skills for the biotechnology industry and create plans to enhance these skills. They will learn to use data and statistical methods to make informed decisions, a crucial ability in this field. The topic will also help students analyze and interpret the latest research, keeping them up-to-date with industry advancements. Students will be encouraged to utilize the latest published research to plan and conduct their own research projects, fostering a deeper understanding and application of current scientific knowledge. Emphasis will be placed on effectively communicating complex scientific information to diverse audiences. By the end of the course, students will have a thorough understanding of the biotechnology landscape and the skills required to excel in their future careers.
learning_outcomes: Assess personal progress towards becoming a Biotechnology professional
Incorporate insights from critical analysis of the scientific research, assessing the quality and relevance of findings to ensure informed and evidence-based conclusions
Communicate scientific findings effectively through written and oral presentations
Evaluate statistical analyses important for decision-making in biotechnology
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1b Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology GE
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Equip students with the knowledge and skills required by postgraduate-level biotechnologists to perform in the Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology industry Develop the understanding and basic skills required to take an industrial and pharmaceutical product or process from discovery to commercialisation Expose students to key areas of industrial and pharmaceutical biotechnology using real-world case studies delivered by guest lecturers from industry

Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology is the application of biotechnology and engineering in the exploitation of living organisms (mostly cells) and their subcomponents for sustainable, large-scale production of industrial bio-chemicals, biomaterials and pharmaceutical products. Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology has the potential to address the environmental sustainability of industry through the development of innovative technological solutions using renewable biomass as feedstock, rather than fossil materials, thereby having a significant impact on the existing chemical and pharmaceutical industry. This topic teaches students at graduate entry level the biological and bioengineering principles that underpin the development of industrial and pharmaceutical biotechnology processes and biological products. This topic provides students training in the development, design, scale-up, integration and commercialisation of bioprocesses, to be qualified as postgraduate-level industrial biotechnologists, capable of performing best industry practice globally.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply skills to search, retrieve and interpret articles published in scientific journals
Develop and apply laboratory skills including technical skills, experimental design and data interpretation
Integrate and synthesise core concepts and information from other interacting disciplines to propose innovative solutions for the Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology industry

Display effective skills in self-directed learning, peer-learning, critical literature analysis, communication, and team work skills with the cultural diversity and social inclusiveness awareness required for global practice

Analyse their knowledge and skills to the development and design of large-scale bioprocesses, for the production of Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology products at the technical level of a beginning practitioner and in accordance with best industry practice
Analyse biomolecular and engineering concepts used in Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology processes and awareness of frontier areas of research and development
Incorporate their knowledge of regulatory requirements and pathways to commercialisation into the development of an Industrial and Pharmaceutical Biotechnology product
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GDPBT-Graduate Diploma in Biotechnology 1a Admission into MNT-Master of Nanotechnology 1b Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Industry Project
school: College of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to immerse Master of Biotechnology students in authentic, industry-driven projects that foster the application of advanced biotechnology knowledge in real-world contexts. Through collaborative teamwork with industry partners, students will develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication skills while addressing genuine challenges faced by the biotechnology sector. The experience is designed to enhance professional readiness and provide meaningful engagement with industry practices.

In this innovative topic, students will collaborate in teams with industry partners to tackle real-world challenges identified by industry. Leveraging the knowledge and skills acquired during the first year of their course, students will engage in hands-on projects that require critical thinking, problem-solving, and effective communication. Each team will be guided by a mentor to ensure successful collaboration and project execution, providing students with invaluable experience and insights into the biotechnology industry.
learning_outcomes: Communicate scientific findings and project outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences
Critically analyse and evaluate industry challenges to develop and propose innovative solutions
Apply advanced biotechnology concepts and techniques to solve industry-specific problems
Demonstrate effective teamwork and collaboration skills by working closely with industry partners in a professional setting
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MBTL-Master of Biotechnology 2 36 units of topics Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

This topic aims to: Convey the breadth of interacting disciplines that comprise Medical Biotechnology Describe in-depth examples and illustrative case-studies representative of key areas of Medical Biotechnology Explain how core scientific concepts and practical techniques are applied in Medical Biotechnology Develop problem-solving and team work skills that incorporate culturally inclusive practices, especially as regards Indigenous groups and other stakeholders
