title: Inorganic Chemistry
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop and use the modern approach of molecular orbital theory to develop chemical bonding concepts and provide an understanding of ligand field theory (The spectral and magnetic properties of transition metal ions can then be understood at a sophisticated level, which allows them to be used diagnostically to identify and characterise transition metal compounds) Provide an overview of the role that metal ions play in biological chemistry and of the inorganic chemistry associated with organometallic compounds Continue the development of laboratory skills associated with synthetic work pertaining to inorganic and organometallic compounds

The aim is to provide students with an overview of the role and importance that transition metal ions play in inorganic chemistry and in organometallic chemistry. Secondly, students will learn to use the modern approach of molecular orbital theory to develop chemical bonding concepts across the periodic table, and so to acquire an understanding of ligand field theory. The spectral and magnetic properties of transition metal ions can then be understood at a sophisticated level, which allows these transition metals to be used diagnostically to identify and characterise compounds. Finally, this topic will present students with the fundamentals of inorganic chemical synthesis through a series of practical experiments. These practical experiments and the associated capstone activities will solidify students knowledge and skills in the inorganic chemistry field.

Demonstrate an understanding about what various types transition metal compounds are and how they can be used
Use the concept of metal ion hydrolysis to understand and make limited predictions of metal ion speciation in aqueous solution
Understand the molecular orbital description for bonding in an octahedral coordination complex
Evaluate and present results from laboratory work in written and verbal form
Understand the chemical bonding in metal carbonyl and metal pi-complexes

Be familiar with the major industrial catalytic processes that employ organometallic catalysts
Be familiar with the method of uptake and retention of metal ions in biological systems

title: Organic Reactions GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an appreciation of the basic reactions encountered in organic chemistry. This topic will teach students why and how organic reactions are carried out as well as an understanding of the underlying mechanism of the main reactions. Further, students will gain an appreciation of the factors affecting the main organic chemical reactions as well as stereochemical and regiochemical characteristics for these reactions. In addition students will be trained to carry out reactions safely and independently in a laboratory and to analyse and characterise the materials produced.

This topic will present students with the fundamentals of organic chemical synthesis. These are introduced initially by discussing the philosophy behind synthesis, a presentation on the mechanistic approach to understanding organic reactions followed by discussion on the main organic chemical reactions. The main organic reactions include for example; nucleophilic substitution and elimination, anion based chemistry (acetylenic anions, enolates, Grignard and organolithium reagents), addition reactions, and both electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution reactions. In addition students will learn about the stereochemical aspects of organic molecules and how these are influenced by organic reactions.

Carry out basic organic chemistry reactions safely and independently in a laboratory and examine and characterise the compounds produced
Predict and rationalise mechanistically the products from a variety of chemical reaction conditions, and factors that may influence them

title: Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a short overview of several fundamental areas within Artificial Intelligence (AI). Students will gain a greater understanding of the theoretical, mathematical, and algorithmic principles behind several AI techniques, along with an appreciation for how modern AI tools are being applied to solve real-world problems. Students will also gain hands-on experience applying the skills and techniques learned to solve practical-based AI tasks across a variety of industry relevant domains. Students will also obtain skills in critical thinking, analytical research, and effective communication of ideas within the wider context of AI.

This topic provides the core fundamentals necessary for many areas within artificial intelligence. This includes both theoretical knowledge and practical skills necessary to form a comprehensive understanding of modern artificial intelligence techniques and applications. Specific areas covered include: Algorithm Design , including how to interpret/write pseudocode and analyse the complexity of different algorithmic processes. Search and Planning, including how to define problems in terms of states and actions, and apply appropriate exploration and decision-making algorithms. Artificial Life , including how natural systems and biological process can be used to inform and enhance AI development. Knowledge Representation and Reasoning , including how information about the world can be formalised in a manner that allows for automated reasoning to answer complex questions. Data Analysis , including how to collect, analyse and interpret real-world data to extract meaning and make predictions. Generative AI , including an explanation of the techniques behind recent generative AI advancements and a discussion of the ethical considerations they present to modern society.
learning_outcomes: Examine how knowledge can be represented in a formalised manner that allows for autonomous reasoning
Write, interpret and contrast basic searching, sorting and planning algorithms presented in pseudo-code form
Implement Artificial Life (ALife) algorithms that simulate natural processes and genetic evolution
Explore the capabilities, limitations and ethical considerations of modern generative AI techniques
Analyse large-scale datasets to extract meaning and make useful predictions

title: Programming Fundamentals
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topic aims to help develop: An understanding of the nature of programming using a modern high-level programming language The ability to read, comprehend and write simple programs An appreciation of the process by which software systems are developed, including their specification, design, implementation, testing and maintenance

The topic is intended as a first topic in programming for students who intend to major in computer science and for students from other disciplines who require programming skills. It aims to introduce students to the basic tools and techniques of software development using the Python programming language. The topic will cover the fundamentals of structured programming, beginning with the nature of programming, how computers process data, and the concept of algorithmic thinking as a process for solving problems. The topic will then explore foundational programming concepts as building blocks for implementing algorithms as computer programs. This includes variables and basic data structures, conditional and looping structures, functions, classes and modules, code tracing and testing, and the application of best practice readability and style conventions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate that they can read pseudo-code and translate it into a readable, working program
Demonstrate that they can use programming development environments and tools within a defined context
Demonstrate that they know the basics of testing and debugging
Demonstrate that they can comprehend basic program control constructs of sequence, selection, and iteration
Demonstrate that they can apply programming principles to solve domain-specific problems

title: UX Fundamentals
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: A working vocabulary to classify, examine, and interpret concepts that drive user focused software development of interactive, web-based systems Skills to develop interactive web-based systems The ability to appraise and recommend human computer interaction and user experience principles in the design and development of web-based, interactive systems Skills to evaluate the usability of a web-based solution based on human factors principles

Modern interactive software is a complex experience with a focus on the user and their needs. This topic will examine the issues associated with human factors in the design, implementation and evaluation of interactive, web-based systems. The core of the topic focuses on identifying and critiquing human factors and user experience (UX) design principles in the construction of web-based systems, acknowledging the importance of and incorporating user involvement in the design and development of engaging interactive systems for an effective user experience. The topic will cover the following material: the complexity of UX design for interactive and web-based systems, the integral nature of the user in the design and development process, the human computer interaction cycle, use of affordance and metaphor in software, application of computing and UX laws and principles, the societal, ethical and security issues associated with software design and construction. Students will explore these concepts through the use of and implementation of web technologies, including HTML, CSS, DOM, PHP, and JavaScript.
learning_outcomes: Determine how human factor principles and system design affects usability
Construct an evaluation procedure utilising the techniques of heuristic evaluations, usability testing and experimental evaluation
Work independently and in a team on designing, creating and maintaining applications for the web
Implement user focused software solutions through the effective inclusion of users in the design and development process
Communicate effectively to a diverse audience following professional practice standards
Reflect on ethical, legal and security issues related to web applications

This topic will examine the issues associated with human factors in the design, implementation and evaluation of interactive, web-based systems. The core of the topic focuses on identifying and critiquing human factors and user experience (UX) design principles in the construction of web-based systems, acknowledging the importance of and incorporating user involvement in the design and development of engaging interactive systems for an effective user experience. With a focus on securing connected organisations, the students will study the principles, standards, processes and technologies associated with networked computer systems and data communications, and the cybersecurity associated with these. school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to familiarise students with the basic concepts, fundamental structures and general techniques that are needed to define, construct and manipulate a database using a database management system (DBMS) with the main emphasis on relational DBMSs. title: Full-Stack Web Development
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: The ability to build complete web applications by learning how MongoDB, Express.js, React, and Node.js work together Skills to create back-end systems that manage and share data through APIs The ability to design interactive websites using React that respond to users Actionable knowledge to secure and deploy web applications

Current web applications demand a holistic understanding of both front-end and back-end technologies to deliver effective and affective user experiences. This topic looks at the requirements of full-stack web development, focusing on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React, Node.js), to equip students with the skills necessary to build dynamic, data-driven web solutions. The core of this topic centres on the practical application of these technologies, enabling students to design, develop, and deploy complete web applications, while emphasising the importance of efficient data management and robust API design. The topic will cover the following material: the architecture and interaction of the MERN stack components, the creation of RESTful APIs with Node.js and Express.js, the implementation of NoSQL databases using MongoDB and Mongoose, the development of interactive user interfaces with React, the management of application state, user authentication and authorisation, and the deployment of applications. Students will explore these concepts through the practical implementation of a full-stack web application, integrating front-end and back-end functionalities to create a cohesive and scalable solution. Students will gain an understanding of the core concepts of software deployment.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and in a team, utilising source control technologies, on the deployment of a full stack web solution
Develop web-based applications using current, popular frameworks
Evaluate and apply appropriate APIs for session management and authentication
Evaluate and apply appropriate strategies, technologies and architectures during development of full stack web solutions

title: Mobile Application Development
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: Skills to build Android apps using Kotlin, by learning its basic rules and good practices Knowledge of how Android apps are made, including designing layouts, handling data, and using internet connections with Android Studio Hands-on experience making intuitive mobile apps, following design and accessibility rules An introduction to cross-platform deployment, exploring alternate languages The steps to get your Android apps ready and published

There are twice as many mobile devices in the world as there are people. This is a technology that is always on and always connected across a number of form-factors, platforms, and operating systems. The complexity of the mobile market requires flexibility, demanding developers with expertise in both native and cross-platform technologies. This topic provides a comprehensive introduction to Android application development using Kotlin, a modern and powerful language, while also exploring the fundamentals of cross-platform development. The core of this topic focuses on building robust and engaging native Android applications, covering essential concepts from UI design and data persistence to network communication and asynchronous programming. Students will learn to leverage Kotlin's features for efficient and maintainable code, and understand the Android ecosystem for effective app deployment. In the latter stages of the topic, a comparative analysis of alternate languages will provide insights into cross-platform development, allowing students to evaluate and understand the trade-offs between native and hybrid approaches. Students will explore these concepts through the practical implementation of multiple Android applications.
learning_outcomes: Create functional and intuitive native Android applications using Kotlin
Evaluate the suitability of native Kotlin development versus cross platform implementation for specific mobile application projects
Analyse and debug complex Android application issues, identifying and resolving errors related to UI, data, and network communication
Reflect on ethical, legal, and security issues related to mobile application development

title: Data Engineering
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: 1. Develop a comprehensive understanding of the data engineering lifecycle and its fundamental concepts, tools, and technologies. 2. Enable students to design and implement scalable data pipelines using cloud-based solutions. 3. Cultivate analytical skills to assess data usability, transformation techniques, and decision points across pipeline stages. 4. Introduce modern data management architectures such as data lakes, data meshes, and DataOps for scalable and efficient data processing. 5. Foster critical thinking in evaluating current data engineering practices, identifying emerging trends, and addressing associated threats and limitations. 6. Reinforce ethical awareness by integrating data quality, privacy, and security considerations across all stages of the data engineering process.

This topic offers an in-depth exploration of the key concepts, techniques, and tools necessary for a career in data engineering. Students will gain hands-on experience in designing and implementing data architectures, building data pipelines, and applying advanced data transformation, modelling, and analytics techniques. By leveraging a modern cloud-based data management platform such as Amazon Web Services, students will learn to process and analyse large, diverse datasets efficiently and at scale. Additionally, the course emphasizes data quality, security, privacy, and ethical considerations, preparing students to tackle real-world data challenges while supporting decision-making in organizations.

Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental concepts, tools, and technologies involved in the data engineering lifecycle

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with the skills needed to solve programming problems of moderate complexity, such as applications that provide an interface to real-world data. The focus is on object-oriented techniques for representing and manipulating program data using either predefined components or custom-designed components.

This topic provides a second-level exploration of programming, with an emphasis on the data structures that frequently occur in programming problems and the algorithms for traversing and manipulating such structures. The syllabus is built around the theme of data abstraction using object- oriented programming. Specific areas covered include: 1. Basic data representations, including arrays, records, and strings 2. Key object-oriented computational techniques, including exception handlers, inheritance, recursion 3. Fundamental linked data structures such as lists, stacks, trees, and graphs, together with the operations for manipulating them 4. Algorithmic strategies, including brute force, divide-and-conquer, and branch-and-bound approaches 5. An introduction to algorithmic analysis, including complexity classes and an appreciation for space-time trade-offs 6. Fundamental computing algorithms, including a variety of common searching, sorting, and traversal algorithms

The scope of the topic incorporates increasingly relevant applications such computer vision, image analysis, data science and the ethical issues associated with these. Students will also obtain skills in analytical thinking, experimental research, and effective communication within the wider context of ML.

title: Computer Mathematics
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic builds a solid discrete mathematics and logic foundation for a computer scientist.

The main themes of this topic are logic and proof, induction and recursion, discrete structures, algorithms and their analysis, and applications. Mathematical reasoning, combinatorial analysis and algorithmic thinking are carefully blended and balanced to provide students with skills and knowledge necessary for a successful career in science and technology.

Understand and apply formal logic system on which mathematical reasoning is based
Use various problem-solving strategies including algorithmic thinking (both iterative and recursive) and various counting techniques to create appropriate solutions to computing problems
Analyse and construct valid mathematical arguments - proofs - and understand mathematical statements - theorems

title: Systems Software
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the fundamentals of systems software and operating systems Illustrate the relationship between systems software, operating systems and process management Demonstrate how the operating system manages security requirements Provide students with a hands-on working knowledge of systems software functions, configuration and management Provide students with a good understanding of how systems software works to control the functionality of computing technologies

This topic introduces the fundamentals of systems software and operating system design concepts and management together with the basics of security and an appreciation of the issues involved in the design and implementation of systems software. Areas of learning include: an overview of systems software, operating systems, evolution of modern operating systems, real-time and embedded systems, central processing unit, drivers, interrupts, kernel, file systems, storage devices, virtualisation, processes, threads, concurrency, memory management, scheduling, basic shell scripting, command-line commands, network fundamentals, account management, resource management and security.

Explain and compare core systems concepts, including processes, threads, scheduling, concurrency, memory management, and file systems.
Produce structured artefacts and documentation for common IT management processes, such as disaster recovery, business proposals, and vendor selection.

title: Probabilistic Machine Learning
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic explores machine learning from a probabilistic and computational perspective. Students will examine core concepts and methodologies from probabilistic machine learning and apply these techniques to real-world applications. Probability theory is explored through multiple computational frameworks to build the foundational knowledge required to understand key probabilistic machine learning algorithms. The topic emphasises algorithmic design, implementation, and analysis within a computing context. Markov modelling is also covered and applied to a range of complex data-analysis problems, providing students with practical tools and insights into the functioning of these algorithms within modern computing systems.

Uncertainty is a fundamental challenge in data-driven decision making, yet many machine learning models overlook this important issue. This topic introduces students to probabilistic machine learning, a powerful and emerging modelling approach that directly incorporates data uncertainty to develop more robust machine learning models. Students will first explore the theoretical and computational statistical concepts that underpin the development and analysis of probabilistic machine learning algorithms. From this foundation students will then investigate probabilistic network representations and apply them to challenging real-world data sets. The topic then deepens its focus on the algorithmic foundations, computational complexity, scalability, and performance of these models. These modules develop a deep technical understanding of how probabilistic algorithms operate within modern computing environments and how they can be optimised for operational deployment. In summary, this topic integrates theoretical depth with practical implementation to develop advanced insights into how probabilistic reasoning strengthens machine learning, particularly in areas such as uncertainty quantification, sequential modelling, and inference in high-dimensional spaces.
learning_outcomes: Implement and analyse Markov models on real-world computational applications
Assess and utilise a range of model estimation and inference algorithms within the appropriate context
Understand the foundations of probabilistic machine learning including probability theory, estimation and inference, statistical machine learning and Markov models

Evaluate, select and apply different probabilistic machine learning algorithms for specific contexts and applications, with understanding of the theoretical computational complexity of each algorithm and the implications for model scalability
Integrate Frequentist, Bayesian and Computational statistical approaches within machine learning applications and appraise the benefits and limitations of each of these approaches within applications
prerequisites: 2 of COMP2031, COMP2711

title: Mixed Reality
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: The ability to critically evaluate and synthesise advanced theories and principles of Mixed Reality, spatial computing, and human-computer interaction. Skills to design and architect complex mixed reality solutions that address real-world problems. The capacity to create high-fidelity, user-centric mixed reality applications using contemporary development technologies. Actionable knowledge to implement sophisticated interaction paradigms, and manage data in shared MR environments. The ability to assess the ethical, societal, and economic implications of emerging mixed reality technologies and their deployment.

Mixed Reality (MR) is transforming human-computer interaction, blending physical and digital worlds to create immersive and intuitive experiences. This topic looks at the theoretical underpinnings and practical implementation strategies for designing, developing, and deploying Mixed Reality applications. Focusing on the creation of innovative solutions, students will critically evaluate existing MR paradigms and development processes. The course will leverage contemporary technologies for immersive 3D environments, as well as web-based AR/MR experiences, providing a versatile skillset for various deployment platforms, including augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) headsets, and web browsers. The topic will cover the following material: advanced spatial computing concepts, human-computer interaction (HCI) principles in MR, multimodal interaction design, perception and cognitive factors in immersive environments, data persistence and synchronisation in shared MR experiences, and ethical considerations and societal impact of MR technologies. Students will engage in complex project-based learning, culminating in the design, development, and rigorous evaluation of a novel mixed reality application, demonstrating prowess of the entire development lifecycle from conceptualisation to deployment and critical assessment.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop solutions for persistent data management and synchronisation in multi-user mixed reality environments
Critically appraise the performance, usability, and user experience of mixed reality applications
Synthesise theoretical knowledge with practical skills to autonomously conceive, develop, and deploy a novel mixed reality application that addresses a defined problem or opportunity
Analyse and articulate the ethical considerations, societal impact, and future implications of mixed reality technologies within diverse contexts
Implement innovative mixed reality experiences that demonstrate comprehension and application of spatial computing and multimodal interaction design principles

title: Capstone Game Project
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: The ability to integrate and apply advanced knowledge and skills from various game development and computing disciplines (design, programming, systems, UX, project management) to a single, cohesive project. Skills to manage and execute a complex, self-directed game development project from conception to completion within a collaborative team setting. The capacity to design, implement, and iterate upon innovative game mechanics, systems, and experiences that align with a defined creative vision. Employ professional game development methodologies, including version control, quality assurance, and comprehensive documentation. The ability to critically evaluate game design choices, technical implementations, and project outcomes, and to adapt strategies based on iterative feedback and testing.

The Capstone Game Project is the final defining experience for students in game development, designed to integrate and apply the comprehensive knowledge and skills acquired throughout their studies. This topic provides students with the unique opportunity to conceptualise, design, develop, and deliver a significant, original game project in a small team environment. With an emphasis on creative freedom and self-directed learning, students will immerse themselves within the complexities of a full game development lifecycle, from initial ideation and prototyping to final production, testing, and presentation. The topic fosters professional practices, including agile methodologies, version control, rigorous quality assurance, and comprehensive project documentation. Students will work collaboratively to realise their unique game vision, tackling real-world development challenges and preparing them for professional roles in the game industry. The topic culminates in a public showcase of their completed game, demonstrating their ability to deliver a high-quality, playable experience.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively the game's vision, design, and technical aspects through professional documentation, presentations, and a public demonstration
Evaluate and debug complex game systems, identifying and implementing solutions for technical challenges, performance optimisation, and user experience improvements
Apply professional project management methodologies and collaborative tools to effectively plan, execute, and deliver a complex game development project within a team
Analyse and critically reflect on the entire game development process, including design decisions, technical implementations, team dynamics, and project outcomes
Create an original, playable game demonstrating the integration of advanced game design, programming, systems, and UX principles

title: Cloud and Distributed Computing
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Students will understand the core concept of cloud computing and its building blocks, including services (IaaS, SaaS, Paas, DaaS), different deployment models (private, public, hybrid), infrastructure (virtualisation, networking, storage), cloud security architecture, and its performance metrics such as scalability, availability, cost etc. Students will develop an understanding of public cloud platforms, its essential API and deployment scenarios for various use cases. Students will analyse a real-world problem, design a solution and deploy it on a public cloud platform.

This topic covers the fundamentals of cloud computing, its services (IaaS, SaaS, Paas, DaaS), different deployment models (private, public, hybrid), infrastructure (virtualisation, networking, storage), cloud security architecture, and its performance metrics such as scalability, availability, cost etc. Students will develop a good understanding of publicly available cloud solutions (Amazon, Google, IBM, Microsoft etc.) and its important APIs. Students will have hands-on cloud deployment and its different services for various use cases.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and assess the business and technical benefits of cloud computing for a real-world use case
Design and deploy a cloud solution for a real-world use case over a public cloud platform
Explain the core concepts of cloud computing, cloud services, deployment models and infrastructure
Analyse the performance metrics of cloud deployment models for a use case
Analyse cloud computing models for security and privacy issues
prerequisites: 1 1 of COMP1102, ENGR1762 2 31.5 units of Level 2 topics 3 Admission into BENGSH-Bachelor of Engineering (Software)(Honours) Must satisfy: (1 and (2 or 3))

title: Information Security and Applied Cryptography
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic develops advanced capability in information security and the applied use of cryptography to protect data and services in modern systems. Students will learn to select, justify, and implement cryptographic mechanisms and security controls, evaluate security properties and trade-offs, and design security solutions that address confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation within realistic operational and organisational constraints.

This topic covers the practical use of cryptography to protect information in modern systems. Students study security goals, threat models, cryptographic primitives and protocols, and key management. They apply established libraries to implement and test secure functions, and evaluate common design and implementation errors. The topic emphasises justified control selection, secure deployment, and professional security reporting.
learning_outcomes: Select primitives/protocols based on threat model and constraints
Design an end-to-end security architecture for a scenario
Communicate security analysis professionally and ethically
Analyse security requirements and suitable crypto + non-crypto controls
Implement cryptographic functionality using established libraries, safe practices and testing
Evaluate common crypto deployment/implementation failures
prerequisites: 1 ENGR1762 2 COMP3723 Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Cloud Security
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic develops advanced capability to design, implement, and assure security controls in cloud environments. Students will learn to secure cloud workloads and data using risk-based security architecture, identity and access management, network segmentation, encryption and key management, logging and monitoring, and incident response, and to justify decisions against realistic threats, compliance needs, and operational constraints.

This topic addresses security design and implementation in cloud environments. Students apply shared-responsibility principles, identity and access management, network and workload controls, encryption and key management, and logging and monitoring. They assess cloud security posture using evidence from configurations and telemetry and propose risk treatments and improvements. The topic links secure architecture decisions to operational constraints and stakeholder needs.
learning_outcomes: Produce professional security documentation and communication (architecture justification, risk treatment, incident summary) consistent with ethical and professional expectations
Implement cloud security controls using industry-aligned practices (least privilege IAM, secure configuration, encryption, secrets management, logging/monitoring)
Evaluate cloud security posture using evidence (logs, configuration findings, control verification) recommending improvements that reduce exposure and increase detectability
Analyse cloud threat models and shared-responsibility obligations to derive security requirements for cloud services and workloads
Design secure cloud architectures (identity, network, data and workload security) that manage risk, availability, and cost-performance trade-offs
prerequisites: 1 COMP3033 2 COMP3781 Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Capstone Project
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide third-year IT students the opportunity to: Apply skills and knowledge gained in their course to the systematic development of a complex computer-based information system Apply their skills and knowledge in a professionally responsible manner Communicate effectively with other computer scientists, IT specialists and members of the wider community using a range of communication technologies Work professionally as an individual and in a team Develop a computer-based solution appropriate to the social, political, economic and environmental context of the project Contribute successfully to project management Search, access, and analyse research literature as part of the process of developing solutions to problems

This capstone topic provides practical experience in designing, developing and testing a non-trivial information technology project. Projects are generally software-based, although sometimes they may involve investigation of theory. Projects cover the whole systems development life cycle from analysis through design to implementation. The project work will involve project management, comprehensive document preparation and a presentation. The project will be supervised by an academic staff member. The projects offered will be determined by the topic co-ordinator in consultation with the potential supervisors. Students are assigned in groups to a project supervisor. There are no lectures in this topic, although students will be expected to do the equivalent of at least 10 hours per week of practical work for a semester including attending regular meetings with their group and with their project supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Gain experience in formal document preparation

Gain first-hand practical experience in aspects of the systems development life cycle, including the development of system requirements, system design, system testing, system implementation and evaluation
Demonstrate skills in practical experience in project management
Apply experience in professional practice
Communicate effectively with clients, users and project group members
Undertake a significant group project in an area of information technology
prerequisites: 72 units of topics

title: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
On completion of this topic, students will be able to: Understand the theoretical foundations that underpin inductive reasoning in data‑rich environments, enabling them to interpret and generalise from complex, noisy, and heterogeneous datasets. Evaluate core and emerging algorithmic approaches in data mining, recognising their strengths, limitations, and the contexts in which these algorithms can be most effectively applied. Analyse and apply architectural frameworks for knowledge discovery, integrating data preparation, modelling, evaluation, and deployment into coherent, end‑to‑end processes. Apply legal, ethical, and professional considerations in data mining and knowledge discovery, including privacy, fairness, transparency, and compliance within relevant regulatory environments.

The ability to transform raw, complex data into meaningful knowledge is a critical skill in the data‑driven world. This topic introduces students to the principles, techniques, and frameworks of Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, integrating statistical reasoning, algorithmic thinking, and systems perspectives. Students will explore a range of representative approaches and tools that are selected to match current and emerging trends for discovering patterns, relationships, and structures in diverse data sources. Practical engagement spans the entire process, from data preparation through analysis to deployment, informed by ethical, legal, and professional considerations. The curriculum combines theoretical depth with practical application, developing the capability of students to design, evaluate, and articulate robust, responsible knowledge‑discovery processes that meet the demands and complexities of contemporary real‑world contexts.
learning_outcomes: Plan and conduct data mining projects, employing suitable methodologies to ensure reproducibility, transparency, and analytical depth.
Communicate data mining results, uncertainty, and limitations to technical and non‑technical stakeholders, utilising appropriate visualisations and documentation to inform decision‑making.
Apply theoretical foundations of data mining and knowledge discovery by designing and implementing prototype end‑to‑end systems, demonstrating the link from theory to practice.
Architect, engineer, and integrate scalable knowledge discovery pipelines, aligning data preparation, modelling, evaluation, and deployment strategies.
Critically analyse the potential and limitations of given data mining approaches, integrating evaluation of their ethical, legal, and professional implications.
Use, compare, and discuss common algorithms found in both commercial systems and scholarly literature, selecting appropriate methods for varied problem contexts.
prerequisites: COMP2031

title: Advanced Algorithms and Programming
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with the skills needed to solve complex programming problems, such as applications that provide an interface to real-world data. The focus is on object-oriented techniques for representing and manipulating program data using either predefined components or custom-designed components.

The topic covers the development of solutions to complex problems based on complex algorithms involving many, possibly distributed, components in complex structures. Problems will be taken from a number of areas such as robotics, image processing, animation and information retrieval and analysis. Various computational models will be used such as mobile agents, distributed processing and evolutionary.
learning_outcomes: Determine the time and space complexity of complex algorithms
Develop programs that solve complex problems using a range of computational models
Analyse complex problems and develop algorithmic solutions
Make use of APIs that support the computational models used in the topic
prerequisites: COMP2711

title: Information Security
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topic provides an overview of cyber security and information security, and their application to managing and securing information systems and technology. Contemporary techniques and technologies are highlighted. It improves student skills in preparing and presenting technical reports on aspects of information management and computer security.

Information security combines a technical control and a managerial approach to the protection of information systems. The topic provides a comprehensive overview of cyber security and information security programs. Examining current and emerging technologies, addressing the contemporary challenges and ethical issues, and introducing cryptography, physical security and digital forensics, are core to the learning in this topic.
learning_outcomes: Analyse security risks and select appropriate security controls
Develop a business report on an organisations’ cyber security and information security program
Identify the security issues associated with the integration of information systems, including the impact of poor software security implementation
Explain the importance of cyber security and information security to business and organisations
Describe the threats to securing an organisation and common attacks associated with those threats
prerequisites: 1 1 of ENGR1762, ENGR1204 2 31.5 units of Level 2 topics Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Theory and Practice of Computation
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
To be able to specify and implement algorithms in an appropriate paradigm with an understanding of how to estimate what performance (efficacy and efficiency) can be expected and what resources will be required To understand and be able to employ Logic Programming, Functional Programming, Object Oriented Programming and von Neumann (Procedural Programming) paradigms To be able to set up, carry out and appropriately report on theoretical and practical evaluation (analysis and benchmarking) of computer routines and use this information to improve the performance of a program To be able to write clear portable code that is independent on machine, language and compiler dependencies To develop an ability to work alone both in a team, including to integrate work and build extensible systems, and to negotiate an ethical solution acceptable to a diverse range of stakeholders

This topic is concerned with the concepts and mechanisms that underlie modern programming languages as well as providing insights into the capabilities and limitations of languages, computers and algorithms. The topic combines both theoretical foundations and practical demonstrations of issues relating to programming and algorithm design. It teaches fundamental skills necessary to selection of an appropriate programming paradigm for a problem, whilst highlighting the distinct and overlapping capabilities of three families of programming languages. The topic examines concepts such as types, variables, binding, abstraction, parameterization, encapsulation, generics, polymorphism, inheritance, recursion, iteration, formal languages, automata, logic, proof, decidability, computability and complexity. It uses as vehicles for illustration and exploration multiple languages supporting a variety of programming paradigms, including the procedural, functional, object-oriented and logic programming paradigms. The topic has an emphasis on design and evaluation of efficient, efficacious programs, including analysis and benchmarking of programs, with close integration of the theoretical and practical components, and workshops to assist in application of theory.
learning_outcomes: Have the basic foundations to deal with the broad range of programming languages, paradigms and libraries/APIs
Utilize concepts from one paradigm in a language or context associated with another paradigm, choosing the most appropriate paradigm for the job
Be adept at styles of programming and system development that are knowledge, rule and logic based rather than depending on low level step by step instructions
Use both theoretical and practical means of assessing the requirements of a proposed system and analysing the performance of an implemented system
Understand the concept of paradigms and the effect of language, paradigm, data structure on the design of algorithms
prerequisites: 1 1 of COMP2711, COMP2741, ENGR2701 2 31.5 units of study Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Advanced Enterprise Security
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic provides practice in the practical application of the techniques and contemporary frameworks used secure information systems and information technology infrastructure in modern businesses and organisations. It develops student skills in assessing risk and preparing and presenting security business reports and technical documents reports on the management of computer and information security in organisations. Student will learn how to lead enterprise security programs.

Strategic security management and the effective protection of an enterprises’ information systems and infrastructure is vital in the global and increasingly interconnected business world. This topic investigates information security governance, developing security programs, creating practical and compliant policy, risk assessment and operation information security management.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse publications in enterprise information security
Develop a cyber security or information security program outline for a specific issue in enterprise information security
Construct a contingency plan that includes incident response, disaster recovery and business continuity
Analyse security incidents and risks and identify controls and prevention techniques
Compare information security management and governance frameworks for use in organisations
Identify significant national and international law, regulation, industry best practice and international standards that relate to the practice of cyber security and information security

title: Extended Industry Experience
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic provides a further period of industry experience following on from a structured practicum. As such it provides students with a further period when students can relate academic theory to industry practice. Student will: Contribute to a technical, ICT or engineering related project Understand the structure and operation of the company or organisation, and its responsibilities to shareholders, employees, customers, and the general public Understand the influences of commercial, economic, social, cultural, political, legal, industrial and environmental issues affecting companies, organisations or employees that undertake engineering work

Industry experience is particularly valuable for the Science and Engineering professions where the industry context of academic theory is necessary to create a well-rounded professional. This topic facilitates an extension to any other Computer Science, Engineering and Mathematics practicum topic by enabling a student to spend a further six months in industry before returning to complete their award. Note that under the Fair Work Act, students enrolled in 0-unit Industry Experience topics must be in receipt of appropriate remuneration from the industry partner. Evidence of appropriate remuneration must be demonstrated before enrolment is permitted in the topic. International students, please be aware that your student visa conditions restrict you from undertaking the topic within Australia. Please see the topic coordinator for further details.
learning_outcomes: Critically describe the influences of commercial, economic, social, cultural, political, legal, industrial and environmental issues affecting companies, organisations and employees that undertake ICT work
Contribute to technical projects as an individual or team member
Participate as a member of a team, understanding the roles and valuing all members of that team
Appreciate the responsibilities, roles, attitudes, values, priorities, judgement and work methods of practising professionals in industry
Appreciate the overall manner in which ICT is practised and managed
Synthesize and apply skills and knowledge already acquired in their course
Understand the structure, operation and responsibilities, and business culture of a company or organisation
prerequisites: 1 ^ 1 of ENGR3704, ENGR3705 2 1 of COMP3792, ENGR3700, ENGR3710, ENGR3403, STEP3700, STEP3710 Must Satisfy: (1) and (2) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

title: Artificial Intelligence
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
To be able to specify, consult, deploy and implement intelligent software and systems To understand and be able to employ Logic Programming, Knowledge Engineering and Knowledge Discovery paradigms and frameworks To be able assess requirements and select or adapt appropriate methodologies, techniques and tools for the achievement of a task, including through interviewing personnel and reviewing literature To be able to communicate with non-computing specialists and interdisciplinary specialists in the design of intelligent systems, learning paradigms or data mining applications To develop an ability to work alone both in a team, including to integrate work and build extensible systems, and to negotiate an ethical solution acceptable to a diverse range of stakeholders

This topic will provide a basic understanding of Intelligent Systems and their applications, including a basic understanding and broad overview of Artificial Intelligence and Heuristic Search methodologies, and supervised and unsupervised Machine Learning and Data Mining technologies. The topic provides a balance of theory and practice, with two lectures on theory or philosophy being complemented by seminar-style case studies on specific applications, including guest speakers. Practical work is largely undertaken and assessed in weekly computing laboratory sessions, with a variety of assignments including specification, programming and written tasks. Specific areas to be covered include methodologies and philosophical issues, the relationship of intelligent systems to human intelligence and cognitive science, applications to knowledge engineering, knowledge discovery, language processing, text and data mining, as well as selected topics relating to cognition, perception, visualization and classification/clustering.
learning_outcomes: Understand the basic foundations to deal with the broad range of intelligent systems, applications and literature, including producing and critiquing proposals and reports appropriate to the field
Become familiar with styles of programming and system development that are knowledge, rule and logic based rather than depending on low level step by step instructions
Achieve basic intelligent behaviours in simple programs and systems

Develop a basic understanding of the power of heuristics and tricks and the human propensities that make for a good or a bad interface, and that either easily convince the user into accepting behaviour as human or conversely irk the user as being somehow inhuman
Weigh up the basic human factors, personal and team relationships and ethical considerations and risks that affect the design and employment of intelligent systems
Understand concept of heuristics and the basic methodologies of designing intelligent systems and developing learning and mining paradigms

title: Computer Game Development
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: The skills to create digital games The ability to critique the complexity of structure and processes associated with a real-time, user driven, interactive system The techniques to relate framework principles in the examination of commercial digital games An appreciation of the history and trends of computer games, their development, and the industry The skills to construct a complete game production life cycle, from concept to deployment, within an Agile development framework

This topic provides a thorough exploration of the field of computer game development, including the design, project management and development of complex, digital, interactive, player-centric experiences. Specific areas will include: Examining the architecture of computer games through various perspectives – design, play, and society Practical experience in the design and implementation of game mechanics, rules, objects and interactions Practical experience working with industry game development engines and the implementation languages Practical application of Agile game development principles across the breadth of the project Investigating the history of computer games and their development
learning_outcomes: Work professionally as an individual and in a team
Incorporate mechanics, aesthetics, narrative, and technology in the production of digital media artefacts
Communicate effectively about computer game artefacts, frameworks, development, and the industry
Develop a functional computer game
Design and execute the project management life cycle components for an Agile game development project
prerequisites: 1 1 of COMP1204, COMP1701, VEED1004 2 18 units of level 2 topics Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Cybersecurity
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Students will gain an understanding of the issues associated with implementing and maintaining network security, and the issues of securing both wired & wireless networks. In addition, it will provide practical experience in both attacking and defending a network, and the fundamentals of cryptography as it applies to network security.

The topic is concerned with the management and security of networks. Areas covered include: cryptography concepts and applications, computer forensics, network threats, security protocols, application of security concepts in specific contexts, attack and defence mechanisms.
learning_outcomes: Analyse cryptosystems for different applications
Evaluate the security posture of an organisational network
Analyse network security threats
Design security at different levels of the OSI model
Perform and document a security assessment of an organisational network

title: Serious Games
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop engineering skills in relation to digital game projects Investigate the diversity of users, platforms, technologies and mechanics that define digital game experiences Critique existing digital game experiences across various scenarios from Indie and AAA, to games for purpose Provide appreciation for the ethical and professional issues surrounding the production, publication, distribution and use of digital games

This topic explores the use of games and game mechanics for non-entertainment purposes: serious games. The topic will present the design, development and evaluation of game artefacts for a serious purpose. Through readings, discussion and presentations, an exploration of the history, future use, motivation and benefits of serious games will be provided. An in depth investigation of the research field associated with serious games will be conducted identifying and contemplating the complex facets that define not just a video game but a serious game for change.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the ethics, nature, usage, limitations, and features of existing digital games
Generate effective team-based workflow and strategies for complex software development in relation to game development
Justify and implement the application of agile software development principles for production of interactive, digital game experiences
Critically evaluate the fields of research related to games, player experience, and purpose
Design and develop functional computer based assets for the purpose of a digital game deliverable
prerequisites: 1 1 of COMP3752, VEED2001 2 18 units of Level 3 topics Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

Construct a contingency plan that includes incident response, disaster recovery and business continuity
Compare information security management and governance frameworks for use in organisations
Explain the purpose of a range of typical business information systems

title: Advanced Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
On completion of this topic, students will have gained knowledge in: The theoretical foundations of induction in data-rich environments The algorithms commonly used in data mining The architectural frameworks commonly used in knowledge discovery Some of the legal and ethics considerations of data mining and knowledge discovery The research methods used in data mining and knowledge discovery Current research issues in data mining and knowledge discovery

Data Mining (DM) and Knowledge Discovery (KD) are concerned with the extraction of useful knowledge from large quantities of more or less structured information. With the continued growth in large data sets and the inability of manual analytical techniques to cope with such volumes, data mining algorithms and knowledge discovery processes and frameworks have emerged as potential solutions. Specifically the topic will cover: Introduction - The role of common sense, trends in information management, fundamental ideas, developing data mining algorithms, applications of knowledge discovery, future directions in DMKD. Data mining techniques - association rule mining, clustering algorithms, classification and prediction, sequential pattern mining, graph mining, text mining, higher order data mining, visualisation techniques, spatial data mining, temporal and longitudinal data mining, interestingness, web mining, ethics in data mining, knowledge discovery frameworks, research methods used in data mining and knowledge discovery.
learning_outcomes: Construct rudimentary knowledge discovery systems
Argue the merits of various research issues in the field
Understand the potential and limitations of given data mining approaches
Understand the theoretical fundamentals underpinning the field
Use common algorithms used in available systems and in the literature
Understand the ethical and legal issues involved

title: Full-Stack Web Development GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide the ability to: Architect and build complete, complex web applications in response to authentic, real-world problems using the MERN stack. Design and optimise resilient, scalable back-end systems for data management and high-performance APIs. Develop highly interactive and user-centric web interfaces in React, addressing performance and experience challenges. Implement and validate advanced security and deployment strategies for production-grade web applications.

Current web applications demand a holistic understanding of both front-end and back-end technologies to deliver effective and engaging user experiences. This topic extends beyond foundational full-stack development by embracing problem-driven learning, challenging students to tackle complex, ambiguous web development scenarios. Focusing on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React, Node.js), the course equips students with the advanced skills necessary to build dynamic, data-driven, and highly scalable web solutions. The core of this topic centres on the critical decision-making involved in designing, developing, and deploying robust web applications. Through focused research and iterative processes, students will critically evaluate technologies and justify their strategic choices in the construction of their solution. This topic emphasises not just how to build, but why specific solutions are chosen, preparing students to lead the development of complex, production-grade web applications.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise, defend and communicate complex architectural choices and project outcomes to diverse stakeholders.
Design and integrate robust, multi-layered security measures and advanced authentication protocols.
Implement scalable, resilient back-end systems, justifying design choices based on critical evaluation.
Analyse and frame complex web development problems, proposing strategic MERN stack solutions.
Evaluate the user experience and performance of interactive web interfaces using advanced React techniques.

title: Data Engineering GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop a comprehensive understanding of the data engineering lifecycle and its fundamental concepts, tools, and technologies. Enable students to design and implement scalable data pipelines using cloud-based solutions. Cultivate analytical skills to assess data usability, transformation techniques, and decision points across pipeline stages. Introduce modern data management architectures such as data lakes, data meshes, and DataOps for scalable and efficient data processing. Foster critical thinking in evaluating current data engineering practices, identifying emerging trends, and addressing associated threats and limitations. Reinforce ethical awareness by integrating data quality, privacy, and security considerations across all stages of the data engineering process.

This topic offers an in-depth exploration of the key concepts, techniques, and tools necessary for a career in data engineering. Students will gain hands-on experience in designing and implementing data architectures, building data pipelines, and applying advanced data transformation, modelling, and analytics techniques. By leveraging a modern cloud-based data management platform such as Amazon Web Services, students will learn to process and analyse large, diverse datasets efficiently and at scale. Additionally, the course emphasizes data quality, security, privacy, and ethical considerations, preparing students to tackle real-world data challenges while supporting decision-making in organizations.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast advanced data management architectures such as data lakes, data meshes, and DataOps to enable scalable and efficient data processing and analysis

Describe the stages of the data engineering pipeline and the key considerations for decision-making at each phase, including how choices in one stage influence the quality and outcomes of subsequent stages
Assess and report on the limitations and threats associated with current data engineering practices and explore emerging trends that shape the future of the field
Implement a data pipeline using a cloud-based technology
Interpret and evaluate data to determine its usability across different real-world scenarios and for various types of data consumers
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental concepts, tools, and technologies involved in the data engineering lifecycle

title: UX Fundamentals GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide: A working vocabulary to classify, examine, and interpret concepts that drive user focused software development of interactive, web-based systems Skills to develop interactive web-based systems The ability to appraise and recommend human computer interaction and user experience principles in the design and development of web-based, interactive systems Skills to evaluate the usability of a web-based solution based on human factors principles Scaffolded experience with iterative design, including user-centric evaluation and testing of features and hypotheses, allowing for rapid integration of feedback into design iterations Actionable frameworks for the design of UX evaluation procedures for interactive, web-based systems Methodological skills for experiment design, data capture, analysis and formulation of conclusions for human-computer interactions

Modern interactive software is a complex experience with a focus on the user and their needs. This topic will examine the issues associated with human factors in the design, implementation and evaluation of interactive, web-based systems. The core of the topic focuses on identifying and critiquing human factors and user experience (UX) design principles in the construction of web-based systems, acknowledging the importance of and incorporating user involvement in the design and development of engaging interactive systems for an effective user experience. The topic will cover the following material: the complexity of UX design for interactive and web-based systems, the integral nature of the user in the design and development process, the human computer interaction cycle, use of affordance and metaphor in software, application of computing and UX laws and principles, the societal, ethical and security issues associated with software design and construction. Students will explore these concepts through the use of and implementation of web technologies, including HTML, CSS, DOM, PHP, and JavaScript. Through a semi-structured, Agile approach, students will design, build, and evaluate a user-centric web solution. Utilising existing research and leveraging their own skills, students will also critically examine existing web solutions, through a UX lens.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on ethical, legal and security issues related to web applications
Practically apply user-centric, iterative design practices incorporating rapid feedback integration to implement user focused web solutions
Determine how human factor principles and system design affects usability
Appraise and utilise human factors research methods to critique web solutions
Work independently and in a team on designing, creating and maintaining applications for the web

title: Programming Fundamentals GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to help develop: An understanding of the nature of programming using a modern high-level programming languages The ability to read, comprehend and write simple programs An appreciation of the process by which software systems are developed, including their specification, design, implementation, testing and maintenance

The topic is intended as a first topic in programming for students who intend to major in computer science and for students from other disciplines who require programming skills. It aims to introduce students to the basic tools and techniques of software development using the Python programming language. The topic will cover the fundamentals of structured programming, beginning with the nature of programming, how computers process data, and the concept of algorithmic thinking as a process for solving problems. The topic will then explore foundational programming concepts as building blocks for implementing algorithms as computer programs. This includes variables and basic data structures, conditional and looping structures, functions, classes and modules, code tracing and testing, and the application of best practice readability and style conventions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate that they can use programming development environments and tools within a defined context
Demonstrate that they know the basics of code management systems for producing code within a collaborative group environment
Demonstrate that they can apply programming principles to solve domain-specific problems
Demonstrate that they know the basics of testing and debugging
Demonstrate that they can apply this understanding, knowledge, and skills within the context of professional contributions to the management of an enterprise's information space
Demonstrate that they can read pseudo-code and translate it into a readable, working program
Demonstrate that they can comprehend basic program control constructs of sequence, selection, and iteration

title: Database Modelling and Information Management GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to familiarise students with the basic concepts, fundamental structures and general techniques that are needed to define, construct and manipulate a database using a database management system (DBMS) with the main emphasis on relational DBMSs. Furthermore students should understand the concept of data models, have practical skills in data modelling using the Entity-Relationship (ER), Extend Entity-Relationship (EER) and relational data models, their diagrammatic representations, normal forms, and the Structured Query Language (SQL). In addition, students will be knowledgeable about current research trends in data modelling.

The aim of this topic is to familiarise students with the basic concepts, fundamental structures and general techniques that are needed to define, construct and manipulate a database using a Database Management System (DBMS) with the main emphasis on relational DBMSs. The topic will cover the concept of data models, basic skills in data modelling using the Entity-Relationship (ER), Extend Entity-Relationship (EER) and relational data models, their diagrammatic representations, normal forms, and the Structured Query Language (SQL).
learning_outcomes: Discuss and practise the various techniques for database system design, implementation and maintenance
Define and manipulate a relational database using SQL
Appreciate of the role of ethics in a data modelling environment and maintaining a database management system and its environment
Discuss current research trends in Data Modelling
Specify the activities that a database management system supports and describe common approaches to supplying this support
Explain the concept of data model and have basic skills in data modelling using the information (or semantics) and the relational data models

title: Neural Networks and Machine Learning GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a theoretical and practical introduction to the development and application of Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) systems. Students will understand the architectures and principles behind selected ML/DL models and gain hands-on experience in employing ML and DL techniques towards solving practical problems in a variety of domains. The scope of the topic incorporates increasingly relevant applications such as computer vision, image analysis, data science and the ethical issues associated with these. Students will also obtain skills in analytical thinking, experimental research, and effective communication within the wider context of ML.

This topic provides a thorough exploration of selected supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques with a working knowledge of Python for examples and assessment. Specific areas covered include: Data representation and feature engineering. Linear and logistic regression, K-means clustering, decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines. Methods of model evaluation and improvement Single and multi-layer neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNN), and Deep Learning systems (DL). Practical experience writing, deploying, optimising, and evaluating systems. Practical applications of machine learning systems in areas such as computer vision and image analysis.
learning_outcomes: Identify the practical and ethical constraints associated with ML systems
Conduct independent individual studies in applications of ML, extending those covered in the topic, with the level of understanding allowing for practical applications of the material
Acquire practical skills to design, implement, train and evaluate ML models including DL systems
Utilise ML and DL systems towards solving a variety of relevant real-world problems
Evaluate and analyse in a scientific manner the suitability and effectiveness of different ML techniques
Utilise principles of ML and understand its capabilities and limitations

title: Advanced Software Development Practices GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to give students a sound understanding of program design, implementation and testing in a team and individual context. It provides essential knowledge for IT professionals

This topic is intended as a second course in programming for students who have completed an introductory Java programming topic such as COMP8702. It aims to extend and consolidate programming skills acquired in the introductory topic and to introduce methods that assist in the design, and implementation of applications. The primary foci of the topic are developing software that conform to a specification and the pragmatics of the assembly, configuration, deployment, and revision control, in an individual and team context.
learning_outcomes: Choose the best tools that support application development and understand how to use them
Demonstrate knowledge of the various areas of application development
Critically evaluate application development techniques
Collaborate within a team to produce reliable software to a specification
Possess fundamental programming skills including the use of commonly used parts of APIs

title: Computer Mathematics GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic builds a solid discrete mathematics and logic foundation for an IT professional.

The main themes of this topic are logic and proof, induction and recursion, discrete structures, algorithms and their analysis, and applications. Mathematical reasoning, combinatorial analysis and algorithmic thinking are carefully blended and balanced to provide students with skills and knowledge necessary for a successful career in science and technology.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and construct valid mathematical arguments - proofs - and understand mathematical statements - theorems
Conduct independent individual studies in discrete mathematics areas, extending those covered in the topic, with the level of understanding allowing for practical applications of the material
Utilise important discrete date structures such as sets, relations, discrete functions, graphs and trees
Understand and apply formal logic system on which mathematical reasoning is based
Understand the importance of formal mathematical structures and techniques for computing applications
Use various problem-solving strategies including algorithmic thinking (both iterative and recursive) and various counting techniques to create appropriate solutions to computing problems

title: Data Structures and Algorithms GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with the skills needed to solve programming problems of moderate complexity, such as applications that provide an interface to real-world data. The focus is on object-oriented techniques for representing and manipulating program data using either predefined components or custom-designed components.

This topic provides a second-level exploration of programming, with an emphasis on the data structures that frequently occur in programming problems and the algorithms for traversing and manipulating such structures. The syllabus is built around the theme of data abstraction using object- oriented programming. Specific areas covered include: Basic data representations, including arrays, records, and strings Key object-oriented computational techniques, including exception handlers, inheritance, recursion Fundamental linked data structures such as lists, stacks, trees, and graphs, together with the operations for manipulating them Algorithmic strategies, including brute force, divide-and-conquer, and branch-and-bound approaches An introduction to algorithmic analysis, including complexity classes and an appreciation for space-time trade-offs Fundamental computing algorithms, including a variety of common searching, sorting, and traversal algorithms
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of data structures and algorithms to compare, evaluate and choose among candidate solutions for specific problems
Discuss key concepts related to: fundamental data structures, searching and sorting algorithms, object-oriented programming, data abstraction and recursion
Write programs in an object-oriented programming language that use appropriate data structures and algorithms to solve complex problems
Critically evaluate academic literature related to specific aspects of data structures and algorithms
Analyse the time and space complexity of algorithms to evaluate their performance
Conduct an empirical investigation into the properties of different data structures and algorithms and report on the findings
