title: Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a short overview of several fundamental areas within Artificial Intelligence (AI). Students will gain a greater understanding of the theoretical, mathematical, and algorithmic principles behind several AI techniques, along with an appreciation for how modern AI tools are being applied to solve real-world problems. Students will also gain hands-on experience applying the skills and techniques learned to solve practical-based AI tasks across a variety of industry relevant domains. Students will also obtain skills in critical thinking, analytical research, and effective communication of ideas within the wider context of AI.

This topic provides the core fundamentals necessary for many areas within artificial intelligence. This includes both theoretical knowledge and practical skills necessary to form a comprehensive understanding of modern artificial intelligence techniques and applications. Specific areas covered include: Algorithm Design , including how to interpret/write pseudocode and analyse the complexity of different algorithmic processes. Search and Planning, including how to define problems in terms of states and actions, and apply appropriate exploration and decision-making algorithms. Artificial Life , including how natural systems and biological process can be used to inform and enhance AI development. Knowledge Representation and Reasoning , including how information about the world can be formalised in a manner that allows for automated reasoning to answer complex questions. Data Analysis , including how to collect, analyse and interpret real-world data to extract meaning and make predictions. Generative AI , including an explanation of the techniques behind recent generative AI advancements and a discussion of the ethical considerations they present to modern society.
learning_outcomes: Write, interpret and contrast basic searching, sorting and planning algorithms presented in pseudo-code form
Survey, evaluate and discuss a selection of emerging AI technologies
Explore the capabilities, limitations and ethical considerations of modern generative AI techniques
Examine how knowledge can be represented in a formalised manner that allows for autonomous reasoning
Analyse large-scale datasets to extract meaning and make useful predictions
Implement Artificial Life (ALife) algorithms that simulate natural processes and genetic evolution

title: Human Factors for Interactive and Web-Based Systems GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: A working vocabulary to classify, examine, and interpret concepts that drive user focused software development of interactive, web-based systems Skills to develop web-based systems across the full stack deployment environment Skills to critique and apply suitable human factors research methods Scaffolded experience with iterative design, including user-centric evaluation and testing of features and hypotheses, allowing for rapid integration of feedback into design iterations Actionable frameworks for the design of UX evaluation procedures for interactive, web-based systems Methodological skills for experiment design, data capture, analysis and formulation of conclusions for human-computer interactions

Modern interactive software is a complex experience with a focus on the user and their needs. This topic will examine the issues associated with human factors in the design, implementation and evaluation of interactive, web-based systems. The core of the topic focuses on identifying and critiquing human factors and user experience (UX) design principles in the construction of web-based systems, acknowledging the importance of and incorporating user involvement in the design and development of engaging interactive systems for an effective user experience. The topic will cover the following material: the complexity of UX design for interactive and web-based systems, the integral nature of the user in the design and development process, the human computer interaction cycle, use of affordance and metaphor in software, application of computing and UX laws and principles, the societal, ethical and security issues associated with software design and construction. Students will explore these concepts through the use of and implementation of web technologies, including HTML, CSS, DOM, PHP, and Javascript. The importance of the user in the design of web-based systems will be consolidated with contemporary research into human factors methods. Development processes will apply the client-centric design principles with rapid integration of client feedback into iterative development processes. As such, you will engage with practical applications of principles and practices that elucidate the inclusion of the feedback cycles within the design and deployment of client focused, web-based, software systems.
learning_outcomes: Appraise human factors research methods for consideration in the planning of user-centric design practices
Practically apply user-centric, iterative design practices incorporating rapid feedback integration
Prepare, conduct and evaluate user experience experiments for interactive, web-based systems
Reflect on ethical, legal and security issues related to web applications
Work independently and in a team on designing, creating and maintaining applications for the web
Determine how human factor principles and system design affects usability
Communicate effectively, using technical language with other IT professionals
Implement user focused software solutions through the effective inclusion of users in the design and development process

title: Cloud and Distributed Computing GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
By the end of this topic, students will understand the core concepts of cloud computing and its building blocks. They will dive into the structure and functionality of various cloud services (IaaS, SaaS, PaaS, DaaS) and explore the different deployment models, infrastructure components (such as virtualisation, networking, and storage), and performance metrics, including scalability, availability, and cost. An integral part of the topic will be cloud risk management and governance, allowing students to critically analyse the challenges and best practices associated with secure and efficient cloud operations. Students will also develop proficiency with leading public cloud platforms and their APIs, acquiring practical skills in deploying cloud services tailored to specific use cases. This topic requires students to analyse a real-world problem, design a solution, and implement it on a public cloud platform, fostering their ability to create scalable and robust cloud solutions. Additionally, the topic will cover emerging trends and issues in cloud computing, preparing students to stay updated in this rapidly evolving field. This focus on current advancements ensures that students engage with both the present applications and the future direction of cloud technology.

This topic covers both foundational and advanced aspects of cloud computing, aiming to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of its key components and applications. Students will explore core cloud services—Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Software as a Service (SaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Desktop as a Service (DaaS)—as well as various deployment models such as private, public, and hybrid clouds. The topic will address essential cloud infrastructure elements, including virtualisation, networking, and storage, alongside critical aspects of cloud security architecture, risk management strategies, and cloud governance. Students will also study performance metrics such as scalability, availability, and cost-effectiveness, which are essential for evaluating cloud solutions. This topic emphasises hands-on experience with publicly available cloud platforms and their key Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Additionally, students will examine emerging trends and challenges within the field, including security risks, governance issues, and the evolving landscape of cloud technologies. Through practical exercises, students will gain experience in deploying cloud solutions for various use cases, allowing them to connect theory with practice in real-world cloud applications.
learning_outcomes: Understand the issues associated with Cloud Governance and Management
Evaluate and assess the business and technical benefits of cloud computing for a real-world use case
Appraise cloud computing models from a security and privacy perspective. Develop cloud risk management strategies in considering these appraisals
Research and critically evaluate emerging trends, solutions and issues in cloud computing
Select, analyse and assess the performance metrics of cloud deployment models for application use cases
Design and deploy a cloud solution for a real-world use case over a public cloud platform
Discuss the core concepts of cloud computing, compare cloud services, evaluate deployment models and infrastructure
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MCS-Master of Computer Science 1a Admission into MCSFP-Master of Computer Science - Flinders City Campus 1b Admission into MDSC-Master of Data Science 1c Admission into MDSCFP-Master of Data Science - Flinders City Campus 1d Admission into GCC-Graduate Certificate in Cybersecurity 1e Admission into MAIDSC-Master of Artificial Intelligence, Data Science and Cybersecurity 2 ENGR8762 3 36 units of topics Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e) or (2 and 3))

title: DevOps and Enterprise Systems Project
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: The ability to appreciate the principles of DevOps and their application to the development and deployment of enterprise systems The ability to explain and discuss the roles of stakeholders and tools within DevOps The skills to set-up a DevOps project environment The practical skills to use DevOps tools to automate integration, testing, and deployment An understanding of the importance of collaboration and automation in cross-functional process implementation

DevOps is the outcome of applying Lean principles to the IT value stream to accelerate flow of work through Product Management, Development, Test, Deployment, IT Operations, and Information Security. This approach removes the boundaries between teams and brings all stakeholders together to work on the same goal of quickly provide enterprise IT solutions with stability, reliability, availability, and security. Building on the skills you have developed throughout your degree, this project-based topic will cover the following material: the need for effective cross-functional workflow management in enterprise system development and deployment, the philosophy and practicality of DevOps methodology, theory and practice of continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD), task and sprint management, managing source code, managing release and deployment pipeline, recording and tagging of tests against releases, as well as the DevOps tools that enable cross-functional process automation and stakeholder collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Develop and automate functional testing, load/performance testing, and regression testing
Manage a project utilising agile methodology supported by DevOps tools
Construct a CI/CD pipeline utilising DevOps tools
Explain the process, stages, roles and importance of the DevOps methodology
Apply change management best practices
Collaborate more effectively with other stakeholders
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MIT-Master of Information Technology 1a Admission into MITNCS-Master of Information Technology (Network and Cybersecurity Systems) 1b Admission into MITFP-Master of Information Technology - Flinders City Campus 1c Admission into MITNCSFP-Master of Information Technology (Network and Cybersecurity Systems) - Flinders City Campus 1d Admission into MDSC-Master of Data Science 1e Admission into MDSCFP-Master of Data Science - Flinders City Campus 2 54 units of topics Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e) and 2)

title: ICT Management and Professional Standards
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic will require students to apply concepts of the governance and management of ICT projects and organisations, with particular emphasis on analysing large industry, complex, and/or interdisciplinary projects. It includes application of the management frameworks, the tools used and challenges faced, in contemporary ICT operations and modern industry programs through project-based work. Professional standards including those expected by professional bodies are also covered.

This topic employs a cross-disciplinary approach to build the technical competence and business acumen to manage large-scale ICT projects and the governance issues of project teams within ICT organisations. It presents professional ICT practices as related to project management in regulatory environments. It focuses on building knowledge, skills, and competencies in business model innovation and project management including scheduling of tasks as well as the management of scope, resources, risk, quality, communication and cost. Relevant industrial trends as well as professional standards, intellectual property and ICT legal issues in the context of ICT management are addressed.
learning_outcomes: Communicate with project stakeholders effectively and professionally
Gather and analyse information and data to determine the principal internal and external aspects affecting ICT governance, management and practice

Analyse and evaluate the responsibilities, roles, attitudes, values, priorities, judgement and work methods of practising professional ICT managers and be able to enact the ACS Code of Professional Conduct
Synthesise the nature of ICT projects and the manner in which they are initiated, planned and managed
Apply management and engineering practices, methods, and tools to successfully manage the life cycle of innovative ICT projects in engineering and technology organisations
Efficaciously create joint innovation and project results in teams
Critically review the relevant literature or data to identify a key project management issue, and take the first steps to analyse and resolve the issue

title: Masters Research Thesis (4.5/18 units)
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
On completion of this topic, students will be able to: Develop an understanding of the open research issues in a given area of investigation Further develop analytical and critical thinking skills appropriate to research Further develop technical skills relevant to the given area of investigation Further develop high level writing and communication skills through the writing of reports including a final thesis and the delivery of presentations related to the thesis Develop project management skills appropriate to research-oriented investigation

The masters thesis is intended to promote the development of research capability including communication and technical skills through an in-depth investigation of a particular area under the guidance of a supervisor. The project is not merely a large system-building exercise. Rather, the principle objective is for students to show initiative, acquire new knowledge, develop basic research skills and develop insight in assimilating and critically evaluating ideas. The nature of the investigation will depend on the project itself but is likely to include a literature search, the identification (in collaboration with the supervisor) of a suitable project, the planning and management of the project, the execution of the plan resulting indefensible results, the development and presentation of results and the production of a thesis embodying the methods and results of the project. Other aspects which may be included in some projects include liaison with other researchers, industry practitioners and/or the community, either working on similar projects or with expertise required for the project.
learning_outcomes: Write a research thesis that presents complex arguments with rigour and conviction, recognising with critical appraisal the circumstances through which data were obtained
Develop and effectively deliver clear and coherent presentations to a diverse audience, and critically evaluate, respond to, and reflect on other views and/or arguments

Demonstrate comprehensive understanding of discipline fundamentals, research principles and methodologies, together with a deep understanding of specialist knowledge and familiarity with the research agenda for a particular area

Exercise initiative and critical thinking in developing and executing a research program with a degree of intellectual independence, demonstrating competency in applying principles and utilising specialist tools or skills relevant to the profession
Critically review and consolidate existing knowledge, analyse alternatives, and synthesise established approaches, appropriately adapted to develop new understanding in a particular research domain
prerequisites: 31.5 units of study

title: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
On completion of this topic, students will be able to: Investigate the theoretical foundations underpinning inductive reasoning in data‑intensive, heterogeneous, and dynamic environments, critically evaluating formalisms and their implications for generalisation, robustness, and interpretability. Demonstrate understanding of advanced and emerging data-mining algorithms, including the ability to adapt or innovate methods, assess comparative performance under complex real‑world constraints, and justify choices using rigorous theoretical and empirical evidence. Design, evaluate, and operationalise knowledge discovery architectures that incorporate data governance, model lifecycle management, and deployment into coherent, scalable, and reproducible pipelines. Evaluate ethical, legal, and professional principles within data mining contexts, incorporating stakeholder engagement and impact assessment alongside privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, and compliance requirements. Analyse, critique, and implement advanced data mining research methodologies to produce reproducible and rigorous studies. Critically engage with the research frontier, analysing innovations, unresolved challenges, and emerging debates, and articulating their implications for future technological, theoretical, and policy developments in data‑driven knowledge discovery.

The ability to critically evaluate, adapt, and extend advanced data mining and knowledge discovery methods is essential in the modern data‑driven world. This topic builds research‑level expertise in the theoretical foundations, advanced algorithms, and architectural frameworks of modern knowledge discovery. Students will design and validate scalable, reproducible pipelines that integrate data governance, feature engineering, and robust evaluation under realistic operational constraints. Ethical, legal, and professional considerations are embedded throughout the topic, alongside critical engagement with current and emerging research. Theory, innovation, and applied practice are united in this topic preparing students to innovate in the design and application of data‑driven systems that address complex challenges with real‑world impact
learning_outcomes: Architect, implement, and validate scalable end‑to‑end knowledge discovery pipelines that incorporate data governance, model management, monitoring, and risk controls for operational contexts
Selecting and adapting data mining algorithms from contemporary systems and literature, extending and comparing alternatives with rigorous, statistically sound evaluation under real‑world constraints
Critically analyse and argue the merits of current research directions and open problems in data mining and knowledge discovery, discussing the implications for practice, policy, and future research

Critically evaluate data mining and knowledge discovery approaches in complex challenging contexts, integrating ethical, legal, professional, and stakeholder perspectives with impact assessment, and justify responsive methodological and governance choices
Integrate the theoretical foundations of data mining algorithms to develop principled modelling and evaluation strategies, demonstrated through high‑quality analysis and implementation
Produce reproducible empirical data mining and knowledge discovery studies that achieve a substantive contribution and convey uncertainty and limitations to diverse audiences
prerequisites: 1 COMP8031 2 Admission into MCSAI-Master of Computer Science (Artificial Intelligence) 2a Admission into BENGRHMEEE-Bachelor of Engineering (Robotics) (Honours), Master of Engineering (Electrical and Electronic) Must satisfy: (1 or (2 or 2a))

title: Advanced Algorithms and Programming GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with the skills needed to solve complex programming problems, such as applications that provide an interface to real-world data. The focus is on object-oriented techniques for representing and manipulating program data using either predefined components or custom-designed components.

This topic is intended for students who have completed several courses in programming, with some background in object-oriented programming. It covers the development of solutions to complex problems based on complex algorithms involving many, possibly distributed, components in complex structures.
learning_outcomes: Make use of APIs that support the computational models used in the topic
Determine the time and space complexity of complex algorithms
Research, apply and evaluate complex algorithms on real-world problems
Develop programs that solve complex problems using a range of computational models
Analyse complex problems and develop algorithmic solutions

title: Information Security GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topic provides an overview of cyber security and information security and their application to managing and securing information systems and technology. There is an emphasis on contemporary techniques and technologies. The topic develops student skills in preparing and presenting technical reports on information management and computer security.

Information security combines technical control and a managerial approach to protecting information systems. The topic provides a comprehensive overview of cyber security and information security programs. Examining current and emerging technologies, addressing contemporary challenges and ethical issues, and introducing cryptography, physical security, and digital forensics are core to this topic's learning.
learning_outcomes: Analyse security risks and select appropriate security controls
Illustrate the importance of cyber security and information security to business and government
Examine the security issues associated with the integration of information systems
Research and critically analyse publications and industry guidelines in the area of computer security
Design industry professional reports on organisational cyber security and information security programs
Analyse the threats and common attacks faced by organisations
prerequisites: 1 36 units of topics 2 31.5 units of topics 3 COMP9812 Must satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3))

title: Theory and Practice of Computation GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
To be able to specify and implement algorithms in an appropriate paradigm with an understanding of how to estimate what performance (efficacy and efficiency) can be expected and what resources will be required To understand and be able to employ Logic Programming, Functional Programming, Object Oriented Programming and von Neumann (Procedural Programming) paradigms To be able to set up, carry out and appropriately report on theoretical and practical evaluation (analysis and benchmarking) of computer routines and use this information to improve the performance of a program To be able to write clear portable code that is independent on machine, language and compiler dependencies To develop an ability to work alone both in a team, including to integrate work and build extensible systems, and to negotiate an ethical solution acceptable to a diverse range of stakeholders To understand and be able to work with the formalisms of the theory of computations and be able to approach research papers in this area or that assume a basic knowledge of theory of computation

This topic is concerned with the concepts and mechanisms that underlie modern programming languages as well as providing insights into the capabilities and limitations of languages, computers and algorithms. The topic combines both theoretical foundations and practical demonstrations of issues relating to programming and algorithm design. It teaches fundamental skills necessary to selection of an appropriate programming paradigm for a problem, whilst highlighting the distinct and overlapping capabilities of three families of programming languages. The topic examines concepts such as types, variables, binding, abstraction, parameterization, encapsulation, generics, polymorphism, inheritance, recursion, iteration, formal languages, automata, logic, proof, decidability, computability and complexity. It uses as vehicles for illustration and exploration multiple languages supporting a variety of programming paradigms, including the procedural, functional, object-oriented and logic programming paradigms. The topic has an emphasis on design and evaluation of efficient, efficacious programs, including analysis and benchmarking of programs, with close integration of the theoretical and practical components, and workshops to assist in application of theory.
learning_outcomes: Understand the concept of paradigms and the effect of language, paradigm, data structure on the design of algorithms

Have demonstrated experience and expertise in logical, functional and hybrid paradigms of programming and system development, along with familiarity with a broad range of languages and styles that are knowledge, rule and logic based rather than depending on low level step by step instructions

Have a deep theoretical understanding of computability and complexity capable of being applied practically in assessing the requirements of a proposed system and analysing the performance of an implemented system
Utilize concepts from one paradigm in a language or context associated with another paradigm, choosing the most appropriate paradigm for the job
Have an advanced understanding and familiarity with the broad range of programming languages, paradigms and libraries/APIs
prerequisites: 1 1 of COMP8741, COMP8801 2 31.5 units of study Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Computer Game Development GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with: The skills to create digital games The ability to critique the complexity of structure and processes associated with a real-time, user driven, interactive system The techniques to relate framework principles in the examination of commercial digital games An appreciation of the history and trends of computer games, their development, and the industry The skills to construct a complete game production life cycle, from concept to deployment, within an Agile development framework Interpreting research findings in the field of serious games and learning theory and their application to develop games for purpose

This topic provides a thorough exploration of the field of computer game development, including the design, project management and development of complex, digital, interactive, player-centric experiences. Specific areas will include: Examining the architecture of computer games through various perspectives – design, play, and society Practical experience in the design and implementation of game mechanics, rules, objects and interactions Practical experience working with industry game development engines and the implementation languages Practical application of Agile game development principles across the breadth of the project Investigating the history of computer games and their development Incorporating contemporary learning theory research and game design for non-entertainment purposes in the development of serious games
learning_outcomes: Critique existing research publications in the domain of serious games
Develop design materials, computer-based solutions and digital media artefacts appropriate for serious game applications
Work professionally as an individual and in a team
Design and execute the project management life cycle components for an Agile game development project
Incorporate mechanics, aesthetics, narrative, and technology in the production of digital media artefacts
Develop a functional serious game
prerequisites: 1 Admission into MIT-Master of Information Technology 2 36 units of topics 3 Admission into GDPCSC-Graduate Diploma in Computer Science 3a Admission into MCS-Master of Computer Science 3b Admission into MCSAI-Master of Computer Science (Artificial Intelligence) Must Satisfy: ((1 and 2) or ((3 or 3a or 3b)))

title: Artificial Intelligence GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Educational aims of the topic: To be able to specify, consult, deploy and implement intelligent software and systems To understand and be able to employ Logic Programming, Knowledge Engineering and Knowledge Discovery paradigms and frameworks To be able assess requirements and select or adapt appropriate methodologies, techniques and tools for the achievement of a task, including through interviewing personnel and reviewing literature To be able to communicate with non-computing specialists and interdisciplinary specialists in the design of intelligent systems, learning paradigms or data mining applications To develop an ability to work alone both in a team, including to integrate work and build extensible systems, and to negotiate an ethical solution acceptable to a diverse range of stakeholders To understand and be able to work with the formalisms of the artificial intelligence, machine learning and formal grammars, and be able to approach research papers in this area or that assume a basic knowledge theoretical background

This topic will provide a basic understanding of Intelligent Systems and their applications, including a basic understanding and broad overview of Artificial Intelligence and Heuristic Search methodologies, and supervised and unsupervised Machine Learning and Data Mining technologies. The topic provides a balance of theory and practice, with two lectures on theory or philosophy being complemented by seminar-style case studies on specific applications, including guest speakers. Practical work is largely undertaken and assessed in weekly computing laboratory sessions, with a variety of assignments including specification, programming and written tasks. Specific areas to be covered include methodologies and philosophical issues, the relationship of intelligent systems to human intelligence and cognitive science, applications to knowledge engineering, knowledge discovery, language processing, text and data mining, as well as selected topics relating to cognition, perception, visualization and classification/clustering.
learning_outcomes: Understand the mathematical and theoretical foundations to deal with the broad range of intelligent systems, applications and literature, including producing and critiquing proposals and reports appropriate to the field
Become adept at styles of programming and system development that are knowledge, rule and logic based rather than depending on low level step by step instructions

Develop a deep insight into the power of heuristics and tricks and the human propensities that make for a good or a bad interface, and that either easily convince the user into accepting behaviour as human or conversely irk the user as being somehow inhuman
Understand concept of heuristics and be able to develop, design and prove desired properties of intelligent systems and developing learning and mining algorithms
Weigh up the complex interactions among human factors, personal and team relationships and ethical considerations and risks that affect the design and employment of intelligent systems
Achieve substantial and surprisingly complex and intelligent behaviours in simple programs and systems

title: Cybersecurity GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Students will gain an understanding of the issues associated with implementing and maintaining network security, and the issues of securing both wired & wireless networks. In addition, it will provide practical experience in both attacking and defending a network, and the fundamentals of cryptography as it applies to network security. Students will also report on current and emerging trends and issues in network security.

The topic is concerned with the management and security of networks. Areas covered include: cryptography concepts and applications, computer forensics, security assessment, network threats, security protocols, application of security concepts in specific contexts, attack and defence mechanisms, current and emerging security research topics.
learning_outcomes: Design security at different levels of the OSI model
Analyse cryptosystems for different network applications
Critically evaluate Network Security Threats
Research and critically evaluate the emerging cyber threats and mitigation techniques for traditional and emerging networks
Perform and document a security assessment of an organisational network
Evaluate the security posture of an organisational network and propose mitigations techniques

title: Systems Software GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the fundamentals ofsystems software and operating systems Illustrate the relationship betweensystems software, operating systems and process management Demonstrate how the operating system manages security requirements Provide students with a hands-on working knowledge of systems software functions, configuration and management Provide students with a good understanding of how systems software works to control the functionality of computing technologies

This topic introduces the fundamentals of systems software and operating system design concepts and management together with the basics of security and an appreciation of the issues involved in the design and implementation of systems software. Areas of learning include: an overview of systems software, operating systems, evolution of modern operating systems, real-time and embedded systems, central processing unit, drivers, interrupts, kernel, file systems, storage devices, virtualisation, processes, threads, concurrency, memory management, scheduling, basic shell scripting, command-line commands, network fundamentals, account management, resource management and security.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and justify approaches to core systems architectures and algorithms across varied applications.
Produce structured artefacts and documentation that justify IT management decisions, such as in the context of disaster recovery, business proposals, and vendor evaluations.
Synthesise literature, theory, and practice to propose and justify solutions to complex systems and/or IT management challenges.
Select and apply systems tools, including virtualisation and performance monitoring, to assess performance and explain observed behaviour using theoretical concepts and empirical reasoning.
Demonstrate proficient use of command line interfaces, including implementing shell scripts to automate multistep tasks.

title: Academic and Professional Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with the necessary skills for reading and thinking critically and writing effectively by: Analysing and evaluating academic texts Cultivating awareness of audience, context and purpose in writing tasks Developing rhetorical skills relevant to academic contexts at Flinders University Engaging in texts from a range of disciplines

This is a foundation topic with the broad aim of enabling students to recognise and use an appropriate style of communication in academic settings related to various fields within university study. The basic premise of the topic is that effective writing is contingent on critical thinking, reading and writing. You will be exposed to a variety of texts to encourage you to critically evaluate and write about issues from multiple perspectives before you develop your own arguments. The need to consider the rhetorical situation and ethical issues is emphasised as you go through the process of planning, writing, and critically revising your own texts based on feedback. The topic is designed specifically for the needs of Flinders University students in order to transition to university studies and many of the texts and study topics are directly related to your studies at the university to aid successful progression in your university education.
learning_outcomes: Produce academic texts appropriate to a disciplinary audience
Develop and deliver presentations on an academic topic
Identify and critically evaluate credible sources
Develop an academic learning strategy by selecting and completing activities to enhance academic communication skills and critically reflect on learning progress

title: Digital and Social Media
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
To develop a comprehensive understanding of social media's evolution, impact, and strategic use in contemporary digital communication. This topic aims to equip students with the analytical skills to critically examine social media platforms, evaluate their societal implications, and apply professional auditing techniques to assess brand presence in the digital landscape.

This topic provides students with a multi-faceted understanding of social media platforms, their development, and their role in shaping modern society and business practices.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate ethical, cultural, and regulatory challenges in professional social media practice
Design a social media content calendar informed by audit findings and platform data
Analyse contemporary social media ecosystems using platform data, audience insights, and industry trends

title: Digital Communication Fundamentals
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the basic principles and theories of digital communication Familiarise students with common digital communication platforms and tools Develop fundamental skills in digital content creation and curation Raise awareness of ethical considerations and best practices in digital communication Prepare students for entry-level roles in digital communication and content creation

This topic introduces students to the fundamental concepts and practices of digital communication in the modern world. It explores the evolution of digital platforms, their impact on personal and professional communication, and the basic skills required to navigate the digital landscape effectively. The course is designed to provide students with a practical understanding of digital communication tools, content creation, and ethical considerations in the digital realm.
learning_outcomes: Conduct social media audit
Analyse the historical development and current landscape of social media platforms
Critically evaluate the ethical implications and societal impacts of social media usage, including issues of privacy and misinformation

title: Crisis Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the ability to: Analyze the communication-driven actions and behaviours associated with organisations Critically evaluate decisions made in communicating about and managing a crisis Analyze ethical factors in organisational communication Understand best practices in crisis and reputation management Understand the causes of misunderstanding and miscommunication in organisational contexts and be prepared to avoid them

This topic provides students with principles and theories of crisis communication in organisatons. It examines the function of communication in professional settings, through analysis of case studies and real world situations and explores the role of different strategies and media in completing successful crisis management projects in a range of organisations. These explorations may include study of public relations campaigns, reputation management, and strategic leadership practices.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate their own role in a professional setting
Analyse strengths and weakness of their chosen project
Apply techniques and skills acquired in the degree in a professional context
Communicate issues related to their industry context, both verbally and in writing
prerequisites: 9 units of Level 1 topics

title: Transmedia & Cross-Platform Communication: Analysis of “Stranger Things”
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
Through this topic, we aspire to: Facilitate a comprehensive understanding of transmedia narrative techniques and principles. Foster the ability to critically analyse and utilise the power of storytelling in digital communication. Develop practical skills for content creation across various platforms. Inculcate ethical considerations in the execution of digital campaigns.

Understand how stories spread across platforms using Stranger Things as your case study. Explore content strategies for streaming, gaming, and social that connect with real audiences. Learn transmedia storytelling principles, ethical engagement, and the tools creators use. Analyse narratives that work across TikTok, Instagram, Netflix, and beyond in today's digital landscape
learning_outcomes: Analyse the principles of transmedia narrative and multimedia storytelling in practical scenarios
Apply transmedia storytelling techniques to develop multimedia narratives
Apply ethical considerations in digital communication
Develop digital content that resonates with various audience segments
Implement the effective use of different platforms for optimal content distribution

title: Emerging Communication Technologies: AI, Blockchain and more
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The comprehensive topic at hand calls upon students to grasp the multifaceted nature of advanced communication technologies that shape our contemporary world. To complement the learning outcomes, the course pursues the following aims: Insightful Exploration: The course aims to unravel each layer of advanced communication technologies, examining their inner workings, foundational principles, and distinctive characteristics. Real-world examples will assist students in visualising complicated concepts, thus fostering a comprehensive understanding. Contextual Analysis: We strive to cultivate an atmosphere of critical thinking. Students will be encouraged to dissect the myriad implications of these technologies across various contexts and industries. This includes the evaluation of potential benefits, the consideration of societal impact, and the anticipation of future trends. Practical Application: A central aim is to ensure that theoretical knowledge transcends the classroom. Accordingly, interactive assignments and group projects have been designed to encourage students to conceptualise and implement innovative uses for the examined technologies. This will serve as an opportunity for students to apply their understanding in a hands-on environment, harnessing their creativity in the process. Ethical Orientation: As we stride forward in this digital age, ethical concerns regarding technology adoption have become increasingly prominent. This course aspires to instil a value-driven perspective among students. Emphasizing responsible decision-making, we will engage in potent discussions regarding the ethical considerations of using emerging technologies.

In the ever-evolving terrain of digital communication, new technologies frequently surface, altering the way we interact and share information. The focus of this topic is to provide students with a robust understanding of these emerging technologies, allowing them to remain at the forefront of the communications industry. Through theoretical knowledge and practical applications, students will explore new platforms, tools, and trends, shaping the future of digital communication. This topic embarks on a journey through the revolutionary landscape of emerging communication technologies. We will examine and interact with influential developments like AI, Blockchain, Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), the Metaverse, and Digital Twinning. Every step of the way, we aim to illuminate the profound effects these technologies offer today and envision their immense potential for the future.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge into practice through innovative uses of adopted technologies
Demonstrate an understanding of emerging communication technologies
Describe ethical considerations in the adoption of emerging technologies
Critically analyse the implications of these technologies in various contexts and industries

title: e-Portfolio
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
Industry Readiness: Equip students with the skills and confidence to create a professional digital ePortfolio that reflects their capabilities and prepares them for entry into the digital communication industry. Professional Identity: Support students in articulating their unique professional narrative through curated content, design, and multimedia integration. Reflective Practice: Encourage critical reflection on academic and professional experiences to foster self-awareness and continuous improvement. Peer Collaboration: Promote constructive peer feedback and iterative development to enhance the quality and relevance of the final ePortfolio.

In today’s dynamic media landscape, the ability to curate and present a compelling digital identity is essential for emerging communication professionals. This topic empowers students to design and develop a professional ePortfolio that showcases their skills, experiences, and personal brand within the field of digital communication. Through a combination of practical workshops, reflective exercises, and peer collaboration, students will explore the strategic use of digital platforms to communicate their academic and professional journey. The ePortfolio serves not only as a tool for career readiness but also as a space for critical self-reflection and creative expression. Students will learn to integrate multimedia elements, articulate their professional narrative, and apply design principles to create a visually engaging and purposeful online presence. By the end of the topic, students will have a fully developed ePortfolio that demonstrates their readiness to engage with industry, clients, and collaborators in a digitally fluent and professional manner.
learning_outcomes: Engage in peer review and incorporate feedback to refine and improve the final presentation of their ePortfolio
Curate content that communicates their professional identity, including bios, résumés, work samples, and credentials
Apply design principles to ensure the ePortfolio is visually engaging, user-friendly, and suitable for professional contexts
Design and build a professional ePortfolio that effectively showcases their academic achievements, creative work, and industry-relevant skills
Integrate multimedia elements (e.g., images, videos, infographics) to enhance the visual impact and storytelling of their portfolio

title: Workplace Experience in Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with the opportunity to explore ways in which skills and knowledge acquired through their study are applied in workplace scenarios Develop the vocabulary to communicate how their skills and knowledge are valuable to employers Assist students in identifying a career path and beginning the transition from study to employment Expose students to current practices in one area of the communication industries

This topic provides students with the opportunity to undertake a workplace-based project, or work placement, in an area related to one of their fields of study. Through this, students will have the opportunity to examine how the skills and knowledge they have acquired through the degree can be applied to work place scenarios. The precise nature of each placement is to be developed in conjunction with the topic coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the strengths and weakness of the placement, both professionally and academically
Assess how your study has prepared you for a pathway to employment
Integrate contemporary themes and issues in communication studies, and present these to a range of audiences
Adapt and combine skills and knowledge acquired during your degree to a workplace setting
prerequisites: 9 units of Level 2 topics

title: AI for Workplace Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to learn how to use generative AI productively and ethically for professional communication in your discipline or field of study, and how to use AI to enhance your writing and communication practice.

In this topic, you will take your communication skills to the next level by exploring the role of generative AI in various professional and industry-specific workplace contexts. You will learn how to use AI tools productively, critically and ethically to support a range of communication tasks including drafting emails, setting meeting agendas, summarising documents, producing outputs, and writing proposals. This topic also examines the ethical use of AI in professional environments, including authorship, data privacy, bias, and accountability. Here, you will apply prompt engineering strategies to critically review and evaluate AI-produced communication, interpreting its purpose, audience, and revising these for professional appropriateness. This topic emphasises collaboration, reflective practice and the use of AI as a tool for problem solving and communication enhancement in your discipline.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective, ethical and audience-appropriate communication skills
Deliver a presentation and demonstration to showcase the efficacy of an industry-specific AI-supported solution
Produce a professional pitch for an industry-specific proposal
Write a consultancy report that applies AI tools to address an industry-specific problem

title: Student Led Agency A
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to encourage students to apply digital innovation principles in a practical context, thereby gaining: An appreciation of the dynamic nature of the digital industry An understanding of how digital tools and strategies can address practical business challenges Proficiency in leveraging digital solutions to drive business outcomes The ability to work collaboratively within a team to solve complex problems

This topic provides students with a thorough understanding of the role of digital communications in the current industry landscape. Through a student-led agency model, participants will engage directly with industry projects, applying digital strategies and tools to solve real-world challenges. The topic aims to not only enhance students' knowledge of digital technologies but also to cultivate leadership, project management, and creative problem-solving skills. This will facilitate the application of students' digital proficiencies to develop, implement, and assess a genuine industry project. Over this topic, students will be immersed in a collaborative venture, working with a prominent industry partner to realise a comprehensive digital communications campaign. Prior to commencement, the topic coordinator will engage with the industry partner to draft a proposal, which will articulate the aims and objectives of the project, alongside the necessary competencies required for successful result. Engagement with the industry partner and the topic coordinator will be integral from the outset, as it will inform the scope of work and ensure alignment with student capability and learning outcomes. This topic is designed to iterate the practical application of theoretical knowledge, ensuring participants emerge with a holistic understanding of the digital communications campaign lifecycle. Upon completion of the project, students will deliver a capstone presentation to the industry partner and academic faculty, detailing the campaign, its outcomes, and the knowledge gained through this immersive experience. Throughout this professionally valuable journey, students are expected to express initiative, engage in critical dialogue, and contribute constructively as they navigate a live digital campaign.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of existing digital strategies in real-world business scenarios
Critically analyse the outcomes of digital projects and pose improvements based on evidence-based insights
Create a comprehensive digital strategy to address a specific business challenge
Implement a digital strategy, including assessment metrics
Evaluate key digital marketing tools and justify their applications in the industry

title: Strategic Communication and Public Relations
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the principles and practices of strategic communication Develop students' ability to think strategically in the context of an organisation Introduce students to ethical and legal considerations when producing media publications Explore issues related to public relations, including ethics, legal requirements, market research, content creation, PR strategies, brand management, and sponsorship

This topic introduces principles of strategic communication and public relations, including media and public relations campaigns, communication strategies, and advertising for a range of media distribution. The topic explores the strategic decision processes in organisations, ethical and legal issues, market research and Corporate Social Responsibility. It discusses public relations both from a practical and a critical perspective.
learning_outcomes: Assess public relations documents in different media
Evaluate ethical standards and their implications when developing public relations documentation for media outlets
Evaluate strategic communication practices
Critically appraise public relations campaigns
Produce public relations documents at professional standards for specified digital or print media outlets

title: Business Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic assists students to: Formulate and implement advanced communication strategies to effectively convey organizational messages to diverse audiences Select and strategically utilize traditional and new media for business and organisational communication Plan, create, and edit a variety of business documents using verbal and visual modes Develop positive and productive interpersonal relationships through effective communication, active listening, and conflict resolution.

This topic prepares students for international work opportunities, placing emphasis on communicating in global business contexts. The emphasis is placed on developing systematic ways of identifying relevant from non-essential information and then effectively and appropriately communicating what is relevant to a wide variety of audiences. Students will learn to regard effective business communication in terms of a series of strategic choices, including choosing from among a repertoire of tones and styles appropriate in different situations and with different audiences.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply ethical standards and assess their implications in business and professional communication
Apply strategic communication and critical thinking skills in evaluating and producing a range of professional documents
Research and analyse stakeholder attitudes and positions in a range of business and professional contexts
Research, assess, and synthesise a range of source materials to produce complex documents for specific purposes
prerequisites: 1 9 units of Level 1 topics 2 9 units of Level 2 topics Must satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Digital Nexus: The Core of Modern Communication
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The primary goal of this topic is to foster an understanding of digital communication foundations and their pivotal role in shaping contemporary society. Through rigorous analysis and dynamic discussion, we aim to: Uncover the multidisciplinary nature of digital communication, bridging concepts from information technology, media studies, and social sciences. Examine the impact of digital technologies on societal norms, relationships, and professional practices. Cultivate a capacity to critically evaluate digital media trends and their implications on global communication dynamics. Empower students to apply theoretical insights into practical scenarios, enhancing their digital literacy and communication skills.

This topic explores the critical role of digital communication practitioners, emphasising the skills and knowledge required to navigate the digital landscape proficiently. It is designed to equip students with a comprehensive insight into the essence and evolution of digital communication. The topic explores how digital platforms have transformed the way we disseminate information, interact, and perceive the world around us. "Digital Nexus: The Core of Modern Communication" is an essential topic for those eager to navigate the complexities of the digital age with confidence. By delving deep into the evolution, impact, and ethics of digital platforms, this topic not only broadens understanding and sharpens practical skills in digital communication. It highlights the fundamental role digital platforms play in shaping public discourse and personal interactions, equipping participants with strategies to tackle challenges and recognise opportunities within the digital landscape. Through an examination of current theories and practices, the topic explores the complexities of the digital landscape, preparing students to navigate and contribute to this ever-evolving domain.
learning_outcomes: Critique the socio-cultural implications of digital trends
Evaluate the influence of digital platforms on personal and professional interaction
Create effective communication strategies using digital tools and platforms
Analyse the fundamental theories and models that underpin digital communication

title: Navigating the Frontier: Emerging Communication Technology
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The comprehensive topic at hand calls upon students to grasp the multifaceted nature of advanced communication technologies that shape our contemporary world. To complement the learning outcomes, the topic pursues the following aims: Insightful Exploration: The topic aims to unravel each layer of advanced communication technologies, examining their inner workings, foundational principles, and distinctive characteristics. Real-world examples will assist students in visualising complicated concepts, thus fostering a comprehensive understanding. Contextual Analysis: We strive to cultivate an atmosphere of critical thinking. Students will be encouraged to dissect the myriad implications of these technologies across various contexts and industries. This includes the evaluation of potential benefits, the consideration of societal impact, and the anticipation of future trends. Practical Application: A central aim is to ensure that theoretical knowledge transcends the classroom. Accordingly, interactive assignments and group projects have been designed to encourage students to conceptualise and implement innovative uses for the examined technologies. This will serve as an opportunity for students to apply their understanding in a hands-on environment, harnessing their creativity in the process. Ethical Orientation: As we stride forward in this digital age, ethical concerns regarding technology adoption have become increasingly prominent. This topic aspires to instil a value-driven perspective among students. Emphasising responsible decision-making, we will engage in potent discussions regarding the ethical considerations of using emerging technologies.

In the ever-evolving terrain of digital communication, new technologies frequently surface, altering the way we interact and share information. The focus of this topic is to provide students with a robust understanding of these emerging technologies, allowing them to remain at the forefront of the communications industry. Through theoretical knowledge and practical applications, students will explore new platforms, tools, and trends, shaping the future of digital communication. This topic embarks on a journey through the revolutionary landscape of emerging communication technologies. We will examine and interact with influential developments like AI, Blockchain, Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), the Metaverse, and Digital Twinning. Every step of the way, we aim to illuminate the profound effects these technologies offer today and envision their immense potential for the future.
learning_outcomes: Create innovative solutions using adopted technologies
Analyse the implications of emerging technologies in diverse contexts
Assess the ethical considerations in adopting new technologies
Evaluate advanced communication technologies and their potential impact on various industries

title: Communicating Research
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Determine the choices needed for effective written and oral communication for research purposes Introduce students how to assess communication styles for different purposes Evaluate the use of clear, concise, and accurate English in research writing Support students to select appropriate language features for communicative impact in research settings Introduce students how to critique self and other's written work for revision and editing

This topic focuses on written and oral communication skills in graduate research. It develops students' academic communication skills at an advanced level within the specific context of their course of study. The subjects covered include linguistic features of academic communication, syntax and idiom; structure and argument; research genres such as literature reviews and research proposals; academic publishing; editing and peer review. Students will gain experience in editing their own and their peers' work.
learning_outcomes: Determine stylistic aspects of writing in a research environment
Critique your own and others' written work
Evaluate expectations of a research higher degree environment
Write in English to a pre-publication standard appropriate to their discipline
Assess grammatical choices in writing

title: Postgraduate English Enhancement
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this topic are to provide students with the skills and knowledge to master important elements of postgraduate communication directly relevant to writing a research dissertation, with particular reference to: The conventions of scientific argumentation The structure of a research thesis Presentation skills used in seminars and conferences

This topic is an academic English enhancement topic suited to postgraduate students who are from a non-English speaking background. This topic is designed to improve the productive (writing and speaking) skills of students with particular reference to postgraduate writing and participating in seminars in English. More specifically, in this topic, students will learn how to construct coherent academic texts relevant to their academic field of study; how to summarise and paraphrase effectively; how to respond to different academic audiences, and how to give an effective academic presentation. We also provide students with an awareness of tools and resources for continued self-study and enhancement of their abilities, as well as aim to increase students’ confidence in the use of academic English. Seminar activities will focus on academic language enhancement through annotation, planning, drafting, peer reviewing, revising, editing, as well as on speaking and listening skills for discussions and presentations.
learning_outcomes: Determine appropriate patterns and conventions of argumentation when thesis writing
Explain their own research topics to academic audiences in English as part of a spoken presentation
Integrate skills and knowledge to actively participate in seminars and workshops

title: Strategic Communication and Public Relations GE
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with in-depth understanding of strategic communication Evaluate ethical and legal considerations when producing media publications Develop students’ writing and oral skills in strategic communication Explore issues related to advertising and public relations, including market research, content creation, PR strategies, brand management, and sponsorship

The topic focuses on the history and theory of public relations, from the age of propaganda to the age of social media. It provides both critical principles and practical conventions of strategic communication and public relations, including media communication, organising media and public relations campaigns, and formulating promotional strategies for a range of media distribution. The different styles for each of these communication types will be explored, as well as techniques for identifying, and meeting, client expectations/needs. Ethical and legal issues, and market research and sponsorship are also covered. Students will be given opportunities to improve their abilities to critically assess their own campaigns, and the campaigns of others.
learning_outcomes: Produce promotional and public relations documents at professional standards for digital or print media outlets
Evaluate ethical standards and their implications when developing advertising and public relations documentation for media outlets
Create public relations media through careful research and preparation
Appraise a range of public relations strategies
Critically appraise strategic communication documents such as annual reports

title: Business Communication GE
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to assist students to: Evaluate the effectiveness of communication strategies employed in business contexts considering clarity, persuasiveness, and appropriateness Apply advanced writing skills to compose a variety of business documents in traditional and new media platforms Examine ethical and legal considerations when producing professional communication in a global context Identify the nuances of business communication, including the impact of diverse cultural contexts

This topic explores different documents and media used in business communication internationally. It examines the functions and structure of proposals, reports, business plans and white papers as well as shorter genres, such as email and memos.
learning_outcomes: Integrate rules of document design and writing style to plan, draft and edit a variety of business documents
Evaluate diverse communication goals of different audiences while making effective choices about the tone, style, and form of the communication
Apply different research methods in collecting evidence to produce different communication documents
Adapt and strategically utilize traditional and new communication media in planning a communication project

Produce an online journal that reflects upon the development of practical and creative skills.

In this topic you will undertake industry-oriented creative projects that will enable you to establish and apply core practical and creative skills in music creation, production, performance, curation and diffusion. You will contextualise your practice alongside the work of other practitioners in a variety of genres of practices, drawing comparisons between the methods and techniques applied.

Review your practical and creative skills development through an online reflective journal
Establish core practical and creative skills in music creation, production, performance, curation and diffusion, through the delivery of industry-oriented creative projects

Analyse and document the extension of your skills in the contextualisation, design, and delivery of creative projects through a reflective online journal

syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with work experience, contacts in the industry, exposure to current practices in the production and management of projects in the creative industries Assist students in identifying a career path and beginning the transition from study to employment Produce a significant creative work to a professional standard

Hours are flexible but a minimum of 120 hours per semester is required. This topic allows students to gain work experience in the creative arts industries by taking up a project or position with an industry partner, or by conceiving and producing a creative project to a professional level.
learning_outcomes: Plan and produce a major creative work in creative writing, drama, digital media or screen production, and be able to demonstrate an analytical understanding of its potential industrial context and process of construction
Describe how the workplace operates, how you can best contribute to the working environment, and recognise a realistic sense of the path ahead if you choose a career in this field

title: Exegesis
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop student capacities for verbal and written communication of creative research including methodologies, theories and outcomes reflecting on an initial research proposition Provide opportunities for students to reflect on their creative development Develop students' critical thinking in relation to their individual creative practice Develop students' abilities to synthesise relevant theory from a practice-led project Deepen students' knowledge of methodologies across the creative arts beyond their personal creative practice Develop students' awareness of scholarly conventions, intellectual integrity, and ethical considerations in practice led research Communicate issues related to creative-led research both verbally and in writing

The purpose of this topic is for Honours students who will separately complete a creative artefact for their thesis to also produce an accompanying exegesis. Students will reflect on the theoretical and creative influences on their creative work, with a focus on practice-led research and other methodologies. Students will have the opportunity to focus on particular aspects of exegetical practice that meet their individual needs and focus.
learning_outcomes: Appraise and analyse your creative practice, within the scope of a specific research design
Sustain an exegetical project to resolution, including planning, problem-solving and reflection on its relationship to research aims, and developmental milestones
Evaluate the research outcomes and appropriateness of the original research design
Communicate issues related to creative-led research both verbally and in writing

title: Cultural Policy and the Arts
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce the subject area of cultural policy Introduce the history of cultural policy Provide an understanding of the different models of cultural funding seen internationally today Provide a detailed understanding of the model of cultural funding used in Australia Develop the critical skills necessary to interpret and assess a range of cultural policy documents

This topic is designed to introduce cultural policy to students whose interests concern the areas of public policy in the arts, culture and society. The relationship between arts, culture and the state is at the core of the subject. It requires the development of a critical understanding of the relationship between public policy and artistic and cultural expression in order to successfully negotiate its objectives. It will provide an overview of the critical factors which affect the development of cultural policy. It will investigate the nature of cultural policy by looking at the history of cultural policies in different countries under various political regimes and analyse the structure of institutions which have been put in place to promote policies. The course will be held in seminar style and approached on a thematic basis.
learning_outcomes: Discuss definitions of cultural policy
Construct a matrix of the different mechanisms of cultural provision, their costs and benefits
Critically evaluate a range of different kinds of cultural policy documents
Develop your professional identity in relation to cultural policy within the cultural sector
Integrate the history and practice of cultural policy

Critically evaluate current practice in the creative industries

Plan and produce a major project to industry standard

title: Understanding Research Methods in the Creative Arts
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to deepen participants' skills and knowledge in research methods in the creative and performing arts, enabling participants to deepen their methodological knowledge and to develop the skills to effectively undertake and complete their Honours creative project and exegesis.

This topic provides a grounding in research methods for creative artists in creative writing, dance, drama, visual arts, screen production, digital media, fashion, and visual effects and entertainment design. Issues relating to practice-led research and related creative arts methodologies will be explored, including the organisation and communication of creative research outcomes and the relationship between theory and practice. Participants will acquire cross-disciplinary skills and knowledge while preparing for their own major creative project and exegesis. Participants will deepen their understanding of how to construct a creative arts practice-led research project, including research proposals, methodologies and methods, literature and artefact reviews, ethics and evaluation processes.
learning_outcomes: Defend the research proposal prepared for your Honours creative project and exegesis
Develop and sustain a research methodology applicable to your area of specialisation, including understanding the principles of ethical research
Critically evaluate research theories
Model research at a high level via oral and written communication/assessment using advanced critical writing skills

This topic aims to: Develop students' producing skills required for major projects Develop students' skills in creative, aesthetic and managerial problem solving Develop skills in the practical application of creative research Develop students' skills in successful collaboration in project production

In this topic students will produce a major project demonstrating practise led research in the field of entertainment design. Students will manage their own production under supervision of an academic staff member from VEED, including pre-production planning and collaboration with key project personnel.
learning_outcomes: Support the completion of the proposed project to final production stage
Appraise and manage all logistical tasks required for the project, including risk assessment
Demonstrate an understanding of pre-production planning
Create a production process (including both the scheduling and managing of it) in the field of digital entertainment design
