title: Research Methods for Literature and Creative Writing
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with the research tools needed to complete an Honours project Instil in students an awareness of the creative and/or critical methodologies that they use in their creative and/or critical practices

In this topic students will explore discipline-specific research methodologies during an intense six program (i.e. over the first six weeks of the topic). This six-week program includes discussion/application of the following: Benchmarking Honours-level research/practical research skills Working with secondary sources Theoretical approaches to research Methodologies for creative research; methodologies for literary research Ethical research Writing at Honours level In the final four/five weeks of the topic, students will present a research proposal to be delivered as a presentation and in written form
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in a range of research activities including database/internet research, ethical research, primary and secondary analysis, applying secondary material and theory, and advanced creative/critical writing skills
Communicate research skills and knowledge via oral and written communication/assessment
Demonstrate advanced oral and written communication skills
prerequisites: Admission into HBA-Bachelor of Arts (Honours)

title: Crafting Narratives in the Digital Epoch: Transmedia Content and Multimedia Storytelling
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
Through this topic, we aspire to: Facilitate a comprehensive understanding of transmedia narrative techniques and principles Foster the ability to critically analyse and utilise the power of storytelling in digital communication Develop practical skills for content creation across various platforms Inculcate ethical considerations in the execution of digital campaigns

This topic provides students with practical knowledge on creating compelling digital content and engaging storytelling across multiple digital and social media platforms. It focuses on transmedia narratives, multimedia techniques, and content creation tools essential to connect with diverse audiences in this digital era.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of designing coherent storyworlds across multiple platforms
Apply transmedia storytelling techniques to develop original multimedia narratives
Design an original transmedia storyworld and content strategy
Define key concepts related to transmedia storytelling and multimedia narratives
Critique transmedia content strategies and provide recommendations for improvement

title: Research Methods in the Creative Arts
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Help postgraduates' transition from undergraduate study to postgraduate study Help postgraduates to develop a clear conception of research in the creative arts Develop understanding of specific modes and methods of research in the creative arts Develop independent research skills in the creative arts Facilitate postgraduate research and to provide ongoing support during candidature

This topic explores research methods appropriate to the creative arts and other non-traditional and/or new university disciplines. It takes an inter-disciplinary approach, investigating current theories and modes of practice in order to facilitate postgraduate research projects and theses. To this end, it discusses the critical as well as creative aspects of research in the arts. On a practical level it offers opportunities for students to discuss research proposals and workshop research questions, as well as providing ongoing support during candidature. In addition, it allows postgraduates to refine presentation skills. Occasional targeted workshops will be available (for example, Illuminating the Exegesis).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate refined independent research as well as presentation skills
Revise and refine that proposal as necessary
Demonstrate an understanding of the variety of research methods utilised in the creative arts
Formulate appropriate research questions
Design an appropriate research proposal
prerequisites: 1 Admission into PHD/EH-Doctor of Philosophy 1a Admission into MA/EHR-Master of Arts by research Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a))

title: Cultural Policy and the Arts GE
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to introduce students to the subject area and history of cultural policy to provide an understanding of the different models of cultural funding seen internationally today and compare these to the model of cultural funding used in Australia. Students will develop knowledge and understanding as well as the critical skills necessary to interpret and assess a range of cultural policy documents, and the issues that frame them.

This topic is designed to introduce cultural policy to students whose interests concern the areas of public policy in the arts, culture and society. Students will gain theoretical knowledge of the relationship between arts, culture and the state, and a critical understanding of the relationship between public policy and artistic and cultural expression. This topic will provide an overview of the critical factors which affect the development of cultural policy. It will investigate the nature of cultural policy by looking at the history of cultural policies in different countries under various political regimes & analyse the structure of institutions which have been put in place to promote policies. Students will develop an understanding of theoretical and policy issues as they relate to their own creative practice.
learning_outcomes: Integrate a knowledge of cultural policy in any career within the cultural sector
Critique key issues and debates in cultural policy
Appraise different mechanisms of cultural provision, their costs and benefits
Critically evaluate a range of different kinds of cultural policy documents
Evaluate the history of cultural policy

title: Entrepreneurship in the Creative Industries GE
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this topic include: Understanding Context: To explore the historical and contemporary forces that led to entrepreneurialism in creative fields. Developing Practical Skills: To equip students with essential skills for undertaking entrepreneurial ventures within the creative sector. Analysing Success Stories: To study successful creative entrepreneurs and learn from their experiences. Exploring Business Models: To delve into various business models relevant to creative enterprises.

Entrepreneurship in the creative industries refers to the application of entrepreneurial principles and practices within artistic, cultural, and media-related domains. It involves identifying opportunities, developing innovative ideas, and creating sustainable ventures in areas such as design, music, film, fashion, and digital media. This field explores the intersection of creativity, business acumen, and risk-taking, enabling individuals to turn their artistic passions into successful enterprises.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge of business entrepreneurship concepts specific to creative industries
Create a strategic business plan that leverages unique creative talents while addressing market demands
Assess practical skills essential for entrepreneurial ventures in artistic, cultural, and media-related fields
Critique industry standards and expectations within various creative domains

title: Industry Project
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an opportunity to identify and research an industry problem, create a solution, and communicate the benefits of the solution.

In this topic, students will define a research problem applicable to a defined industry setting, conduct a literature review, and collect and analyse data to create an evidence-based solution. This may be presented in the form of a practice-based object or a project brief identifying benefits, risk, a budget, project timeline, and including a communication and evaluation plan. The project will be conducted under the supervision of an academic supervisor in a relevant discipline.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a problem to propose an evidence-based solution in a defined industry setting
Influence industry relevant research including a literature review and data collection and analysis
Discuss the outcomes and relevance of practice-based or practice-led research in a variety of formats
Evaluate opportunities to lead change and generate support
Formulate a practice-based or practice-led research question

title: The Digital Communication Practitioner Brand Development
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
To facilitate the comprehensive understanding and practical application of the five dimensions critical to becoming a successful micro-Social Media Influencer (micro-SMI), equipping students with the skills to navigate and engage with the digital landscape effectively.

This topic is designed to equip participants with the essential knowledge and practical skills needed to develop and enhance their personal brand as a digital communication practitioner. It offers a comprehensive exploration into the realm of micro-social media influencers (micro-SMI), guided by the foundational theoretical model delineated in Chapter 3 of "Research Perspectives on Social Media Influencers." Students will engage deeply with the five dimensions integral to developing a successful micro-SMI presence, enabling them to craft a nuanced, impactful professional digital brand strategy. Through a dynamic blend of theoretical grounding and hands-on activities, students will navigate the multifaceted landscape of digital branding, including strategy development, online presence management, and content creation. Aimed at fostering a deep understanding of digital branding's impact in professional settings, this topic prepares students for successful careers in the digital age.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate practical content creation and online engagement strategies for effectively managing students' professional digital footprints
Analyse the role of micro-SMI in the current digital landscape, considering its historical context
Create a professional brand implementing digital strategy skills for navigating the social media domain in a professional context
Evaluate the critical dimensions that underpin a successful micro-SMI persona, synthesising scholarly insight and practical examples

title: Digital Communication Practitioner Professional ePortfolio
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
1. Empowerment: Equip learners with the knowledge and skills needed to construct a compelling digital ePortfolio that showcases their expertise in digital communication 2. Self-Reflection: Encourage self-reflection and critical thinking about one’s professional journey and growth 3. Career Readiness: Prepare participants for successful digital communication careers by emphasising practical application and real-world relevance

Digital Communication Practitioner Professional ePortfolio serves as an online showcase of your skills, experiences, and expertise in the field of digital communication.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate different ePortfolio platforms to select one that effectively showcases your work and aligns with your personal brand
Create engaging multimedia content tailored to various digital mediums for your ePortfolio
Design a customised ePortfolio layout that effectively showcases your work and aligns with your personal brand
Evaluate the effectiveness of ePortfolio elements and personal branding strategies through peer review and self-reflection

title: Introducing Crime and Criminology
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a basic grounding in the causes, forms and impacts of crime as well as an introduction to the writing and research skills in the area.

This topic provides a basic grounding in the causes, forms and impacts of crime. In this topic students will explore: The phenomenon of crime, its extent and location Individual and social explanations for criminal behaviour Various types of crime The portrayal of crime in the Australian media
learning_outcomes: Recognise, identify and apply a range of criminological theories about the nature and causes of crime
Read, analyse and communicate succinctly criminological knowledge
Identify and use research databases about crime research
Identify and summarise knowledge across a range of criminological topics

title: Criminal Justice System
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
In this topic, students will explore the institutions and operations of the criminal justice systems within Australia, and with reference to global contexts. Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of the system in achieving ‘justice’.

This topic critically examines the aims and practices of agencies within the criminal justice system, focusing on the investigation, prosecution, and adjudication of crime, as well as correctional responses. The topic explores whether, when and for whom the criminal justice system achieves ‘justice’. Finally, the topic critically assesses the system’s effectiveness using contemporary criminological/socio-legal evidence.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise the structures and systems of the CJS and evaluate how these may impact the community
Illustrate how the concept of ‘justice’ is a social construction using various theoretical frameworks.
Identify the proposed purposes and mechanisms of the criminal justice system (CJS) in Australia, and particularly South Australia.
Apply these theoretical frameworks to the proposed purposes of the CJS

title: Criminal Law in Practice
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the basic principles of criminal law and procedure Provide knowledge of the criminal process, including the role of its constituent institutions and actors (courts, lawyers, prosecutors, police) Provide an understanding of key areas of criminal law in action, eg. Drug laws, bail, sentencing, one-punch laws

This topic explores how criminal law is constructed by the legislature, the courts, lawyers and law enforcement agencies. Students will study the nature of criminal law and criminal procedure, including criminal responsibility, offences, defences, evidence and police powers. Particular areas of criminal law will be examined in some depth in order to explore how the criminal law works in practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the role of criminal law role in social life and social policy
Describe and apply elements of the criminal justice processes and criminal law
Interpret criminal statutes (legislation) and case law

title: (Mis)Interpreting Crime Data
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic encourages students to unpack how crime is reported or represented and interpreted, and to think critically about how this shapes community knowledge of and/or attitudes to crime. It will also introduce students to basic research methods and analysis.

This topic aims to uncover how crime is reported and/or represented, often in the media or by governments, and how these representations are used to construct the phenomena of crime, which in turn shapes community reactions to crime. In doing so, the topic will introduce students to basic research concepts and methods (including identifying various forms of data, building of graphs/infographics, and preliminary analysis) and encourage reflection on how these shape social reactions to crime.
learning_outcomes: Apply and/or engage with basic issues, concepts, and debates regarding social research methods and the presentation of crime data
Interpret, visually represent/graph, and apply key sources of crime data
Classify various sources or representations of crime and describe their role in the presentation of official crime data/policy
Apply basic research methods to examine how crime data and methodologies are shaped key criminological perspectives or epistemologies

title: Understanding Victims and Trauma
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop understanding of the victim and victimology.

This topic examines the origins of, and developments in, victimology. Students explore the relationship between victims and agencies of criminal justice, including police, prosecution, courts and corrections. Students will become familiar with concepts related to the identity, experiences, and rights of victims of crime. Students will learn about trauma-informed practice and effective criminal justice responses to victims of crime.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate concepts and process of victimology
Evaluate and apply trauma- and theoretically-informed approaches and good practice principles to Criminal Justice System policy and practice responses to victims of crime
Discuss the impact of crime on victims and critically appraise the different ways the criminal justice system, welfare system and society respond to victims of crime
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 1 topics

title: Protecting the Safety of the Community: Sentencing and Corrections
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Examine the degree to which corrective services can contribute to the protection and creation of safer communities. Evaluate how to achieve the primary purpose of sentencing, which is to protect the safety of the community.

This topic examines the purposes of sentencing and corrections in promoting community safety. It explores the emergence of modern forms of punishment, the rationales for various types of punitive techniques (e.g., fines, conferencing, suspended sentences, imprisonment), and the effectiveness of sentencing and corrective practices in keeping the community safe. The topic places a particular emphasis on the role and impact of imprisonment, the experience of living and working in prison, as well as the challenges faced by those released from adult custodial environments.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate ethical and effective correctional service practices
Assess the ability of correctional service agencies and the sentencing model to promote community safety
Appraise the current theories underpinning correctional practice
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 1 topics

title: Children, Young People and the Justice System
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
In this topic, students will identify how children and young people encounter the justice system. Students will develop their theoretical understanding of youth crime, critically examine media and political portrayals of “youth crime epidemics”, as well as assess justice and welfare responses to children at risk and children who offend.

This topic examines which children have contact with the justice system and in what contexts. Students will explore crimes committed by children and explanations proposed for this behaviour. Students will also consider “justice” as it applies to children and young people by critically assessing current justice and social welfare policies and practices and proposing new ways of working.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise contemporary issues and debates about youth justice and related social issues
Identify contemporary challenges to the youth justice system, and discrepancies between the ideal and real youth justice system
Develop an evidence-informed response to a contemporary issue concerning children and the justice system and formulate an implementation strategy.
prerequisites: 18 units of level 1 topics

title: Policing for the Future: Innovations and Social Impacts
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a range of key concepts and debates about policing and law enforcement Place modern police organisations into context regarding diverse approaches to social control in Western society Examine the different police functions and the nature of police organisations and police personnel, to encourage reflection upon and challenge current knowledge and perceptions of police/policing Explore and critique current and future trends in law enforcement

Police are known to be the ‘gate keepers’ to the criminal justice system, and one profession relied upon to uphold the law, prevent crime and protect the community. This topic focuses on policing in the Australian context, exploring the history and development of policing over time, before evaluating the role of police in modern society, exploring a variety of policing topics, such as use of discretion, policing powers, use of police force, police accountability, investigations of crime, and policing real world issues.
learning_outcomes: Apply understanding of contemporary policing methods to real-world problems
Evaluate and reflect on internal and external factors that shape the perceptions and misperceptions of policing practice in Australia
Appraise current theory and models that underpins and shapes contemporary Australian police practices
Examine and discuss key concepts of policing practices within Australian communities
prerequisites: 18 Units of Level 1 Topics

title: Basic Criminological Research Methods and Data
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
In this topic, students will develop: An understanding of the process of research design A critical understanding of the main criteria for assessing research quality An appreciation of the different approaches to social science research practices The skills to be able to apply basic research methods to the collection and analysis of social science data An understanding of how to communicate research findings An understanding of the main principles that underlie ethical research practice

This topic will provide students with a basic understanding of the process of conducting research, starting with framing research questions and research design, through to methods of data collection and data analysis. Students will also gain an appreciation and knowledge of the different epistemological and methodological approaches to research design and practice. They will also be introduced to the main principles of ethical research practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate research designs and apply them to the study of criminology using ethical practices
Critically analyse and interpret data
Identify and make use of different ways in which constructs can be defined and measured
Communicate empirical findings for social impact
prerequisites: 1 9 units of any Level 1 topics 2 CRIM1104 Must satisfy: ((1 and 2))

title: Analysing Cybercrime and Digital Risk
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to criminological dimensions vis-a-vis cybercrime Provide opportunity for students to develop open-source research skills Introduce students to various cybercrimes, the actors involved, and how law enforcement investigates them Appreciate the rapid social and technological changes that are ongoing due to changes in internet capabilities, shifts in technological adaptation, and how societies adopt those technologies to their lives

For all of human history, people have used technology to make their lives easier. Today, this is just as true if not more so as we enter "the information age." In this era, the internet is often the common denominator which these technologies are built upon. Cyberspace is an immense realm that facilitates communications and actions in a vast array of everyday applications. Unfortunately, the opportunities afforded by the internet can also be used for nefarious purposes. This module looks at some of the many crimes which use ICT systems, either fully or in part, to commission a criminal activity and the difficulties in developing responses to these crimes domestically and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Examine and critically reflect upon the intricate connections between cybercrime and various social categories, including but not limited to race, sexuality, sex and gender identity, religion, and immigration status
Conduct thorough research and effectively communicate findings, emphasizing a high standard of professionalism in both content and presentation
Explain and analyse the perpetration and victimisation of cyber-enabled and cyber-dependent crimes
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 1 topics

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop students’ understanding of the importance of understanding, hearing, and working with previously incarcerated people to develop criminal justice policy and to advocate for change.

This topic is based on the presentation and analysis of key national and international issues in criminal justice. It is taught by visiting international scholars and/or current staff. In any year, the topic will centre on particular issues shaping the nature of criminological theory, policing, courts or corrections in particular jurisdictions. Issues which might form the basis of the topic from year to year include: the relationship between race, social marginalisation and mass imprisonment; national and international innovations in court practices; what works in probation and/or prisoner reintegration; how theory and practice diverge and/or converge in various criminal justice settings. In 2025 this topic will develop students’ policy and advocacy skills. Students will reflect on how the criminal justice system and associated agencies can better promote its fundamental purpose of community safety and how to collaborate with people with lived experience in the justice system.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the complex interconnections between marginalisation and crime.
Develop knowledge of a range of criminological perspectives, including convict criminology, queer criminology, etc
Demonstrate effective advocacy skills
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 2 topics

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice: Rehabilitation and Desistance from Crime
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic serves as an umbrella topic to accommodate special or one off offerings in a topical area of criminal justice not currently part of the law curriculum in circumstances when availability of visiting or other staff resources permit. Aims will be drawn up on an ad hoc basis for each offering.

This topic is based on the presentation and analysis of key national and international issues in Criminal Justice. It is taught by visiting international scholars and/or current Law School Staff. In any year, the topic will centre on particular issues shaping the nature of criminological theory, policing, courts or corrections in particular jurisdictions. Issues which might form the basis of the topic from year to year include: the relationship between race, social marginalisation and mass imprisonment; national and international innovations in court practices; what works in probation and/or prisoner reintegration; how theory and practice diverge and/or converge in various criminal justice settings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate achievement of the expected learning outcomes associated with the topic description and content that may be approved from time to time in light of the special nature of this umbrella topic
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BA-Bachelor of Arts 1a Admission into BBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Psychology) 1b Admission into BJS-Bachelor of Justice and Society 1c Admission into BLAWLPR-Bachelor of Laws and Legal Practice 1d Admission into BLAWLPRG-Bachelor of Laws and Legal Practice (Graduate Entry) 1e Admission into BLAWLPRGH-Bachelor of Laws and Legal Practice (Graduate Entry) (Honours) 1f Admission into BLAWLPRH-Bachelor of Laws and Legal Practice (Honours) 1g Admission into BPSY-Bachelor of Psychology (Honours) 1h Admission into BLS-Bachelor of Law and Society 2 18 Units in CRIM1101, CRIM1102, CRIM2201, CRIM2202, CRIM2203, ENGL2130, HIST2043, LLAW3271, LEGL2116, SOCI2015, WMST2015, CRIM1003, CRIM1004, CRIM2003 2a 72 units of LLAW topics Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g or 1h) and (2 or 2a))

title: Building Criminology Careers: Industry Project
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This industry project topic aims to: Partner students with and/or involve community and government justice agencies to produce research on pressing social problems Help students develop career-oriented skills by fostering students’ reflective practice in an innovative capstone skill-focused topic

This industry project topic supports the development of reflective skills, crucial for advancing students’ learning and improving their awareness of the need to reflect. The theoretic underpinnings discuss the concepts of structural/cultural injustice – justice, which can help students to recognise and address underlying causes of harm and disadvantage in applied projects. The topic provides students with extensive support, is scaffolded and allows for participation of the industry to promote students to gain skills in critical reflection and forward planning. CJ agencies and other service providers will be involved in different ways, including by providing industry projects, and hands-on advice on potential careers. Through its theoretical underpinnings, industry focus and support of productive reflection the topic will stimulate students’ self-reflective ability so they can develop a career in criminal justice and cognate sectors.
learning_outcomes: Develop professional competencies which can be used to apply for, and work in, industry related positions
Discuss CJ related issues from a range of perspectives and within local, national and international contexts
Create written and oral presentations using coherent, sophisticated arguments independently and in a group
Formulate research projects using skills, knowledge and understanding of the CJ sector and its demanding socio-cultural and political contexts
Integrate criminological knowledge and reflective practice skills acquired during the course of the Criminology degree in multiple and diverse industry-oriented projects
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCRIM-Bachelor of Criminology 1a Admission into BCRIMH-Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) 1b Admission into BLS-Bachelor of Law and Society 1c Admission into BA-Bachelor of Arts 1d Admission into BAGIS-Bachelor of Applied Geographical Information Systems 1e Admission into BAHA-Bachelor of Arts - Enhanced Program for High Achievers 1f Admission into BASC-Bachelor of Arts and Science 1g Admission into BBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Psychology) 1h Admission into BEDSTBA-Bachelor of Education Studies, Bachelor of Arts 1i Admission into BCRIMC-Bachelor of Criminology (Cybersecurity) 1j Admission into BCRIMFP-Bachelor of Criminology - Flinders City Campus 1k Admission into BCRIMHFP-Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) - Flinders City Campus 1l Admission into CACCR-Bachelor of Accounting/Bachelor of Criminology - Flinders City Campus 1m Admission into CACCRH-Bachelor of Accounting/Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) - Flinders City Campus 1n Admission into CLAWCR-Bachelor of Laws/Bachelor of Criminology 1o Admission into CPSCR-Bachelor of Psychological Science/Bachelor of Criminology - Flinders City Campus 1p Admission into CLAWHCR-Bachelor of Laws (Honours)/Bachelor of Criminology 2 Admission into any BCRIM course variation 3 18 Units of Level Two CRIM topic Must Satisfy: (((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g or 1h or 1i or 1j or 1k or 1l or 1m or 1n or 1o or 1p) or (2)) and 3))

title: Criminology Industry Placement
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with work experience in criminology through an industry placement, and to cover the key elements of work practice necessary for the development of successful careers in the sector. The topic involves practical experience in a criminology-relevant organisation, under the supervision of an industry professional.

This topic gives students the opportunity to apply their academic skills and knowledge to a real-world workplace and gain a clearer insight into the day-to-day functioning of a workplace in the criminology sector, e.g. Department for Correctional Services.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic knowledge and skills to a complex work environment within the criminology sector
Reflect on and evaluate workplace practices that lead to effective and ethical organisations
Prepare for and engage in professional behaviours
prerequisites: 1 Admission to any BCRIM variation 2 18 Units of Level Two CRIM topics Must satisfy: ((1 and 2))

title: International Criminal Justice: Modern Slavery
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Expose students to the fundamental issues and principles of modern slavery as it may operate in the international and national geo-political and legal spheres Facilitate student awareness of relevant contextual matters that can shape the nature and operation of international criminal justice Provide students with a coherent theoretical framework with which to understand the increasingly prominent discourses operating in the field of modern slavery Allow students to understand the reality and significance of the global dimension of crime Provide students with the tools to be able to rationally critique understandings, theories and applications of international criminal justice Motivate students to engage in independent research about international criminal justice

The topic addresses concepts related to the 'internationalisation' of criminal justice including globalisation, non-territoriality, changing conceptions of state sovereignty and the network state. These concepts are elaborated upon in relation to a range of substantive areas of study under the umbrella of human trafficking and modern slavery. Illustrations of subject matter include: typologies of modern slavery; organised crime and human trafficking; global sex markets, i.e. sex traffic and sex tourism; risks and indicators of modern slavery; human rights and the scales of justice, i.e. national, European, international, global, with emphasis on Australia; police cooperation in modern slavery.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate selected issues of modern slavery and their implications through the application of coherent theoretical and contextual frameworks
Synthesise key themes and contested debates within the field of International Criminal Justice
Write well-reasoned arguments in support of a defined position on modern slavery, grounded in empirical evidence and normative frameworks
Analyse selected subject matter in International Criminal Justice using appropriate analytical, legal, and socio-legal methodologies
Systematically apply and evaluate a range of research tools and methodologies to locate information relevant to International Criminal Justice
Communicate independent research on a substantial topic within International Criminal Justice.
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 2 topics

title: The Psychology of Unmaking a Murderer
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to introduce students to: The knowledge base that underpins the psychology of, and psychological engagement with, the criminal justice system The practical application of psychological theories in the criminal justice system (i.e., the assessment and management of people who commit crime) Ethical issues associated with correctional settings Psychological understandings of justice

This topic examines how psychological theories and research can contribute to efforts to reduce recidivism and enable rehabilitation. It covers the basic principles of the psychology of criminal behaviour, and how psychology is applied to the classification, treatment, and management of people who commit crime to reduce risk and improve public safety. This topic also examines the psychological understandings of "justice" and how public perceptions influence public policy in relation to sentencing and punishment.
learning_outcomes: Apply psychological principles to the study of criminal behaviour
Evaluate approaches to rehabilitation
Critique how the criminal justice system assesses and manages people convicted of crime
Describe how social and public policy contexts influence justice practices
Develop an ethical approach to working in correctional settings
prerequisites: 1 18 units of study at level 1 2 18 units of study at level 2 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Netflix and Kill: Encountering Crime Through the Media
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the different ways that crime pervades our lives (on the news, in books, on Social Media and on the screen as entertainment etc.) Provide a conceptual overview of the complex ways that we consume crime in society (and how this has evolved in the past 100 odd years) To prompt students to explore why - despite being fearful of/disturbed by crime - we find it alluring and crave vicarious exposure to it

This topic draws on popular culture and the meditated nature of our contemporary digital world to explore how we encounter crime. The topic engages with a vast array of phenomenon (e.g. news media, film, documentary, television shows and podcasts) to explore the ways that crime is packaged, represented and consumed. This topic prompts students to appreciate that sensory exposure to crime permeates our lives. It seeks to empower students to appreciate the complexities and contradictions at play when they encounter crime and to critically consider crime narratives when engaging with the world they live in.
learning_outcomes: Conduct some independent research into one of the themes of the topic using quality academic resources to elucidate an appreciation of the complexities of that chosen area of study
Identify the different ways that people encounter crime and be able to comment on the nuanced ways that such an encounter occurs
Identify the key social debates and/or controversies attached to the particular ways that people encounter crime
Critique the mode(s) through which people encounter crime (e.g. news media, television, film, social media, video games) to elucidate how that mode shapes or influences perceptions of crime
prerequisites: 36 Units of study

title: Trauma-informed Practice in Criminal Justice
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: teach students to effectively apply their theoretical and academic criminological knowledge to real-world situations, equip students with foundational counselling skills and effective communication skills, and develop students’ self-regulation and self-care strategies to promote trauma-informed practice in criminal justice settings.

Students will learn and apply professional skills to promote trauma-informed practice. They will develop ways of working with clients to promote safety, trust, collaboration, voice, and choice. Students will also develop skills to empower clients by acknowledging their unique strengths, as well as their gender, culture, and historical factors that influence engagement and well-being. This topic draws from the expertise of practitioners, victims/survivors, and people with lived experience of criminalisation and incarceration.
learning_outcomes: Practice foundational counselling and interviewing micro-skills, including reflective listening skills
Apply trauma-informed principles of practice to their work and in reflective practices
Demonstrate effective communication skills in a professional context
Apply self-regulation and self-care strategies to promote better psychosocial health
prerequisites: 18 units of level 2 topics

title: Analysing Cybercrime and Digital Risk
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to criminological dimensions vis-a-vis cybercrime Provide opportunity for students to develop open-source research skills Introduce students to various cybercrimes, the actors involved, and how law enforcement investigates them Appreciate the rapid social and technological changes that are ongoing due to changes in internet capabilities, shifts in technological adaptation, and how societies adopt those technologies to their lives

For all of human history, people have used technology to make their lives easier. Today, this is just as true if not more so as we enter "the information age." In this era, the internet is often the common denominator which these technologies are built upon. Cyberspace is an immense realm that facilitates communications and actions in a vast array of everyday applications. Unfortunately, the opportunities afforded by the internet can also be used for nefarious purposes. This module looks at some of the many crimes which use ICT systems, either fully or in part, to commission a criminal activity and the difficulties in developing responses to these crimes domestically and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Examine and critically reflect upon the intricate connections between cybercrime and various social categories, including but not limited to race, sexuality, sex and gender identity, religion, and immigration status
Explain and analyse the perpetration and victimisation of cyber-enabled and cyber-dependent crimes
Conduct thorough research and effectively communicate findings in assessments and peer-based learning contexts, emphasising a high standard of professionalism in both content and presentation
prerequisites: 18 units of Level 1 topics

title: Children, Young People and the Law
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
In this topic, students will: explore the many complex forces that shape youth crime and criminalisation; build rich understandings of how these systems are experienced by, and often harm, criminalised young people; develop their theoretical understanding of youth crime and critically examine media, political and research portrayals of “youth crime epidemics”; compare and contrast dominant carceral approaches with community driven, welfare-based responses.

Drawing from the narratives of criminalised young people and the wisdom of current youth justice practitioners, this topic critically appraises dominant representations of youth crime and the systemic, structural and interpersonal forces that shape and drive it. The topic then explores the impacts of carceral interventions and innovative approaches offering a new way forward.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise contemporary issues and debates about youth justice and related social issues
Develop an evidence-informed response to a contemporary issue concerning children and the justice system and formulate an implementation strategy
Identify contemporary challenges to the youth justice system, and discrepancies between the ideal and real youth justice system
prerequisites: 18 units of level 1 topics

title: Advanced Criminology Research Methods and Data
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Examine major epistemological frameworks for understanding research methodologies Develop a critical understanding of the criteria used for assessing research quality Develop a reflective understanding of a range of quantitative and qualitative social science research methods Develop the skills to be able to analyse quantitative and qualitative data, including being able to use major analytical software packages Examine ethical issues relating to the conduct of social science research

An understanding of social and socio-legal research methods is highly regarded in the workplace and essential for successful completion of honours and postgraduate studies. This research methods topic brings together a range of essential research skills designed to provide students with a grounding in social science research skills. This topic will provide students with a conceptual understanding of research methodologies, practical skills in employing different research methods, and skills in analysing both quantitative and qualitative research data.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate a range of quantitative and qualitative social science research methods
Critique ethical issues in relating to the conduct of social science research
Analyse quantitative and qualitative research data
Apply epistemological frameworks underlying research methodologies and methods
prerequisites: 1 of SOCI2025, CRIM2205

title: Criminal Justice Honours Thesis (18 units)
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to offer Honours students the possibility to develop a comprehensive discussion on current issues in criminology and criminal justice in an independent manner, making use of the knowledge and academic skills acquired during the degree programme.

With the guidance of a supervisor, students will devise a thesis proposal and execute this proposal by conducting research and writing a thesis. The thesis may be a critical survey of existing knowledge or a exploration of a particular area that requires the student to conduct their own research. In both cases the study should make an original contribution to the subject of criminological inquiry. The completed thesis should demonstrate the student's ability to collect and evaluate information; to test and defend an argument or thesis; and to examine critically the major theories in the area of enquiry.
learning_outcomes: Design and present a piece of criminological research
Read and reflect critically, contextually and independently upon criminological literature
Identify, comprehend and analyse a criminological problem
Define the criminological problem in an appropriately circumscribed way

school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to offer Honours students the possibility to develop a comprehensive discussion on current issues in criminology or socio-legal studies in an independent manner, making use of the knowledge and academic skills acquired during the degree programme.

With the guidance of a supervisor, students will plan, conduct research and produce a research thesis. title: Honours Thesis in Law and Criminology (4.5/22.5 units)
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to offer Honours students the possibility to develop a comprehensive discussion on current issues in criminology or socio-legal studies in an independent manner, making use of the knowledge and academic skills acquired during the degree programme.

With the guidance of a supervisor, students will devise a thesis proposal. The proposal details the aims and methods of their Honours thesis. The thesis may be a critical survey of existing knowledge or the exploration of a particular area that requires the student to conduct their own research. In both cases the study should make an original contribution to the subject of criminological or socio-legal inquiry. The completed thesis should demonstrate the student's ability to collect and evaluate information; to test and defend an argument or thesis; and to examine critically the major theories in the area of enquiry.
learning_outcomes: Define the criminological problem in an appropriately circumscribed way
Identify, comprehend and analyse a criminological problem
Design and present a piece of criminological or socio-legal research
Read and reflect critically, contextually and independently upon criminological and spcio-legal literature
prerequisites: ^ CRIM7300B - Honours Thesis in Law and Criminology (9/22.5 units) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

school: College of Business, Government and Law

The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire the appropriate research skills and training to enable them to work independently and complete a body of research at the level of a Masters by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Master's degree by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Masters by Research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Master's degree by research.
learning_outcomes: Validate research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Demonstrate your capacity to formulate a significant problem
Explain your understanding of chosen methodological practices
Justify and transmit required knowledge and skills through the presentation of well written work
prerequisites: Admission into MA - Master of Arts by research

title: Advanced Theory and Research Applications
school: College of Business, Government and Law
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an intensive exposure to criminological and socio-legal research. It will assist in the development of competencies supportive of knowledgeable civic engagement. It will arm students with tools for unpacking policy into theoretical or ideological assumptions. It will prepare students for engagement for masters or doctoral level study in criminology or socio-legal studies

In this topic, students will examine and analyse a range of major approaches to understanding crime and legal institutions and will be invited to reflect on potential applications in practice. The approach taken requires students to look thematically at criminological or socio-legal explanations for social problems as well as to study one or two problems in depth. Students will be expected to read intensively for their research essay and show competence in the analysis of case studies by using adequate theoretical underpinning. They will also be expected to understand the policy implications of the different theories examined, including some of the shortcomings associated with particular policy responses. Students will be expected to link theory to practical and empirical cases.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of key theoretical debates and schools of thought in criminology and social legal studies
Contextualize, outline, and be able to explain the key policy issues in a range of contemporary policy areas related to crime and justice
Provide an analysis of one or more key theoretical debates and schools of thought in criminology and socio-legal studies
Discuss and explain ideas and debates within contemporary disciplinary boundaries
Critique the policy arguments arising from the above issues drawing from an advanced literature review
Conduct advanced research using tools relevant to criminological or socio-legal theory
Analyse and write in depth upon a particular research theme in the field
prerequisites: 1 Admission into HBCRIM-Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) 1a Admission into HBLS-Bachelor of Law and Society (Honours) 1b Admission into HBA-CRIM-Criminology 1c Admission into HBA-LWSO-Law and Society 1d Admission into CRIM-HP-Criminology 1e Admission into LWSO-HP-Law and Society 1f Admission into BCRIMH-Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) 1g Admission into CACCRH-Bachelor of Accounting/Bachelor of Criminology (Honours) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g))

Validate the originality of their research topic in relation to a broader framework of knowledge

title: Writing Across Genres
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a range of popular fiction genres, including romance, science fiction, horror and fantasy Explore how different genres are defined, and how writers refresh recurring tropes for contemporary audiences Create two fiction stories that meld popular genres with contemporary settings and issues Practice the process of regularly drafting and submitting creative works

This first-year creative writing topic explores story ideas at the core of different genres—from romance to fantasy, sci-fi to cli-fi, horror to historical fiction. Why do the stories of these genres draw us in, and how can we make them fresh? By reading a wide variety of texts, working with a rotating cast of published writers and creating original works of fiction, this topic will allow students to experiment with their writing voice in a range of popular genres.
learning_outcomes: Compose exegetical writing that investigates creative choices and techniques
Identify and analyse various popular fiction genres
Practice generating and developing story ideas and drafts
Create new works of fiction that combine classic genre tropes with contemporary

title: Story: Who, What, When, Where
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Broaden students' appreciation of the short story genre Encourage students to read some exemplars of the form Help them understand the cultural contexts in which such fictions are produced. The short story is particularly appropriate for encouraging comparative analysis between national cultures and periods of literary development.

This topic is designed to help students conceptualise, critique, and create short written works. In this two-hour workshop, students will read and analyse a diverse range of short texts and will be encouraged to use them as models for their own creative writing. Students will consider how short narratives are constructed and how they function by examining fundamental building blocks of storytelling like structure, voice, characterisation, setting and genre. Close reading of short stories from national and international markets will help students to understand the cultural contexts in which such fictions are produced. Students will be introduced to the crucial process of refining, revising, and polishing creative work for publication.
learning_outcomes: Construct a creative and critical response to a diverse range of short stories
Formulate edited work which provides evaluative feedback to peers
Discuss their textual analysis skills when reading and responding to their peers' creative writing, both orally and in writing
Develop a short story of their own following appropriate form, genre and style
Debate critically the short story form in various genres

title: The Publishing Circuit
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to publishing industries and contexts Evaluate publishing trends Analyse traditional and independent publishing pathways to identify appropriate career strategies Produce creative and professional outputs aligned with industry expectations Consider how creative praxis and professional identity evolve in response to industry needs

This topic introduces creative writers to the Australian publishing industry. By learning about the past and rapidly changing future of publishing, exploring different traditional and indie publishing pathways, and crafting a suitable creative artefact and book pitch, the topic will help creative writers develop their professional identity and plan for a productive future in the industry.
learning_outcomes: Identify publishing contexts and trends
Connect creative praxis to context of industry
Establish strong understanding of the history of publishing
Think critically about the past and future of publishing
Develop awareness of new publishing technologies

title: Workshop: Reading and Writing
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce creative writing students to workshop processes Provide students with opportunities to develop skills in critiquing their own, and others' writing Encourage students to read and respond to published creative writing from local and international authors from a range of literary styles and contexts Explore and contextualise issues relevant to creative writing as a discipline

"If you want to be a writer you must do two things above all others: read a lot and write a lot." - Stephen King. Hit the ground running and get writing in this first-year creative writing workshop. This topic offers first-year BCA (Creative Writing) students an introduction to critically analysing and workshopping creative writing at a university level. The emphasis in this series of two-hour workshops is on reading and responding to published creative writing, for thinking about critical concepts related to creative writing theory, and to the discipline of creative writing. Bearing this in mind, students will devote much of this semester to engaging with articles and professional book reviews, reading and writing like literary critics, and writing critical responses to short works of fiction. There will also be opportunities for students to develop their editing skills, to produce their own creative pieces, to discuss the craft of writing and related matters to do with the publishing industry.
learning_outcomes: Discuss your textual analysis skills when reading and responding to your peers' creative writing, both orally and in writing
Develop a short creative piece of your own following appropriate form, genre, market and style
Respond critically to published creative writing and appraise techniques of the craft through clear and effective written communication
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCACW-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Creative Writing) 1a Admission into BCACWFP-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Creative Writing) - Flinders City Campus Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a))

title: Editing & the Industry
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the current state of Australian publishing Explore the different stages of the editing process Simulate real-world editing practice through interactive activities Consider the impact of new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, as well as changing perspectives on the roles of the author, the editor and publisher in the publishing process Connect students with professionals in the editing and publishing industry

This topic examines the role of editors and prepares students for their future engagements with the publishing industry. Through readings and interactive activities, publishing challenges, controversies, and the impact of new technology are all considered and debated. Students will develop an editorial identity and practice their editing skills on an existing story draft, and then create their own written piece responding to an issue in contemporary publishing of their own choosing. They will also practice using a style guide to edit writing at a professional level. The topic will appeal to students involved in creative writing in the areas of fiction and non-fiction, and it relevant to both aspirational writers and those who have an eye on work in the publishing industry.
learning_outcomes: Identify the different components of the publishing industry
Draft and edit a publishable written artefact on the topic of editing and/or publishing
Analyse current and future challenges to editing and publishing awaiting students when they enter the industry
Create an editorial identity and philosophy
Demonstrate ability to engage with each stage of the editing process

title: Love and Death: Writing Romance and Horror
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Identify and evaluate commercial genres of fiction Discuss examples of literary and cultural theory Practice exegetical writing Compose new works of creative writing Explore the connections between scholarly research and creative praxis

Love and death have always been the heart and soul of literature, and Romance and Horror are two of the biggest-selling commercial genres of the 20th and 21st Centuries. In this topic, we will explore the popular commercial genres of Romance and Horror from the perspectives of writers, cultural theorists and literary critics. We will explore the commercial publishing industry, generic conventions, and relevant literary theory and criticism, while conducting analyses of examples from literature and/or film, and producing written work.
learning_outcomes: Analyse creative and scholarly texts
Compose new creative writing in commercial genres
Apply scholarly ideas to creative praxis
Compose exegetical writing explicating creative praxis

title: The Epic: Writing Epic Fiction
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to create a single piece of prose fiction that engages with concepts, themes, and structures of epic literature. Students will research and read selected examples of epic literature and draw on this as inspiration for their own fiction.

From The Odyssey to Viking Age sagas, One Thousand and One Nights to Star Wars and Game of Thrones, the epic has fascinated readers and writers for centuries. In this topic, students will engage with epic stories - ancient and new - to explore their enduring popularity. We will consider a range of media and texts and analyse key aspects of the epic form, including: heroes, voyages to distant lands, sweeping casts of characters, mythic and memorable tones. Students will reflect upon significant themes and elements of the genre when constructing imaginative works of their own.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to engage with the editing process
Draft a creative piece that engages with epic literature
Develop appropriate responses to literary texts through the production of creative pieces
Debate the relevance of the cultural and historical context of literature to your reading of literature with peers and experts from the field

title: Workshop: Craft and Critique
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Apply advanced understandings of genre and writing strategies Create new work Develop students' skills as workshoppers, editors, readers, presenters and listeners Analyse the creative industries through seminars and special workshops

This topic, conducted weekly in two-hour blocks, allows second-year Bachelor of Creative Writing students to focus on individual projects in an intensive workshop environment. Students develop their editing skills, practise oral presentation, and are given the opportunity to work collaboratively with each other. In addition, they develop their understanding of genre and advanced writing strategies through practical exercises.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate your strengths and weaknesses as writers and set goals
Actively reflect on your creative work
Evaluate your capacity to read, listen and research critically
Produce moderately complex original work
prerequisites: CRWR1100

title: Workshop: Reading and Writing
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:

Hit the ground running and get writing in this intensive creative writing workshop. This topic offers creative writing students an introduction to critically analysing and workshopping creative work at a university level. The emphasis in this series of two-hour workshops is on reading and responding to published creative writing, for thinking about critical concepts related to creative writing theory, and to the discipline of creative writing. Bearing this in mind, students will devote much of this semester to engaging with articles and professional book reviews, reading and writing like literary critics, and writing critical responses to short works of fiction. There will also be opportunities for students to develop their editing skills, to produce their own creative pieces, to discuss the craft of writing and related matters to do with the publishing industry.
learning_outcomes: Respond critically to published creative writing and exegetically to your own new writing
Appraise techniques of the craft through clear and effective written communication
Evaluate skills as writers and set clear goals
Develop a short creative piece of your own following appropriate form, genre, market and style
Discuss your textual analysis skills when reading and responding to your peers' creative writing, both orally and in writing
prerequisites: Admission into BCRWR-Bachelor of Creative Writing

title: The Fantastic: Writing Speculative Fiction
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the concept of metaphor in fantasy fiction Empower students with the critical and creative skills to turn areas of socio-political interest into an engaging fantasy story Simulate a real-world context by inviting students to distil their fantasy concept into a story treatment and respond to critical feedback Combine critical thinking and imagination through the model of practice-led research

This topic explores genres of the Fantastic, which may include Science Fiction, Fantasy, Speculative Fiction, Alternative History, Utopias and Dystopias, and Myths and Legends. In this reading intensive topic, we will explore generic conventions alongside relevant literary theory and criticism. The process involves close analysis of examples and production of writing in class. It is therefore essential that students do the relevant readings before attending lecture/workshops, where active participation is encouraged.
learning_outcomes: Research a subject of personal interest to you and devise a metaphorical representation of that research
Argue the link between real world issues and fantasy fiction
Apply external critical feedback to your creative process
Integrate the core creative and research skills into the planning and mapping of an original creative work
Evaluate existing creative works to identify the processes the creators have undertaken
Determine your own creative process through self-reflection

title: Workshop: Anthology A
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Identify creative thinking and practice; Explore writing techniques and processes Explore writing techniques and processes Extend skills in developmental editing Practice professional editorial communication Enhance knowledge of the writing and publishing industry Extend skills in creative writing Practice reading and writing reflexively Develop the capacity to work with teams to produce polished creative work Showcase skills learned in the degree to produce high quality creative output

This topic is the first stage of the Creative Writing Anthology project. In this topic, students will analyse examples of short story anthologies and develop a reflective editorial practice as they craft editorial responses to existing collections. Students will design the theme and outline of the group Anthology project. They will then write to the chosen theme of the anthology and collaborate in creating an effective workshop environment as they workshop their creative writing. At the conclusion of the semester, students will have a draft manuscript of an anthology of short stories.
learning_outcomes: Produce high quality creative writing
Effectively communicate editorial feedback
Extend creative thinking and creative practices
Demonstrate the capacity to be a cooperative team member
Model ethical and professional beahvior in publishing and writing processes
Extend understanding of the contemporary publishing industry
Demonstrate synthesis of editorial feedback in creative drafting process
Effectively and actively participate in collaborative workshopping

title: Workshop: Anthology B
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Extend creative thinking and creative practices Practice editorial skills developed over the course of the degree Engage with professional editorial and publishing practice in collaboration with industry partners Produce high quality polished creative work Collaboratively lead the creation of a workshop environment Showcase the high level writing and editorial skills in a complete developed manuscript anthology of creative work

In this topic students will be taken through the editorial process, taking the manuscript developed in the Anthology A topic and will work in editorial teams to copy edit the manuscript and then edit the publishing galleys. Working with a publisher, students will produce neccessary elements for publication of the manuscript, such as cover briefs, blurbs, marketing plans and more. By the conclusion of the topic they will have a manuscript ready to be published.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capacity to be a cooperative team member
Demonstrate synthesis of editorial feedback in creative drafting process
Extend understanding of the contemporary publishing industry through a professionally written editorial report on an anthology collection and through a professional interview
Effectively and actively participate in collaborative workshopping
Extend creative thinking and creative practices
Effectively communicate editorial feedback
Model ethical, professional behaviour while critiquing others' work with positive and actionable language

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 1
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide the students with: The skills necessary in a range of contemporary dance techniques at an increasing level of complexity The necessary physical learning skills and approaches for contemporary dance practice Dance partnering capabilities and skills that can be used in a variety of settings The skills necessary to explore and perform dance improvisation

This topic is designed to introduce various forms of contemporary dance training, their associated concepts and philosophies. The body of work will explore approaches and structures of training utilised in professional contexts including anatomical design and stylistic interpretation. As part of that genre there will be sessions dedicated to partnering work and improvisation in order to employ these skills and understandings in a range of contexts.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and apply concepts to improvisation
Facilitate collaborative dance partnerships
Synthesise principles of technical dance training into contemporary movement form
Construct expressive movement language
Reflect on process and performance of contemporary dance
prerequisites: Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance)

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 2
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the skills to: Use musical rhythm and pitch notation Recognise how musical elements are interpreted by human anatomy Apply the principles of Yoga as a technique and philosophy employed in body conditioning for dancers Explore the nature, causes, management and methods of preventing dance injuries and strategies for coping with injury

This topic introduces students to a range of auxiliary disciplines related to the life of a professional dancer, including music studies, anatomy and conditioning. Students will develop an understanding of musical structures, epochs, and styles and how these transform into movement and dance. This will relate to an understanding of how a dancer's body transforms music through investigating anatomical functions such as breathing and the kinesiology of body movement. The topic will develop methods through which dancers understand their bodies as part of their craft, and methods through which they can employ methods and training to ensure continued good health, fitness, and injury mitigation and rehabilitation.
learning_outcomes: Use basic musical notation in sound scores
Apply the principles of safe dance practice to conditioning
Apply anatomical knowledge to promote health and prevent injury in dance practice
Apply anatomical knowledge to manage immediate and long-term dance injuries
Integrate musical elements into movement practice
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 ^ DANC1100 - Dance Workshop and Theory 1 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 3
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce classical ballet exercises, concepts, and terminology at a developing level Build on the dancer’s flexibility, strength and coordination in the technique Encourage a self-disciplined approach to training Instil critical thinking about contemporary dance practice and theory Connect the processes of analysis to the artist’s practice

This topic combines the traditional training of Classical Ballet and the theoretical study of Contemporary Dance Performance with its origins. Students will develop a critical approach to the study of dance, including the relationship between practice and theory, the ability to place dance in an historical framework, and political, social, and culture issues that affect dance performance. The classical training is an integral and complementary aspect of a contemporary dancer's training and provides physical rigor that strengthens the body.
learning_outcomes: Execute classical ballet exercises
Adapt instruction to strategies of self-directed improvement
Critique dance artists, genres and practices using theory
Synthesise practice and feedback to exhibit control in set ballet vocabularies
Research and evaluate performance in the contemporary dance genre
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC1101 - Dance Workshop and Theory 2 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 4
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with skills to: Consolidate, refine and develop contemporary dance techniques and practical and theoretical knowledge Build on the knowledge of the functionality and design of movement Further develop diverse approaches to training in contemporary dance through improvisation Explore and practice compositional structures and devices as they relate to recent and current industry practice Work collaboratively in group devised choreography

In this topic the technical dance training is designed to extend and refine the skills of the students. They will be offered the opportunity to develop their own classroom exercises under supervision to support their understanding of the discipline. It will also include advanced improvisation sessions, tumbling and mat work. Compositional studies will be reintroduced to further the creative collaborative skills of the performer. A particular emphasis will be placed on the exploration of the relationship between dance and music
learning_outcomes: Integrate theory and technique in dance practice
Choose appropriate approaches in the creation of original movement content
Critically reflect on process of movement creation
Produce choreography through engagement with compositional elements
Create contemporary dance sequences using technical processes
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC2100 - Dance Workshop and Theory 3 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 5
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop: The ability to research, analyse, interpret and evaluate dance works, both the student's own and others Greater proficiency and versatility in writing about dance and in discussing ideas in an academically appropriate manner An appreciation of the dancer as actor, and the multi- disciplinary nature of current dance/theatre practice An increased ability to rehearse and performance in a safe manner Knowledge of the movement disciplines of Yoga which engender efficient, integrated mind/body use

Students will be introduced to theoretical approaches to enable the analysis, interpretation, evaluation and contextualising of dance works in the 20th and 21st Centuries. The role of dance writers and critics in documenting and communicating dance will be explored. Modern and Postmodern dance innovators and their works will be studied and compared. Students will examine issues such as gender, popular culture, and social cultural issues, both through a critical investigation of the history of dance, but also through the development of acting skills though which these, and other, ideas and issues are presented to an audience. Through further exploration of how dancers represent these ideas through performance, they will continue to develop health and fitness tools for a career as a professional dancer.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise acting with dance performance
Synthesise dramaturgical approaches with dance performance
Communicate the theory and process of professional dance practice
Analyse the processes of theatre making
Determine physically safe practices in dance preparations
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC2100 - Dance Workshop and Theory 3 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Dance Production 1
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to: Assist in the development of original material for a dance work Use rehearsal techniques and practice to develop a performance Work effectively as part of an ensemble Apply correction and dance techniques to deliver the requirements of live performance Experience performing in front of a live audience

This topic requires students to participate in a major dance production. This includes the creation, development and rehearsal of works under the direction of industry choreographers. The process will involve the transference of the work from a rehearsal room to a staging and performance context.
learning_outcomes: Produce concept-devised movement through physical based research
Reflect on processes for rehearsal and performance
Produce a sustained and holistic performance
Collaborate in creative and performance processes
Collaborate with others to create duo and ensemble performances
Apply individual awareness and movement skills to performance
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC1101 - Dance Workshop and Theory 2 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Dance Workshop and Theory 6
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with opportunities to: Develop complex performance attributes that are associated with the various genres of contemporary dance practice, through research and performance application Increase the performer's technical dance capacity and range Expand the practice and knowledge of advanced improvisation techniques Build a proactive physical training practice that allows for external as well as self-managed improvement/development
