In this topic students will experience a range of approaches and undertakings that reflect professional contemporary dance practice. The practical sessions will focus on advanced technical performance and research skills including structured improvisation. All students will be expected to participate through discussion that will include self and peer analysis and reflects on concepts and ideology of the work explored. To further support the demands of the training students will extend their fitness through advanced classes in a physical exercise discipline (e.g. Yoga or Pilates)
learning_outcomes: Compose innovative choreographic content
Improvise in response to provocations and instruction
Embody expression into movement
Critically reflect on processes for dance making
Execute variations of set and improvised movement
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC2102 - Dance Workshop and Theory 5 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Dance Production 2
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to: Develop an understanding of professional rehearsal techniques and practices as used in dance Realise a complex dance performance, through the application of dramaturgy and choreography developed in group contexts Contribute conceptual and creative ideas in a constructive and collaborative manner Critically review and process all aspects of own performance with the intension to improve/progress the standard of work and practice

In this topic students will produce and perform their graduate performance piece. The work will be selected, choreographed, and developed as an ensemble, with all students contributing to the final performance piece.
learning_outcomes: Respond creatively to complex choreographic questions using advanced compositional insight
Reflect on the outcomes of performance
Express emotions into complex abstract movement ideas
Create holistic performances as part of an ensemble
Exhibit professionalism in all creative processes
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 2 DANC2222 - Dance Production 1 3 DANC3100 - Dance Workshop and Theory 6 Must Satisfy: (1 and 2 and 3)

title: Theatre in Context
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a diverse range of historically and stylistically significant dramatic texts within the context in which they were initially created and presented Interrogate and consider the contemporary relevance and meaning of key dramatic texts and theatre movements Develop students’ critical thinking skills and the ability to contextualise artistic work Develop students' research and writing skills in a variety of forms Assist students in the transition to university life by providing opportunities for learning with peers and colleagues

As an introduction to theatre, this topic examines the relationship between text and performance and the role of the audience as it encounters and responds to live performance in space and place. Students will learn to interrogate theatrical conventions in key periods of theatre history, consider how theatre reflects social, political, and cultural forces, and identify how spatial dynamics are encoded in performance texts. The topic aims to develop students’ skills in reading and understanding both text and performance, enhance their discussion skills, and further their ability to think and write analytically, critically, and creatively.
learning_outcomes: Apply research skills in the formulation of essays and short writing assignments
Apply knowledge of the set texts including their context and significance within the history of drama
Contribute effectively to group discussions
Analyse the role of space and place in the theatrical theatrical encounter
Appraise live performance in written and oral forms
Critically analyse key concepts in written and oral forms

title: Contemporary Drama
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a range of historically and stylistically significant 20th and 21st Century theatrical texts including film and demonstrate their implications in performance as well as their cultural contribution Explore the history of representations of gender on stage Develop students' critical thinking and their ability to consider key issues in both group settings and individual study Develop students' research and writing skills in a variety of forms

Contemporary drama wrestles with the legacy of theatre history that excluded non-male and non-white bodies from the stage. This topic examines a wide range of modern and post-modern theatrical and film texts that seek to create new representations of gender and identity. The topic aims to develop analytic and critical skills, prepare students for second- and third-year study, and provides opportunities for practical and creative activity.
learning_outcomes: Research and formulate both an essay and a creative pitch
Analyse set texts and understand their significance within the recent history of drama and film
Contribute to group discussions including presenting seminars
Apply knowledge of staging practices to understand a range of representations of gender and identity

title: Voice and Movement 1A: Breath, Awareness, Presence
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Assist the student to identify idiosyncratic habitual patterns that limit the expressive potential of body and voice Assist the student to develop the ability to embody breath, muscularity, and resonance in the moment of speaking Assist the student in beginning the process of investigating the body’s diverse range of psycho-physical expression Assist the student to develop an embodied understanding of the concepts of Weight, Space, Time, and Flow Assist the student to connect knowledge from voice/movement/acting

This topic will introduce students to key Voice and Movement methodologies, providing them with the foundations for their psycho-physical awakening and development.
learning_outcomes: Locate connection between breath, sound imagery, and movement
Apply an awareness of breathing that is responsive to, and in support of, impulse and release
Map specific anatomical landmarks
Demonstrate an understanding of the connection between voice/movement/acting
Demonstrate an embodied understanding of the concepts of Weight, Space, Time and Flow
Critically reflect on performance practice
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Acting 1A: Laying the Foundations
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Empower the student to start to allow kinaesthetic response to drive action Assist the student to develop critical awareness of actor training practices and their contexts Assist the student to begin to develop an ability to monitor and regulate growing connections they are experiencing Equip students with the fundamental tools they need to approach text in both the live and screen space

This topic introduces students to foundational actor training approaches that have significantly shaped creative practice for the live and screen space.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate clarity in impulse, action, thought and connection
Facilitate collaboration in the rehearsal and presentation of embodied performance tasks
Execute first-principle improvisation
Critically reflect on performance practice
Activate first-principle story telling
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD - Bachelor of Performance (Directing) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Voice and Movement 1B: Connection, Embodiment, Authenticity
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Assist the student to understand and utilise the potential of the body-voice in transformation, style, and inhabitation Assist the student to extend kinaesthetic connection towards application to text work, devising and making Continue to develop and extend the sensation of freedom in the voice, with deep connection to the body and impulse Begin to expand the students’ movement range and observational skills via Movement analysis frameworks (Laban Movement Analysis and Viewpoints) Assist the student to connect knowledge from voice/movement/acting

This topic will deepen and expand the student’s Voice and Movement knowledge, enhancing the connection between breath-sound-imagery-movement, and commencing the journey of applying Voice and Movement skills to the process of transformation.
learning_outcomes: Detect specific psycho-physical movement patterns in others, and the self
Critically reflect on performance practice
Demonstrate an understanding of the connection between voice/movement/acting
Deepen the connection between breath, sound, imagery and movement
Demonstrate muscularity, imagination and a responsive embodiment of language
Map sites of resonance across the body
prerequisites: DRAM1005

title: Acting 1B: Developing the Language of Performance
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Activate the imagination by connecting self-awareness with the extant needs of character and/or text Develop and challenge the students’ sense of range and its possibilities Assist the student to create new pathways in themselves: expanding the toolkit Assist the student to shape a sophisticated and conscious approach to structure and text in both the live and screen space

This topic builds on the skills and knowledge developed in Semester One. Students will deepen their sense of personalisation and ownership through the enhanced activation of imagination, and via the application of action work to text, for the live and screen space.
learning_outcomes: Practice the principle of clear and simple transitive action work in collaboration and in monologue work
Apply the principle of endowment, to activate the imagination
Detect the dialogue between camera (technology) and body
Critically reflect on performance practice
prerequisites: DRAM1006

title: Production Laboratory: Foundations
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to assist students to: Apply and integrate performance and research skills within production contexts Develop collaboration and group communication skills in creative contexts Analyse and evaluate their knowledge and skill in production contexts

In production laboratories, students develop and apply their performance and production skills in the context of a specific project. This topic provides students with opportunities to learn foundational collaborative skills in the development of creative projects, to respond to creative briefs, and to evaluate their skills development and progress. The topic also introduces students to principles of research-led practice, including applying individual research skills to collaborative performance outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Apply performance and research skills in collaborative practice
Interpret and respond to creative briefs in production contexts
Create outcomes for performance and production contexts
Evaluate creative outcomes and personal skills development
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) 1c Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Acting Fundamentals
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to major performance training practices and methodologies Assist the student to develop critical awareness of actor-training practices and their contexts Allow students to explore performance practices as they relate to text in both live and digital (screen) spaces

This topic will introduce students to select fundamental actor training practices and methodologies. Students will explore select practices in Movement, Voice and Acting, and examine how they are synthesised to live and digital (screen) spaces.
learning_outcomes: Identify and execute fundamental ‘Stanislavskian’ principles
Improvise with confidence
Locate the connection between breath, sound, and movement
Demonstrate fundamental and foundational skills in Movement, Voice, and Acting
Apply basic action work to monologue and scene work
prerequisites: 1 Admission into UCA-Undergraduate Certificate in Acting 1a Admission into BCITP-Bachelor of Creative Industries (Theatre and Performance) 1b Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b))

title: Voice and Movement 2A: Dynamism and Range
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Strengthen the students’ technical control of voice and movement choices Extend the students’ psycho-physical connection towards application in text-based, and devised outcomes Assist the student to consciously harness and guide vocal choices with deep connection to the body and impulse Assist students in applying expressive gesture as a tool for psycho-physical communication

This topic focuses on the expansion of the students' Voice and Movement range, challenging them to move beyond familiar patterns of expressive action and behaviour, and deepening their psycho-physical awareness and readiness.
learning_outcomes: Practice the concept of self-monitoring safety in the use of the voice and the body
Demonstrate a strong understanding of the connection between voice/movement/acting
Construct an approach to the voice and body as eloquent and subtle communicators of refined and specific thought
Employ psycho-physical, expressive movement skills across a range of text-based and devised tasks
Integrate the balance of technique and psycho-physical awareness
Examine your sophisticated understanding of movement/voice performance practices
prerequisites: DRAM1007

title: The Actor and the Text
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Explore major analytical concepts relating to performance and text. Develop students' capacities to undertake textual analysis. Investigate playwrights and their work as part of the creative process. Apply performance skills through staged readings of theatrical texts.

This topic will introduce students to textual analysis, contextual and character-based research skills, and the page to stage process. Students will apply their fundamental acting techniques to the staging of a rehearsed reading of a classic or contemporary work included in the broader Drama curriculum. They will engage with the socio-political context of the work, the history of its performance, and the ideology of the playwright to deliver their own version to their peers.
learning_outcomes: Develop independent research skills into theatre texts and their playwrights
Apply an understanding of fundamental skills in Movement, Voice, and Acting to an existing performance text
Evaluate how techniques are effectively applied to performance
Implement performance techniques and research in the creation of a staged reading
Identify how acting techniques and research skills are combined in creative practice
prerequisites: 1 Admission into UCA-Undergraduate Certificate in Acting 1a Admission into BCITP-Bachelor of Creative Industries (Theatre and Performance) 1b Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) 1c Admission into BEDSHPE-Bachelor of Education (Secondary Health and Physical Education) 1d Admission into BEDSEC-Bachelor of Education (Secondary) 1e Admission into BFTVSI-Bachelor of Film and Television (Screen Industries) 1f Admission into BFTVSP-Bachelor of Film and Television (Screen Production) Must satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f))

title: Acting 2A: Developing Methodology
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Assist students to begin to develop and articulate a bespoke working process Provide students with a variety of tools for interpreting a range of contemporary and twentieth century texts to create interpretative performance Build the students’ ability to apply their developing skills across a variety of styles and performance demands Assist students in transferring psycho-physical, interpretive and expressive skills to digital (screen) spaces

This topic focuses on deepening students' psycho-physical, interpretive and expressive skills, and the synthesis of this embodied knowledge into contemporary and heightened-language texts. Students will be empowered to begin to develop their own processes of work for live and digital (screen) spaces.
learning_outcomes: Modify the scene analysis framework (action/objective) for screen
Unify complex layers (i.e. facts v invention/imagination) in both live and digital spaces
Employ advanced, embodied text analysis techniques to complex text, both contemporary and heightened
Integrate psycho-physical, interpretive awareness with text and outwardly-directed energy
Examine their sophisticated understanding of acting practices
prerequisites: DRAM1008

title: Production Laboratory: Devising and Collaboration
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to collaborative and intermedial ways of working Develop students’ skills in devising, movement, and film Provide opportunities for students to plan, devise, create, and present a short-format piece Develop students’ ability to think, research and write about collaborative and intermedial methods for creating new work

Creating original performance and production outcomes in interdisciplinary mediums and contexts are vital skills in the performing arts. This production laboratory topic introduces students to collaborative, imaginative and interdisciplinary methods for creating new work. Students will explore and apply a range of devising techniques, as well as dramatic and film languages, to create innovative intermedial performance and production outcomes. Students will develop skills in undertaking individual research to inform collaborative devising processes, as an introduction to practice-led research.
learning_outcomes: Discuss a variety of collaborative and intermedial ways of working
Evaluate collaborative ways of working and your personal development in devising, movement and film making skills
Create outcomes for performance and production contexts
Apply devising, movement and film making skills in collaboration with peers
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) 1c Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Voice and Movement 2B: Transformation and Power
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Continue to assist students to integrate psycho-physical, interpretive, and expressive skills to contemporary and complex texts Empower students to make powerful, dynamic, and heightened choices in a safe and supportive environment Continue to assist students to integrate skills from Movement and Voice into diverse live and digital (screen) spaces Develop a strong sense of heightened awareness, listening, compassion and readiness.

This topic continues to develop the students’ psycho-physical, interpretive, and expressive skills. Students will be empowered and challenged to deepen awareness, release and readiness, and to imaginatively diversify their movement-vocal choices.
learning_outcomes: Combine principles of text structure, pitch, rhythm, and image/metaphor
Synthesise stamina, range and articulation into extant and improvisatory text
Integrate psycho-physical skills to an extant, and improvised/devised dramaturgical score
Adapt expressive psycho-physical and interpretive skills to an established dance-theatre choreography
Produce an artist journal/self-reflection examining your sophisticated understanding of learning tasks associated with the expansion of expressive range
prerequisites: DRAM2011

title: Acting 2B: Harnessing Methodology
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Continue to assist students to integrate psycho-physical, interpretive, and expressive skills to contemporary and heightened (Shakespeare) text Empower students to make powerful, dynamic, and heightened choices in a safe and supportive environment Continue to assist students to integrate skills from Movement and Voice into diverse live and digital (screen) spaces Develop a strong sense of heightened awareness, listening, compassion and readiness

This topic deepens and furthers skills and knowledge harnessed in Semester one. It empowers students (actors, directors and/or makers) to harness an autonomous psycho-physical process for a range of live and digital (screen) spaces.
learning_outcomes: Examine your sophisticated understanding of acting practices
Create an embodied response to the varying demands of a range of dramatic texts
Combine interpretive, dynamic vocal and physical choices within an extant text score
Formulate an autonomous working process
Adapt nuanced psycho-physical skills to screen performance/digital technologies
prerequisites: DRAM2012

title: Production Laboratory: Extension and Experimentation
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide students with an opportunity to employ experimental, innovative, and exploratory ways of working Develop students’ skills in independently producing a multi-faceted work of performance Equip students with hands-on experience in planning, devising, creating, presenting, and documenting a short-format piece Enhance students’ conceptual skills, by conceiving a performance project as a strategy for enquiry into an area of new knowledge

This topic builds on the foundations established in the first-year production laboratory by providing an opportunity for students to interrogate chosen areas of form, style and content through research and creative work. This topic will extend and expand students’ interpretive, expressive, technical and design skills through the development of more complex performances. Students conceive a performance project designed to explore a particular challenge in process, form, or genre, then identify the combinations of developing skills they want to employ in new ways to meet the demands of that research question.
learning_outcomes: Create outcomes for performance and production contexts
Evaluate experimental and intermedial methods for creating new work, and your personal development
Apply interpretive and expressive skills in collaboration with peers
Synthesise a range of different working methods and techniques to devise an approach to meeting a specific creative challenge
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) 1c Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Popular Performance: From Bankside to Broadway
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to the significance of popular performance traditions to the development of contemporary theatre Enable students to explore selected performance works drawn from the history of popular performance Provide opportunities for students to learn to recognise and articulate the function of music and song in popular performance traditions Develop students’ ability to think, speak, and write about popular performance of the past, present, and future in a critically-engaged and aesthetically-informed way

For much of its history, theatre has been a popular performance tradition that catered to a broad cross-section of society. This topic explores performance forms from the Early Modern period through to the present day, with a focus on popular entertainments that feature music and song. Beginning with the legacy of the Jacobeans, students will travel through melodrama, Grand-Guignol, and worker’s theatre, before arriving at contemporary stand-up comedy and the Broadway musical. This topic explores how popular performance developed across time and cultures, and invites students to consider how contemporary theatre might draw on its roots in popular entertainment as it seeks out new audiences.
learning_outcomes: Research, formulate and present dramaturgical reports and research essays in a clear, coherent and confident manner
Discuss potential future alignments of contemporary theatre and the popular tradition
Appraise what is popular about performance across time and in different cultural contexts
Analyse the set theatrical texts, their landmark presentations and significance in relation to the development of popular theatre
Apply knowledge of the function of music and song in theatre to written and verbal analysis of popular performance

title: Making Meaning: Space and the Body
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop students’ understanding of the dynamics of space in performance, and how those dynamics may be incorporated into the creative process of conceiving and delivering a production Equip students with the skills to shape and control meaning in non-determinative live and virtual spaces including in-the-round/installation/virtual reality Enhance students’ awareness of both the innate spatial dynamics of various architectural forms of real and virtual performance spaces, and the capacity of the creative team to instigate spatial dynamics through design and the interaction of the performers’ bodies

This topic develops the ability of directors, designers, and dramaturgs to shape meaning in dramatic narratives through the dynamic interplay of space and the body. The topic traces the evolution and contemporary manifestations of the drive to break down barriers between spectators and performers, and to engage the audience’s complicity in the act of performance. Students will engage with performance making for non-traditional theatre spaces, including in-the-round, traverse, immersive, and virtual reality spaces. At the heart of this work is the study of storytelling through space via the body, and the body in space.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how spatial dynamics enhance and inform performance in non-determinative live and digital spaces
Develop a design response to performance text which prioritises the communication of meaning through body in space and proxemics
Communicate concepts related to spatial dynamics to actors and creative collaborators in the production of a new or extant scene for live or virtual spaces
Demonstrate a practical and intellectual understanding of spatial dynamics in performance for live and digital space
prerequisites: Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing)

title: Creating Performance: Ethical Practice
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to Develop students’ awareness of ethical issues arising when handling complex dialectics in performance in relation to interpretation, context, and visualisation Enable students to apply semiotic analysis to identify potential ethical issues and evolve solutions

This topic assists directors, designers, and dramaturgs in building an ethically aware practice of both the aesthetics of live performance, and the collaborative processes involved in its creation. Students will interrogate the interplay between the ethics of representation and the ethics of practice, developing skills in managing complex intersectional identities in the rehearsal room and on stage. The topic considers issues such as representation and cultural appropriation, the power dynamics of the rehearsal room, respectful multi-stakeholder collaboration, and intersectional equity. Across each issue, students will be introduced to the ethics and cultural protocols of working with Indigenous collaborators, aesthetics, and processes.
learning_outcomes: Develop a series of protocols to foster a creative and culturally safe working rehearsal room environment
Apply a practical, ethical, and intellectual understanding of semiotic analysis to various tasks
Discuss potential issues of appropriation and cultural representation in legacy theatrical texts and original creative responses
Engage actors in collaborative exploration of a dramatic text in a manner that empowers them to begin devising a creative interpretative response
prerequisites: Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing)

title: Modern Theatre: The Rise of the Director
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce a range of historically and stylistically significant 19th and 20th century landmark performances and demonstrate their implications for subsequent theatrical development Introduce the development of the director's role through a range of key playwrights and practitioners from Europe and beyond from the 1880s to the 1950s Provide students with the opportunity to develop an historical perspective by recognising, articulating and evaluating these theories and performances in the light of current theatre practice through contemporary adaptations Develop students' ability to think, speak and write about performance in a critically engaged, aesthetically informed and ethically responsive manner.

This topic is concerned with the emergence of the director in modern theatre and the concomitant development of theatrical modernism. This includes a study of some of the major playwrights and practitioners in Europe and beyond whose work codified and challenged realism and naturalism as dominant theatrical styles from the 1880s to the 1950s.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the set theatrical texts, their landmark presentations and significance in relation to the emerging concept of the director
Investigate directing as an interrogative practice through contributing to group discussion and responding constructively
Question the historical distinction between realism and naturalism, and appraise its implications for contemporary theatrical practice
Research, formulate and present performance reviews and essays in a clear, coherent and confident manner
Apply appropriate aesthetic criteria and historical perspective in analysing performances and the cultural contexts from which they have come

title: Adaptation and Audiences
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Increase students' knowledge and appreciation of a range of ways theatre and audiences interact and inform one another Introduce students to the field and practice of adaptation Encourage students to adopt a reflexive, inquiry-based approach to adapting stories for target audiences Provide opportunities for students to develop practical skills in preparing, writing and presenting a performance

The relationship between audience and performance is dynamic and diverse. Theatre makers might seek to attract, challenge, empower or engage specific audiences through the form and content of their work, and specific audiences can inform how and where theatre is made, funded, marketed and delivered. This topic introduces students to the dynamic relationship between audience and performance through the particular lens of adaptation – translating a story from one context into theatre. Students learn a variety of intentions and approaches for adapting work for theatre, analyse adapted performances, and write their own adaptations for target audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles and practices of adaptation to create and evaluate a performance for a target audience
Discuss and describe the impact and relationship of target audiences on theatre and performance activities
Analyse and evaluate the principles and practices of adaptation in performance texts
Evaluate your skill as a maker and collaborator for target audiences

title: Voice and Movement 3A: Synthesis
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Empower students to begin to develop an autonomous preparatory Voice-Movement practice Assist students to further develop awareness, readiness, and dynamism Develop the students’ ability to work with curiosity, dexterity and play Assist students in integrating dynamic and nuanced choices to a range of texts and styles

This topic enhances the students' ability to synthesise acquired Voice and Movement skills and knowledge, empowering them to develop an autonomous process that supports the process of transformation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the connection between voice/movement/acting
Implement conscious awareness and control of vocal/physical choices
Construct an autonomous preparatory practice (Voice and Movement) for performance
Employ conscious deployment of vocal and physical power and range
Produce an artist journal/self-reflection articulating an advanced knowledge of learning tasks associated with the synthesis of performance methodologies
Integrate the vocal/physical choices any text might demand, with deep psycho-physical connection
prerequisites: DRAM2014

title: Acting 3A: Developing Autonomy and Authority
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Guide students towards a resilient, optimistic, and autonomous practice Empower students to develop and refine their own unique creative process Assist students to approach complex characters with authority

This topic advances skills and knowledge developed in previous years. It provides students with strong foundations to work autonomously across a range of live and digital (screen) spaces.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an advanced knowledge of professional acting practices
Integrate sophisticated psycho-physical, interpretive skills in the development and presentation of heightened language in a variety of styles
Modify principles of transformation and heightened language to the screen environment
Synthesise psycho-physical and interpretive skills to the virtual (screen) environment
Produce independently developed performances informed by a range of texts, techniques and conceptual frameworks
prerequisites: DRAM2015

title: Voice and Movement 3B: Consolidation
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Prepare the students' body-voice for the many demands of psycho-physical expansion Assist the students to transfer Movement-Voice skills from one creative practice to another with authority and ease Continue to assist students to develop a rigorous and aware psycho-physical process Assist the students to make powerful connections between voice/movement/acting Assist the students to make nuanced, sophisticated and imaginative psycho-physical choices for the live and digital space

This topic expands on Movement and Voice skills acquired over the years of the students' study. It will empower them to work with psycho-physical authority and ease, and to make sophisticated and nuanced choices for live and digital (screen) spaces.
learning_outcomes: Integrate acquired psycho-physical, interpretive skills to diverse directorial methodologies
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the connection between voice/movement/acting
Produce an artist journal/self-reflection articulating an advanced knowledge of learning tasks associated with a consolidation of acquired movement and voice skills
Synthesise acquired psycho-physical, interpretive skills to an eclectic range of contemporary and classical text
Combine significant theoretical and practical, interpretive concepts and methodologies
Compose an autonomous, rigorous working practice that is resilient and vibrant
prerequisites: DRAM3011

title: Acting 3B: Consolidation
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Enable students to synthesise heightened and complex language through sophisticated textual interpretation and performance Enable students to create advanced character-driven screen work through bold, authentic creative offers and collaborative ensemble practice Enable students to apply the comprehensive range of acting and directing techniques acquired throughout the degree Enable students to implement sophisticated independent rehearsal and preparation techniques for autonomous creative work

This topic consolidates and extends skills and knowledge acquired over previous years. Students will strengthen their autonomous processes, and apply skills acquired over the course of the degree to solve performance challenges of increasing complexity and stylistic diversity.
learning_outcomes: Implement independent rehearsal processes and preparation methods with professional autonomy.
Critically analyse complex theatrical texts using advanced vocal and physical techniques for heightened language
Articulate an advanced knowledge of acting practices
Create compelling character-driven screen performances through bold creative choices and effective ensemble collaboration
Integrate acting and directing methodologies flexibly across different performance contexts
prerequisites: DRAM3012

title: Production Laboratory: Engaging Audiences
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Allow students to refine their acquired skills and knowledge via the rehearsal, performance or production of a complex text Provide students with a platform to work under the conditions that mirror the professional industry Equip students with an advanced understanding of how performance and design choices are interpreted by a general public audience to draw meaning from the performance Analyse and evaluate students’ intentions for further study or work-place engagement

This topic explores the co-creation of meaning in performance, by the meeting of a creative ensemble and an impartial audience in the live encounter. Students are invited to assemble a broad range of production tools including sound, lighting, design, costume, and digital assets with the embodied work of the performer in space, to communicate meaning in a performance that is coherent and perceptible to a general public audience. Students gain an in-depth understanding of how audience reception shapes and informs creative practice, enhancing their ability to apply a range of advanced research and production skills to a performance outcome.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise the elements of production into a sustained and holistic outcome
Collaborate in professional-standard rehearsal and performance processes
Combine the complex array of skills acquired with an ethical and sensitive professional approach to both process and performance
Evaluate the conceptual gap between the creative intent of the collaborating artists and the perception of the audience
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BCADR-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Drama) 1a Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1b Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) 1c Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c))

title: Arts Practice and the Community
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Increase students' knowledge and appreciation of a range of industry stakeholders and community organisations who collaborate with artists on creative outcomes Enhance students' ability to initiate and respond to collaborative opportunities with external stakeholders in reflexive and inclusive ways (including processes of communication, negotiation, scheduling, implementation of mutually agreed objectives and evaluation of outcomes) Provide opportunities for students to develop practical skills in designing, planning and evaluating a collaborative community engaged arts project

Collaborating with industry stakeholders and engaging with community groups and organisations is a vital skill for working in the creative industries. This topic develops these skills through the exploration of various strategies, policies and approaches to collaborating with external stakeholders in creative projects. Starting with the initiation of a project through to the projects evaluation, the topic culminates in a presentation of students’ original community-engaged arts projects.
learning_outcomes: Design, pitch and evaluate a community engaged arts project (including suggested processes for communicating with stakeholders, proposed schedules and timelines for completion, acknowledgement of potential barriers to the project, examples of creative practice and a description of the expected project outcome)
Discuss and analyse professional collaboration processes, policies and practices in community engaged projects
Design, justify and evaluate a process of documentation for a community engaged arts project
prerequisites: 36 units of topics

title: Making Meaning: Inside the Frame
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to Provide students with an understanding of the ways in which spatial and compositional dynamics lie at the heart of visual storytelling Develop students’ awareness of the ways in which other visual and non-visual elements such as lighting, costume and sound/music may compliment the core spatial and compositional performance artefact Develop skills in deploying visual elements to create mood, convey emotion, and support the dialectic of the performance Enhance students’ capacity to effectively communicate their creative vision to actors and creative collaborators

This topic develops the skills and knowledge required by directors, dramaturgs, and designers to create compelling and meaningful visual storytelling. Students will consider how meaning in performance is curated within a frame, whether the fourth wall of the proscenium arch stage, the film frame, or the digital screen. This curation includes the control of space, object, colour, and texture, as well as the dynamic interplay between the body of the performer and visual cues. Students will experiment with different media and technologies to develop their skills and understanding of visual storytelling, including live theatre, film, and television.
learning_outcomes: Integrate spatial and compositional dynamics to create an original interpretation of a new or extant text in either live or digital form
Evaluate the ways spatial and compositional dynamics enhance and communicate meaning within a range of performance spaces, both live and digital
Evaluate the ways visual and non-visual elements create mood as well as convey emotion and meaning within a range of performance spaces, both live and digital
Synthesise visual and non-visual elements to create an original response to a new or extant text in either live or digital form
prerequisites: Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing)

title: Creating Performance: From Concept to Vision
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop students’ understanding of the role of director/creative team/actor collaboration in the development of new ideas Introduce students to an intellectual framework for generating creative inspiration for performance from recurring personal interests and instinctive response to external stimuli Examine the role of design elements in shaping the creative vision, including set, lighting, sound, and costume Create a practical plan for realising the creative vision in a production

This topic guides directors, dramaturgs, and designers in harnessing their own creative and intellectual preoccupations as inspiration for conceiving original work. Through a combination of practical exercises, research, and critical reflection, students will learn how to use their own unique perspectives and interests to generate original concepts and content for performance. Students will explore the process of curating and developing such concepts into a unified and unique artistic vision which informs all aspects of a production, including design, acting, and dramaturgy.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the process of generating original and innovative ideas in the production of theatre
Synthesise design, costume, sound, and lighting elements into a pratical production and/or learning tasks
Adapt discoveries made in collaboration with a creative team to the preparation and delivery of various learning tasks
Integrate personal responses to creative stimuli into the dynamic creation and interpretation of new, devised and extant texts for live and digital space
prerequisites: Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing)

title: Contemporary Australian Repertoire
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to key practitioners in contemporary Australian theatre and film Consider broader thematic and representational trends in contemporary Australian repertoire Assist students in articulating future directions for Australian performance practice

Since the turn of the millennium, contemporary Australian performance has embraced identity and authenticity as organising principles. Along with the advances powered by global movements including Black Lives Matter and Time's Up, contemporary Australian repertoire is more diverse than ever before. This topic introduces students to the broad thematic trends in contemporary Australian repertoire for stage and screen, empowering them to imagine their own place in this dynamic industry.
learning_outcomes: Assess the dominance of identity and authenticity in evaluating contemporary Australian repertoire
Critically discuss thematic trends in contemporary Australian repertoire for stage and screen
Critique contemporary Australian repertoire in the context of specific ecologies of practice
Appraise potential future directions for Australian stage and screen

title: Production Laboratory: New Work Development
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Allow students to deploy their acquired skills and knowledge to a range of professional creative development scenarios. Provide students with advanced training in professional practice workplace conditions. Provide students with an exciting opportunity to collaborate with a range of academics, professional artists and/or students from other disciplines. Equip students with knowledge and experience to begin to identify desired areas of specialisation in their creative practice.

This topic will provide opportunities for students to develop advanced skills in collaborative creative development for works of live and digital text-based performance which contain a component of originality. Working in peer-to-peer professional-practice simulacra, students are required to synthesise performance skills developed in the first two years of training in acting, directing and theatre-making, in order to originate new collaborative solutions to the challenge of creating original works of performance.
learning_outcomes: Integrate diverse creative practice techniques to devise original solutions to a range of production and dramaturgical challenges.
Analyse and evaluate the principles and practices of creative development in collaborative contexts
Apply the principles and practices of creative development to conceive and deliver a performance work that contains elements of originality.
Simulate professional industry processes in the creation of performance works.
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BPFA-Bachelor of Performance (Acting) 1a Admission into BPFD-Bachelor of Performance (Directing) 1b Admission into BPFTM-Bachelor of Performance (Theatre Making) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b ))

title: The Artist as Researcher
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Increase students' knowledge and appreciation of the recent evolution of contemporary performance theory and practice Provide opportunities for students to recognise, articulate and evaluate the relationship between time, space, and the body in contemporary performance theory and practice Enable students to appreciate the hermeneutic relationship between theory and practice in creative arts research Develop students' ability to think, speak and write about performance in a critically-engaged, aesthetically-informed and ethically responsive manner

This topic explores the role of the artist as a researcher, across both theory-led and practice-led models of creative research. To do so, it introduces significant contemporary theories of performance that focus on the operation of space and place, time and event, the body in action, kinesthetic empathy, embodiment, performativity, and presence and desire. Each theoretical exploration is accompanied by a creative response, so that students develop an appreciation of the hermeneutic relationship between theory and practice. Students also conceive, develop, and execute a small individual research project that explores theoretical and/or practical questions drawn from their own artistic practice and as suited to their degree.
learning_outcomes: Determine opportunities for engaging with aesthetic criteria using related ethical considerations in your own practice as creative researchers
Appraise relevant performance work using appropriate theoretical and aesthetic criteria
Evaluate contemporary performance practice and theory with respect to the operation of time, space, and the body
Evaluate the significance of selected performance works and place them within larger frameworks of contemporary performance practice
Synthesise practice-led and theory-led approaches to creative arts research in the design and execution of an individual research suited to your degree specialisation
prerequisites: 36 units of topics

title: Dramaturgy and New Writing
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Outline developments in the history, theory and practice of dramaturgy Introduce aspects of dramaturgical practice, including new writing for performance Provide students with an opportunity to develop skills in dramaturgical research and analysis Develop students appreciation of new writing for performance

This topic introduces aspects of dramaturgical practice in theatre production, with a focus on new writing for performance. Dramaturgy involves applying skills in research and analysis to theatre production. It includes study of the culture, society and conventions that form the context of play scripts, and an enquiry into the significance of making theatre for audiences today. What kind of world does the play represent? How is that world best represented on stage? And what will make the play work in the theatre for an audience today?
learning_outcomes: Apply dramaturgical research skills to the development of new performance work
Appraise dramaturgical practice, with reference to new performance
Critically discuss and critique key developments in the history, theory and practice of dramaturgy in theatre production
Create and evaluate original performance work
prerequisites: 1 72 units of topics 2 Admission into BCADN-Bachelor of Creative Arts (Dance) 3 36 units of topics Must satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3))

title: Advanced Ensemble Performance Practice
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Expose students to professional production practices in the performing arts and entertainment sectors. Deepen students’ knowledge of workplace skills and expertise specific to the live and digital performing arts. Provide students with advanced, collaborative ensemble performance creation skills. Provide students with opportunities to work collaboratively or individually on original work, and in response to industry-style briefs.

This topic provides advanced professional development in performing arts ensemble practice for actors and directors, including voice and movement skills, live and virtual production practices, the embodied creation of original works and collaborative leadership roles.
learning_outcomes: Effectively collaborate on the conception, design and creation of industry standard live and digital projects in the performing arts.
Consistently and dynamically apply or direct the use of collaborative performance skills at an industry-ready standard, to a range of tasks for the live and screen space.
Dynamically, consistently and safely deploy or direct the use of ensemble vocal and physical performance techniques to meet industry needs in a range of live and digital media performances.
Critically evaluate and adapt current practices in performer preparation in the performing arts and entertainment industries, to suit a range of scenarios.
prerequisites: 1 Admission to HBPF-Bachelor of Performance (Honours) 2 DRAM3014 Must satisfy: ((1 and 2))

title: Entering the Profession
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Expose students to emerging trends in the performing arts and entertainment industries, related to their area of expertise. Assist students in identifying a career pathway and beginning the transition from study to employment in the performing arts sector. Provide students with an environment in which they will undertake a supervised project in an industry simulacrum setting. Provide students with the skills and opportunity to develop a professional portfolio and industry contacts that may assist their entry to the workforce.

In this topic students respond as actors or directors to a range of real-world industry provocations and tasks in the Australian performing arts and entertainment industries. Evaluating skills and strategies developed in the undergraduate training for their suitability to meet the needs of such tasks, students conceptualise and deliver an original, embodied creative response, in live or digital (screen) media as appropriate.
learning_outcomes: Critique your own professional practice expertise, and select strategies for autonomous preparation of audition and screen-test material and/or pitching materials in the industrial context.
Evaluate a range of advanced voice/movement skills and apply them to ensemble scenarios that meet the priorities of prospective employers.

Evaluate professional scripts (performance texts) in use in the performing arts sector, and paradigms of employability in the casting industry, to determine appropriate material for a professional portfolio.
Appraise professional tasks set by prospective employers and conceptualise and deliver an appropriate embodied creative response to meet the needs of those tasks.

Evaluate the needs and priorities of the prospective employers in the performing arts and entertainment industries, and formulate a persuasive case regarding the suitability of your skills and creative practice, to meet such needs and priorities.
prerequisites: 1 Admission into the HBPF-Bachelor of Performance (Honours) 2 DRAM7010 Must satisfy: ((1 and 2))

title: Higher Degree Thesis (Master)
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire the appropriate research skills and training to enable them to work independently and complete a body of research at the level of a Masters by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Master's degree by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Masters by Research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Master's degree by research.
learning_outcomes: Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work
Validate research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Demonstrate their review and application of the literature in writing and orally (where appropriate)
Demonstrate their capacity to formulate a significant problem and synthesise a complex body of knowledge
Explain their understanding of chosen methodological practices
prerequisites: Admission into Masters degree by research

title: Higher Degree Thesis (PhD)
school: College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire high-level research skills and training, to enable them to work independently and complete a body of original research at the level of a Doctorate by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Doctorate by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Doctorate by research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Doctorate by research.
learning_outcomes: Assess research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work
Demonstrate their review and application of the literature in writing and orally (where appropriate)
Validate the originality of their research topic in relation to a broader framework of knowledge
Explain their mastery of appropriate conceptual and methodological skills
Independently assess evidence of an original investigation or testing of ideas and competence in independent research or experimentation
prerequisites: Admission into Doctorate by research

title: Design for Sustainable Manufacture
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Comprehension and practical referencing to both historical and modern day mass manufacturing techniques Comprehension of raw material resource acquisition and processing into modern materials used in mass manufacturing along with the cost associated with such Understanding of Environmental concerns of raw material acquisition and processing along with Circular Economy advocacy and recycling challenges within modern manufacturing Case Study analysis of a common consumer product and thus advocating improvement in the manufacturing techniques and material choices made Sustainable manufacturing applications and TRUE costing analysis: Specifically considering the eventual waste product into the environment and the reduction of such negative environmental effects

History of manufacturing and materials to modern day. The understanding of early material discovery and development, the Industrial Revolution, the emergence of ISO Standards and precision manufacturing (the first lathe, hand tools, the first CNC machine, Injection moulding technologies, through to rapid prototyping, additive manufacturing and 3D printing Design Engineering - Supply Chain and raw material Resource Management and global awareness of Logistics and Costing of such Materials, processes, fabrication techniques, assembly, testing, product standards and their role in design and engineering Design Management in optimising costs and the BOM, reliability, Finite Element Analysis (FEA), simulation and modelling, safety, time-to-market, and Quality Assurance schemes within the management of New Product Development (NPD) Sustainable Design and Manufacturing expectations of todays modern consumer society and the advocacy of Circular Economy within Waste and Resource Management framed by the realities of recycling truths
learning_outcomes: Comprehend mass manufacturing techniques, materials and related technologies and the application of this awareness to product analysis
Have knowledge of the historical and current manufacturing methods used in mass manufacture and rapid prototyping activities in consumer product production
Provide critical analysis of a common consumer product from the perspective of Design Engineering and the decisions made in its manufacture
Apply and analyse Sustainable Product Design Strategies with a specific goal to reduce, reuse and recycle whilst implementing a circular economy approach within mass manufacturing

title: Design Studio
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topics aims to introduce students to: Design Management and effective use of Advanced Manufacturing in the concept development of a consumer product Design Thinking and Design Strategy as a core competency in NPD New Product Development Human Centred Design approaches applied to the prototyping stage of discovery The Role of the Chief Design Officer (CDO) within a modern organisation and their role's competencies Sustainable Design consumption and the true cost of mass consumerism through the lens of resource management The understanding of Logistics and Supply Chain activities and challenges expected in NPD The concept of exploratory failure in the development of prototypes and POC Proof of Concept experimentation Encouraging the student to engage local industry and concept discovery for external advice and advocacy in a potential for a sponsored project and/or continuation of a WIL placement or activity. This will provide students with reality driven design development rigour, hopefully delivering an industry and client focused "real world" experience.

A Design and Advanced Manufacturing industry focused consumer or medical device project encouraging a formal platform in providing students with an experience of the multi-disciplinary nature of design and business problem solving. The project will be developed in conjunction with selected professionals and/or a client who presents a current business problem. This will require the application of innovative design, manufacturing and business model techniques in a consulting framework integrating topics studied throughout the Bachelor of Design and Technology. This effort will be considered a Capstone Project utilising Ethnographic and User Experience Research.
learning_outcomes: Work as a member of a team to design a product or process
Gain competency in the Supply Chain aspects of a product category including Advanced Manufacturing control mechanisms
Apply appropriate techniques and tools in the development of a modern consumer product design
Utilise Sustainable Design strategies and Less is More approaches to NPD and design development
Have a better appreciation of the application of Design Strategy and Human Centred Design
prerequisites: ENGR1711

title: User Experience and Ergonomics
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The topics aims to introduce students to: User Experience (UX) as the core tenet of this topic and its qualitative research activity Identify the differences of UI and UX and why there is a legacy of misunderstanding within the field Human Centred Design approaches to accruing actionable insights within the problem definition stage Nuances of Ergonomics within product design and service contacts with a consumer Adverse Event and causation identification within a case study evaluating system errors and product failures The role of the Chief Design Officer (CDO) within a modern organisation and their role's competencies Sustainable consumption and the true cost of mass consumerism through the lens of resource management Design Management and effective use of Ergonomics as a driver in understanding the consumer Design Thinking and Design Strategy as a core competency in the management of an organisation

Corporate Design Management and Consumer Product Design require a Human Centred approach to its modern execution. Many efforts simply qualify the experiences of the consumer to nominally identify the gaps in the ‘system’ or product. The greater need is the qualitative research side of the equation: with the Human (consumer) at its core. Human Computer Interaction (HCI) along with Human Machine Interface (HMI), are the guide rails of this ethnographic research initiative. UX Design and User Experience Mapping will highlight Ergonomics in Design and Design Management as the core tenets of this topic. Specifically focusing on the core differences of UI Design terminology and UX Research and qualitative approaches to consumer reasoning. UI and UX are most often spoken of in the same sentence and this topic expressly differentiates UX Research activities relating to consumer facing design activities. Design for Sustainable Manufacture DFsM related to consumables will be an additional practicum effort. Embracing User Experience Mapping activities along with available trade software as iterative prototyping tools, students will gain the appreciation of qualitative research versus quantitative and the need to define the consumer sentiment rather than a statistical bias for a decision. Iterative prototyping approaches framed within the focal point of a consumer experience is the core driver of this topic. Application of Design Management principles referencing Design Strategy within management decision trees. Emphasising the need to empower autonomy within an organisation's structure for better corporate outcomes. Activities will utilise Ergonomics to embrace Human Centred Design.
learning_outcomes: Identify specifications for a New Product Development (NPD) effort through the application of User Experience Mapping aligned to your chosen field: i.e. medical product design
Utilise modern UX prototyping tools and software applications that drive the iterative concept discovery process
Coordinate the elements of Design Thinking and Strategy and the application of such in consumer problem definition activities (NPD)
Utilise Human Factors and Ergonomic principles in evaluating Adverse Event case studies and identify causal effect analysis to the system or human error
Advocate and apply the use of Design Strategy and Design Thinking activities within a defined management Case Study and anticipate the outcomes
Frame Qualitative Research activities with the intent to more accurately gauge the consumer sentiment with effective use of Focus Group evaluations

title: Design for Sustainable Manufacture GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
Comprehension and practical referencing to both historical and modern day mass manufacturing techniques Comprehension of raw material resource acquisition and processing into modern materials used in mass manufacturing and production and the cost associated with such Understanding of Environmental concerns of raw material acquisition and processing along with Circular Economy advocacy and recycling challenges within modern manufacturing Case Study analysis of a common consumer product and thus advocating improvement in the manufacturing techniques and material choices made Sustainable manufacturing applications and TRUE costing analysis: Specifically considering the eventual waste product into the environment and the reduction of such negative environmental effects Management of the Supply Chain and Logistics of modern global manufacturing and resource acquisition

History of manufacturing and materials to modern day. The understanding of early material discovery and development, the Industrial Revolution, the emergence of ISO Standards and precision manufacturing (the first lathe, hand tools, the first CNC machine, Injection moulding technologies, through to rapid prototyping, additive manufacturing and 3D printing Design Engineering - Supply Chain and raw material Resource Management and global awareness of Logistics and Costing of such Materials, processes, fabrication techniques, assembly, testing, product standards and their role in design and engineering Design Management in optimising costs and the BOM, reliability, Finite Element Analysis (FEA), simulation and modelling, safety, time-to-market, and Quality Assurance schemes within the management of New Product Development (NPD) Sustainable Design and Manufacturing expectations of todays modern consumer society and the advocacy of Circular Economy within Waste and Resource Management framed by the realities of recycling truths New Product Design (NPD) and Management's role in defining PRODUCT costing along with BOM Bill of Materials and SUPPLY CHAIN logistics and the realities of such, including disruptive events analysis. i.e. think Covid effects on supply chain resources Initialising NPD proposals using SUSTAINABILITY as a core tenet of the discovery activities into the viability of a mass consumer product and its downstream effects on the environment
learning_outcomes: Have knowledge of the historical and current manufacturing methods used in mass manufacture and rapid prototyping activities in consumer product production
Apply and analyse Sustainable Product Design Strategies with a specific goal to reduce, reuse and recycle whilst implementing a circular economy approach within mass manufacturing
Evaluate Product Specification determinants with the understanding of Intellectual Property protection of novel mechanical structures and the purpose of a Utility Patent
Provide critical analysis of a common consumer product from the perspective of Design Engineering and the decisions made in its manufacture
Comprehend mass manufacturing techniques, materials and related technologies and the application of this awareness to product analysis
prerequisites: 1 of ENGR1711, ENGR8711

title: Perspectives on Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Examine the interrelationship of social discourse, historical, legislative and human rights frameworks and the connection these have to the experience of disability and evolution of service provision Introduce and critically discuss theoretical concepts, definitions, perspectives and representation of diversity Encourage critical self-reflection on values, assumptions and biases and how this influences professional interactions and practice

This topic discusses the experience and constructed understanding of disability using a variety of theoretical frameworks. Attitudes towards diversity and disability will be explored and examined in relation to history, legislation, human rights and service practices.
learning_outcomes: Research and think critically about how current literature and media influences the understanding and experience of disability
Articulate and critically self-reflect on personal values, biases, assumptions and learning and discuss how this applies to future practice
Distinguish and discuss the influence of theories and perspectives of disability and how they impact on experience of disability

title: Disability Across the Life Course
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to develop a broad understanding of the key issues arising for people with disability across the life course.

This topic focuses on disability across the life course, including childhood, adolescence, adulthood, becoming older and end of life. Considerations, challenges, and supports for people with disability at these different life stages will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Examine change and growth of people with disability across the life course, that is, from infancy, through childhood, adolescence, adulthood, ageing and end of life
Assess theories of development, including their application across various stages of life for people with disability
Build an understanding of life course approaches to disability

title: Introduction to Disability and Neurodiversity
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Encourage students to critically consider the influence of different conceptual models of disability and neurodiversity Develop student’s understanding of the human nervous system, neuroanatomy and sensory systems Explore the various ways that people live with different disabilities Identify strategies and supports to promote access and inclusion

In this topic students build their understanding of the ways that people live with a range of sensory and physical disabilities and neurodivergence. We critically consider different conceptual models of disability and neurodiversity to appreciate the enormous diversity of lived experience, debunk common myths and misconceptions, and apply a human rights framework to understanding and meeting the challenge of inclusion.
learning_outcomes: Examine and discuss strategies and supports to promote access and inclusion
Critically examine and discuss the features and role of the medical, social, biopsychosocial and neurodiversity models
Identify and describe the basic functions of the human nervous system, neuroanatomy and sensory systems and the role they play in a range of sensory and physical disabilities and neurodivergence

title: Introduction to Communication Diversity and Support Needs
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Explore the diverse ways people develop language and communicate across the lifespan Identify effective strategies to support people with communication diversity and their communication partners

This topic will broadly introduce speech, language, and communication development across the lifespan. It will explore communication for people with disability and introduce effective support strategies to best support individuals with diverse methods of communication, and their communication partners.
learning_outcomes: Discuss an understanding of speech, language and communication development across the lifespan, specifically pragmatic and lexical development
Apply an understanding about the diversity of ways people may communicate and understand the foundations of communication access
Identify and describe effective support strategies to assist individuals with diverse communication methods, and their communication partners

title: The Disability Service Landscape
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Highlight the way that current service systems and policies operate in Australia with the aim to support people with disability Identify the practices required to support a person with disability to navigate service systems Explore how disability professionals can identify and work in partnership with people with disabilities, family, partners, friends and kinship groups Build awareness of the role(s) of disability service professionals

This topic focuses on the current policy and practice landscape in which people with disability receive supports. Students will explore the network of systems within which support to people with disability is provided and consider their role(s) in these systems. This will include the ways they will work in partnership with people with a disability and their family, partners, friends and kinship groups, other allied health professionals, advocates, and the wider community. It also builds awareness around the role of disability service professionals.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the roles of disability service professionals and how this intersects with key stakeholders, including people with a disability and family members, partners, friends and kinship groups, other allied health professionals and the wider community
Demonstrate appropriate interpersonal and interprofessional strategies for working in the disability service landscape
Apply current knowledge of the contemporary practice landscape in which people with disability receive support in a range of contexts

title: Critical Issues in Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to raise students' awareness of wider social justice issues faced by people with disability and the role disability professionals play in working to ameliorate these issues.

This topic explores some of the systemic issues and attitudes facing people with disability that lead to persistent discrimination, inequity and disadvantage. These include inaccessible housing, transport and public spaces; criminal justice; violence and abuse; and access to health care.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategies for working towards systems-level change to address the longer-term causes underpinning the problems
Distinguish own role in supporting people with disability who experience persistent discrimination, inequity and disadvantage
Articulate key systemic issues facing people with disability
Build an understanding of human rights approaches to disability

title: Advocacy and Working in Partnership
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims: to examine how to foster effective collaborative partnerships and explore advocacy principles and strategies for working with people with disabilities and significant people in their lives

This topic introduces students to the role of practitioners in developing and fostering effective collaborative partnerships with people with disability, families, supporters, and service providers. It will also provide an overview and application of advocacy and self-advocacy principles to maximise quality of life and the potential for people with disability for self-determination, empowerment and independence.
learning_outcomes: Examine the effect of having a family member with disability and considerations in the development of collaborative relationships with families, such as culture, family systems and family structure
Identify and evaluate strategies and practices for positive collaborative partnerships with people with disability, family members, and other stakeholders to maximise quality of life
Apply advocacy principles and theoretical frameworks and concepts to working in collaborative partnerships with people with disability, family members and other stakeholders
Identify, analyse and evaluate the role, purpose and practices surrounding various forms of advocacy with and for people with disability, including self-advocacy
prerequisites: 1 18 units of DSRS Level 1 topics 2 Admission into BHS-Bachelor of Health Sciences 3 13.5 units in DSRS Level 1 topics 4 Admission into BBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Psychology) 4a Admission into BSW-Bachelor of Social Work 4b Admission into BSWFP-Bachelor of Social Work Must Satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3) or (4 or 4a or 4b))

title: Practicum 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
