This topic aims to introduce students to professional practice in supporting people with disability and provide opportunities to apply and build foundation skills as a competent practitioner through hands on experience with people living with disabilities.

In this topic students will build skills as a competent practitioner; applying foundation skills in a professional context through a 100 hour supervised placement in a disability setting. Students will work closely with people living with disabilities to effectively support them in their chosen daily activities. The topic will also introduce students to critical and reflective practice within their fieldwork experience.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on placement experience including ways in which you are working in a culturally responsive, safe and inclusive way
Implement respectful and professional communication with people living with disabilities and significant others demonstrating effective inter-professional practice
Implement person centred care to support people living with disabilities to make choices that have positive impact on their chosen daily activities
Demonstrate critical and reflective thinking processes to evaluate one’s own professional practice and performance against placement learning goals
prerequisites: 1 18 units in DSRS 1st year topics 2 Admission into BHS-Bachelor of Health Sciences 3 13.5 units in DSRS topics 4 Admission into BBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Psychology) 5 2 of DSRS1201, DSRS1209, DSRS1218 6 Admission into BPSY-Bachelor of Psychology (Honours) 7 9 units of DSRS level 1 topics 8 4.5 units of DSRS level 1 topics 9 Admission into BSHPA-Bachelor of Sport, Health and Physical Activity 10 Admission into BEDSTBDS-Bachelor of Education Studies, Bachelor of Disability Studies 11 13.5 units of DSRS level 1 topics Must Satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3) or (4 and 5) or (6 and 7) or (8 and 9) or (10 and 11))

title: Instructional Strategies
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to: Apply strategies to increase opportunities for learning and independence for people with disability Identify models of instruction such as: Active Support and various self-management and cognitive strategies

This topic explores evidence-based strategies for supporting people with disability in developing functional living skills that promote independence, inclusion, and quality of life. Students will learn how to design, implement, and evaluate skill-building programs using approaches such as systematic instruction, video modelling, and assistive technology. Emphasis is placed on understanding individual needs and applying person-centred practices. Through case studies and practical activities, students will gain the knowledge and skills to support meaningful learning outcomes in areas such as personal care and community participation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate various instructional procedures and assess those that may provide the desired outcome/s
Determine the appropriate procedures that can be used to develop functional daily living skills
Examine strategies of instruction such as Systematic Instruction and Video Modelling
Identify instructional methods that promote generalisation and maintenance of learned skills
prerequisites: 1 18 units of DSRS Level 1 topics 2 Admission into BHS-Bachelor of Health Sciences 3 18 units of DSRS Level 1 topics 4 Admission into BBSC-Bachelor of Behavioural Science (Psychology) 5 9 units of DSRS Level 1 topics 6 Admission into BHSMPT-Bachelor of Health Sciences, Master of Physiotherapy Must Satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3) or (4 and 5) or (6))

title: Practicum 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to consolidate practice skills in the disability sector and provide opportunities to apply and build skills as a competent practitioner. Students will have the opportunity to contribute to quality service delivery by working effectively as a member of a team and to gain experience in project management.

In this topic students will apply their developing knowledge and skills through a 150-hour supervised placement in a disability setting. Students are required to plan, implement, and evaluate a project during their placement hours. The topic will also build on student’s critical and reflective practice within their fieldwork experience.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective strategies and practices associated with quality service delivery and relevant policies through effective person-centred and inter-professional practice
Demonstrate critical and reflective thinking processes to evaluate one’s own professional practice and performance
Critically reflect on placement experience including ways in which you are working in a culturally responsive, safe and inclusive away
Integrate disability knowledge, skills and professional values though planning, implementing and evaluating a project in a practice environment
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BDCI-Bachelor of Disability and Community Inclusion 1a Admission into BDDE-Bachelor of Disability and Developmental Education 2 45 units of Level 1 and Level 2 DSRS topics 3 DSRS2232 Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a) and 2 and 3)

title: Employment and Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to assist students to develop: Knowledge and skills to effectively assist people with disabilities to access and maintain meaningful employment experiences A repertoire of specific employment support strategies

This topic provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the key concepts, challenges, and practical approaches involved in supporting people with disability to secure and maintain meaningful employment. It explores both theoretical frameworks and applied strategies that promote inclusive, person-centred employment outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the roles/responsibilities of employment professionals in assisting people with disabilities to gain meaningful employment
Offer suggestions for improvement on the impact of various legislative and policy reforms on the employment outcomes of people with disabilities
Determine a variety of work and employment options for people with disability
Identify and explore the issues facing people with disabilities as they attempt to access and maintain meaningful employment
prerequisites: 18 units of DSRS Level 1 topics

title: Disability: Health and Wellbeing
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Identify and examine a range of health issues that may impact the lives of people living with disability Examine the experiences of individuals with disability in accessing health services Identify and discuss strategies and supports which will enable a person with disability to engage effectively with relevant health care services

Like all members of the community, people with disability have health-care needs. However, a large proportion experience difficulty accessing mainstream health care services, including physical access issues, discrimination by health professionals, communication difficulties, financial barriers, diagnostic overshadowing, poor health literacy, and abuse and neglect. This topic explores common healthcare needs of people with a disability and discusses the challenges and strategies to support health literacy and access to mainstream health services. Strategies and supports to optimise the health and wellbeing of people with disability will be discussed. Students will be equipped with knowledge to provide constructive input to team discussions of an individual's health care needs, and skills to support individuals to access and engage with mainstream health services in a positive way.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and summarise the literature describing barriers in accessing mainstream health services that exist for people with disability
Identify and discuss accommodations, supports and strategies to support individuals with disability to access mainstream health services
Critically evaluate the social and medical factors that affect the health and wellbeing of people with disability
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BSHPA-Bachelor of Sport, Health and Physical Activity 1a Admission into BEDSTBDS-Bachelor of Education Studies, Bachelor of Disability Studies 1b Admission into BNE-Bachelor of Nutrition and Exercise 1c Admission into BND-Bachelor of Nutrition and Dietetics 1d Admission into BSAR-Bachelor of Sport and Active Recreation 1e Admission into BSARFP-Bachelor of Sport and Active Recreation - Flinders City Campus 2 18 units of DSRS Level 1 topics Must Satisfy: (((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e)) or (2))

title: Introduction to Principles of Learning and Instruction
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to enable students to understand the theoretical underpinnings and principles of effective learning. Students will also identify and consider the application of fundamental theories and principles of human learning to instructional techniques and support strategies for people with disabilities.

This topic introduces students to human learning theories and principles, including behavioural, cognitive, and socio-cultural influences on the learning process and subsequent behaviour support. It emphasises the importance of critical thinking when considering: definitions of learning; learning styles; social influences; intersectionality; power; developmental perspectives; reinforcement; motivation; self-efficacy; memory and attention. The content is set within the context of working with people with disabilities and learning is related to philosophies and principles within the disability field.
learning_outcomes: Explain fundamental theories and principles of human learning
Identify how environmental, social and cognitive factors influence behaviour
Critically examine how theories and principles of human learning apply to instructional techniques and behaviour support strategies for people with disabilities
prerequisites: 1 22.5 units of Level 1 topics 2 Admission into BLITTHLG-Bachelor of Letters (Health) (Graduate Entry) Must Satisfy: ((1) or (2))

title: Introduction to Positive Behaviour Support
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to enable students to identify appropriate positive behaviour support strategies within a tiered approach for supporting people with behaviour support needs and consider PBS service provision in the context of policy and practice guidelines.

This topic will provide the foundations of theory and implementation of assessments and strategies for supporting people with behaviours of concern to engage meaningfully within their natural environments. It will also consider individualised positive behaviour support plans in the context of broader/universal strategies and approaches to support positive social interactions and maximise community participation.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the underlying principles of positive behaviour support to key stakeholders, including people with disability, family members and support networks
Explain how effective PBS practice is situated within an organisation (i.e across service roles) and within policy and practice guidelines in Australia
Explain positive behaviour support in the context of systems-wide practices that support effective PBS provision within a human rights approach
Illustrate collaborative practices to effectively engage key stakeholders in behaviour support planning

title: Introduction to Counselling Skills
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic focuses on the theory and practice of basic counselling skills that are useful in a variety of work and personal settings, with an emphasis on: Understanding counselling theories and their links to practice in a range of human service roles Opportunities for purposeful practice of counselling micro-skills Completion of an effective and structured counselling interview using basic counselling skills Facilitating personal reflection and peer feedback in skills development Understanding the importance of ethical issues and self-care in human service roles

This topic focuses on developing introductory counselling skills for professional practice. These skills are critical in developing communication skills that are applicable for interprofessional practice and providing therapeutic supports within a variety of human service work settings. Students are encouraged to draw on existing work and practicum experiences gained up to this point in their program of study, and to apply basic counselling skills as an integral part of their future professional practice. This includes understanding basic counselling theories and techniques such as: the practise of micro-skills, trauma informed practice and communication techniques applicable to positive behaviour support.
learning_outcomes: Examine the impact of personal values and attitudes on effective counselling skills, and the ability to articulate these

Identify the ethical and professional issues associated with the counselling process, including awareness of limitations of their own role and skills, and multicultural considerations for clients and professionals
Demonstrate and evaluate basic micro-skills and counselling theories, and how these may be applied in a range of human service roles and settings

title: Communication Rights and Access
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to: Explore communication access from individual and systemic perspectives, providing students with an understanding of the issues impacting upon people who use AAC Evaluate evidence-based and personalised strategies to promote communication access in community settings, including AAC and communication partner instruction Equip students with models to support the analysis of systemic access barriers and propose relevant communication access strategies

This topic will introduce a range of individual and systemic strategies to promote Communication Access as informed by human rights paradigms. The strategies presented in the topic relate to individual approaches such as augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), as well as systemic approaches to enhance communication access in social, educational, and healthcare settings. Topic content emphasises the importance of communication for participation in everyday life and the role of disability professionals in making communities more communication accessible.
learning_outcomes: Propose collaborative processes to design and implement individual communication systems with people who use AAC, communication partners, and other professional stakeholders
Evaluate community-based services using a rights-based model to assess communication access barriers and plan communication access strategies
Synthesise and evaluate key concepts related to the design and implementation of personalised communication strategies (including AAC and multi-modal communication)
Critique communication access strategies against communication rights and legislation

title: Practicum C - Disability and Community Rehabilitation
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide opportunities to be mentored by professionals who will create opportunities to work autonomously and within teams Understand and increase professional competencies Develop and evaluate programs/projects and gain expertise around case management for people living with disability Work collaboratively with a range of professionals to implement and evaluate a task or project Identify effective strategies and practices associated with quality service delivery Contribute to quality service delivery by working effectively as a member of a team Demonstrate an ability to use a systematic approach to case management Demonstrate Professional Practice within a disability organisation

This topic provides opportunities for students to extend their experience working alongside professionals in the field to build upon awareness and professional competencies gained from previous paid or practicum experience. Examination of the role of service provision in the lives of people living with disability and their families continues. Community, education, health and lifestyle provide the context for exploration of practices that support a life of choice for people living with disability with a focus on individual supports and relationships. Students from the Bachelor of Disability and Developmental Education enrolled in this topic will be commencing their third Practicum placement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to use a systematic approach to case management
Reflect on their professional development
Identify effective strategies and practices associated with quality service delivery
Demonstrate Professional Practice within a disability organisation
Work collaboratively with a range of professionals to implement and evaluate a task or project
Contribute to quality service delivery by working effectively as a member of a team
prerequisites: 1 DSRS2236 - Practicum B - Disability and Community Rehabilitation 2 22.5 Units of DSRS2 topics Must Satisfy: (1 and 2)

title: Case Management and Support Coordination
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic focuses on the theory and practice of case management skills that apply to a range of disability and community rehabilitation service settings, as well as an introduction to support coordination in the context of the NDIS, with an emphasis on gaining: An understanding of the knowledge and skills required to facilitate the central roles, functions and stages of case management and support coordination Skills in report writing, negotiation and advocacy in a team environment An understanding of the ethical, professional and self-care issues associated with the case management and support coordination processes in multidisciplinary team environments

This topic provides an introduction to the theoretical principles which enable and underpin effective case management practice in disability, rehabilitation and other human service settings, as well as the practice of support co-ordination in the context of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Areas covered include: determining eligibility and assessment needs; developing, monitoring and evaluating individual program plans; advocacy and negotiation in a team environment; timeliness and cost-effectiveness of service provision; record keeping and report writing. Differences between case management and support co-ordination are outlined, and issues relevant to particular client groups are explored.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the issues and concerns necessary to consider in providing or facilitating case management/support coordination for specific client groups
Evaluate how government social policy influences the delivery of human service roles
Appraise and understand case management and support coordination processes

title: Building Community Capacity
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to explore and learn about: Current research within local, national and international perspectives relating to community development and funding sources Recent social history and benefits of community development in facilitating opportunities for the social inclusion of individuals who are socially isolated, or at risk of social isolation from their communities, including Indigenous communities Role of community development and relevance of participation in community activities of choice and the link to quality of life Principles of identifying and preparing a community development project to create increased opportunities for socially marginalised individuals Principles of preparing a community development project for funding submission

This topic examines both the concepts and role of community development in the lives of people who are marginalised in our communities. Community participation and lifestyle choices provide the context for exploration of the issues, principles and practices related to community development. This topic also provides an opportunity for students to learn about basic principles of community development, project management and submission writing. Particular populations who are currently, or who are at risk of social isolation and limited community participation will be considered, including individuals living with disability.
learning_outcomes: Deduce community needs/issues and strengths for a specific population who are, or at risk of, social isolation from their communities
Develop a sound knowledge of the meaning and benefits of community access, inclusion and participation for people who are socially isolated or at risk of social isolation
Critically analyse current literature relating to community development
Design a community development project proposal and funding submission to increase opportunities for participation in community activities

title: Supporting Early Childhood Development
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to contemporary guidelines for working with young children with disability or developmental differences. Explore current research and evidence-based practice relating to supporting the development of children with disability or developmental differences. Apply contemporary frameworks to the development of goals and selection of supports for young children with disability or developmental differences.

This topic will build on students' knowledge of therapeutic supports when working with children and families. The emphasis will be on working with families, inter-professional approaches and strengths based models of learning. Using play and coaching to promote early learning will be a focus of the topic.
learning_outcomes: Effectively synthesise and discuss the practice implications of key recommendations for supporting the early development of children with disability
Critically evaluate contemporary guidelines and research in early developmental support
Apply appropriate frameworks to the development of goals and support strategies for children with disability and their families

title: Independent Study 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a comprehensive body of research information exploring a specific issue and/or service models to support individuals with a specific support need Advance students' understanding of the theoretical and critical debates pertinent to their chosen area of inquiry Develop students general analytical skills and their capacity for independent research

This topic is designed to enable students to develop areas of interest arising out of theoretical and research literature in disability studies and community rehabilitation. A range of activities is permissible. In each case students must indicate their ability to work independently and demonstrate mastery of the literature in an area of disability studies and community rehabilitation. Students will require supervision from an academic staff member in order to formulate a program of study. Independent studies can be linked to a Practicum Specialisation or be completed as part of an honours program, which will facilitate a student gaining an increased depth of knowledge about supporting individuals dealing with a particular issue or living with a specific support need. Securing the approval of and academic staff member to supervise the study is essential.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional behaviours around the ability to work independently, plan and undertake a research project and submit a report within established time frames
Analyse and evaluate the literature in order to show its strengths and limitations in relation to a specific issue or practice relevant to individuals with specific support needs
Critically evaluate research and practice in relation to individuals with specific support needs
Discuss how the literature might apply to the analysis and understanding of particular problem areas for individuals living with a specific issue or support need
Discuss the possible uses or implications of the research literature and how it might be tested by linking findings to recommendations for service delivery
prerequisites: 22.5 Units in DSRS3 topics

title: Practicum 3: DE Specialisation
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to further enhance student’s skills in assessment, report writing and therapeutic support, and develop relevant competencies as an entry-level developmental educator.

In this topic students will refine their skills as a developmental educator through a 150 hour supervised placement in a disability setting. The topic will build on student’s critical and reflective practice and provide the opportunity to apply and build specialist skills in delivering therapeutic supports, including assessment and functional skills training to improve participation and independence in daily living skills of people with a disability.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical and reflective thinking processes to evaluate one’s own professional practice and performance
Demonstrate effective person-centred and interprofessional practice
Acknowledge the importance of working in a culturally responsive and culturally safe way
Integrate disability knowledge, skills and professional values as a developmental educator in a practice environment

title: Practicum Specialisation
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to further enhance professional skills through: Opportunities to design, implement and evaluate an intervention, service model or management system designed to improve the quality of life of individuals living with disability The facilitation of critical thinking and debate in relation to theory and practice in disability service provision Opportunities for self-reflection about personal performance

The practicum specialisations provide students with choice to apply in practice a specialist area of study within a more focussed organisational setting. A practicum specialisation should be linked to in-depth study into a specialist area or issue and can be linked to independent study.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their practice and professional development
Integrate research and practice in designing, implementing and evaluating a support program for an individual or small group of people with specific support needs
Apply critical evaluation and research to practice, in relation to individuals with specific support needs
Recognise and discuss best practice in relation to individuals with specific support needs around management of disability and other relevant human service organisations

title: Delivering Therapeutic Supports
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Develop advanced practice skills required to deliver therapeutic supports to people with disability, with a focus of functional skills training Develop advanced skills in the ethical administration, interpretation and report writing of standardised and individualised assessments commonly used by developmental educators and other allied health professionals Develop advanced skills in writing case notes, supervision and supporting health professionals and informal supports

As future developmental educators, students in this topic will build their skills in delivering therapy services, including assessment and functional skills training to improve participation and independence in daily living skills of people with a disability. Professional practice skills in ethical administration, interpretation and report writing of standardised and individualised assessments commonly used by developmental educators will be developed.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of ethical administration in standardised and individualised assessments
Implement instructional strategies to increase independence of a learner with a disability
Accurately interpret assessment findings and present recommendations in professional reports for key stakeholders

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Theory to Practice 1
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to: Work collaboratively with key stakeholders to guide planning and assessment to underpin evidence-based PBS practices that uphold a person’s rights. Conduct functional behaviour assessment and interpret assessment data to inform holistic formulation that explains why target behaviours occur in the context of a person’s life and circumstances.

Within this topic, we will explore positive behaviour support (PBS) assessment and planning for people with disability. Specifically, students will develop the knowledge and skills required to (1) be responsive to situations that present risk of harm for a person and others and (2) work alongside key stakeholders to conduct relevant assessment and analysis to inform a functional and contextual understanding of target behaviours. Students will be guided by evidence-based practices that promotes and protects a person’s human rights, aligning with current Australian legislation.
learning_outcomes: Conduct evidence-based PBS assessment and planning guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Develop functional behaviour assessment and formulation reports using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders
Interpret assessment data to appraise risk of harm to the person and others and prioritise the focus areas for intervention
Critically analyse indirect and direct assessment data to inform holistic formulation that provides functional and contextual understanding of behaviour.

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Theory to Practice 2
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to work collaboratively with key stakeholders to develop and implement evidence-based PBS plans that uphold a person’s rights.

Within this topic, we will explore the development and implementation of positive behaviour support (PBS) plans for people with disability. Specifically, students will develop the knowledge and skills required to work collaboratively with people with disability and other key stakeholders to develop and implement function-based PBS plans that support quality of life improvements. Students will be guided by evidence-based practices that promote and protect a person’s human rights, aligning with current Australian legislation
learning_outcomes: Present targeted intervention plans using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders
Formulate PBS goals and targeted intervention plans informed by a functional and contextual understanding of behaviour
Develop evidence-based PBS plans guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Develop implementation plan to monitor the fidelity of PBS implementation

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Practicum and Mentoring Program
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to: Apply PBS theory in practice, including the formulation, development and implementation of evidence-based PBS plans that uphold a person’s human rights. Develop skills in practice leadership required to support interdisciplinary teams in a PBS context

This topic provides student with the opportunity to formulate, develop and implement positive behaviour support (PBS) plans for and with people with disability. Students will apply theoretical knowledge in the field under the supervision of experienced staff and mentors. Specifically, they will carry out risk appraisal and risk response planning and conduct targeted assessment to inform the development of evidence-based PBS plans in collaboration with key stakeholders. Theory and practices will be closely linked, allowing students to further develop PBS knowledge and skills through practice-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Conduct evidence-based PBS practices guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Work in collaboration with key stakeholders to develop targeted intervention plans, including a plan for implementation, using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders
Evaluate behaviour support planning to guide practice improvements
Conduct, compile, and critically interpret individualised assessment data to develop formulation informed by a functional and contextual understanding of a person’s behaviour

title: Capstone for Professional DE Practice and Leadership
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to examine and reflect on current Developmental Educator practice issues and competency standards; facilitate student's ability to develop and manage their own learning and transition to becoming and Developmental Educator; and integrate knowledge and skills gained in the degree as a whole by completing an industry generated project.

This capstone topic in the Bachelor of Disability and Developmental Education provides students the opportunity to bridge the gap between their undergraduate studies and professional future by critically reflecting on their development as a practitioner. Students will engage in a series of workshops and activities designed to hone their critical thinking, reflection and theoretically informed practice on a range of ethical, policy and practice issues core to developing a strong professional identity. This topic also gives students the opportunity to undertake in-depth study related to research, evaluation, quality management or development of an innovative resource relevant to Developmental Education. Students will develop an industry generated project plan and then work independently to complete the project in collaboration with agencies as clients. Students will present their project as a poster presentation in the final seminar to peers, agency representatives and academic staff.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on educational experience, current competency levels and develop a plan to address future learning and competency needs
Work collaboratively with an agency as client to develop and enact a project brief
Design, implement and present industry project findings back to the DE community at a professional level commensurate with an entry-level therapist
Collaboratively identify issues and strategies in the transition from University student to practitioner including contemporary practice frameworks.
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BDDE-Bachelor of Disability and Developmental Education 1a Admission into BDDEFP-Bachelor of Disability and Developmental Education - Flinders City Campus 2 18 Units of DSRS4% topics Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a)) and 2)

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Theory to Practice 2 GE
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to work collaboratively with key stakeholders to develop and implement evidence-based PBS plans that uphold a person’s rights.

Within this topic, we will explore the development and implementation of positive behaviour support (PBS) plans for people with disability. Specifically, students will develop the knowledge and skills required to work collaboratively with people with disability and other key stakeholders to develop and implement function-based PBS plans that support quality of life improvements. Students will be guided by evidence-based practices that promotes and protects a person’s human rights, aligning with current Australian legislation
learning_outcomes: Develop implementation plans and processes to monitor the fidelity of PBS plan implementation and support plan improvements in partnership with key stakeholders
Formulate PBS goals and targeted intervention plans informed by a functional and contextual understanding of behaviour
Develop evidence-based PBS plans guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Compose targeted intervention plans using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Theory to Practice 1 GE
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to: Work collaboratively with key stakeholders to guide planning and assessment to underpin evidence-based PBS practices that uphold a person’s rights. Conduct functional behaviour assessment and critically interpret assessment data to inform holistic formulation that explains why target behaviours occur in the context of a person’s life and circumstances.

Within this topic, we will explore positive behaviour support (PBS) assessment and planning for people with disability. Specifically, students will develop the knowledge and skills required to (1) be responsive to situations that present risk of harm for a person and others and (2) work alongside key stakeholders to conduct relevant assessment and analysis to inform a functional and contextual understanding of target behaviours. Students will be guided by evidence-based practices that promotes and protects a person’s human rights, aligning with current Australian legislation.
learning_outcomes: Critically interpret assessment data to appraise risk of harm to the person and others and prioritise the focus areas for intervention
Compose functional behaviour assessment and formulation reports using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders
Conduct evidence-based PBS assessment and planning guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Critically analyse indirect and direct assessment data to inform holistic formulation that provides functional and contextual understanding of behaviour
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCPBS-Graduate Certificate in Positive Behaviour Support 2 Admission into MDPLDE-Master of Disability Practice and Leadership (Developmental Education) 3 18 units of study at level 8 or 9 Must satisfy: ((1) or (2 and 3))

title: Positive Behaviour Support: Practicum and Mentoring Program GE
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic enables graduates to: Critically appraise and apply PBS theory in practice, including the formulation, development and implementation of evidence-based PBS plans that uphold a person’s human rights. Develop skills in practice leadership required to support interdisciplinary teams in a PBS context.

This topic provides student with the opportunity to formulate, develop and implement positive behaviour support (PBS) plans for and with people with disability. Students will apply theoretical knowledge in the field under the supervision of experienced staff and mentors. Specifically, they will carry out risk appraisal and risk response planning and conduct targeted assessment to inform the development of evidence-based PBS plans in collaboration with key stakeholders. Theory and practices will be closely linked, allowing students to further develop PBS knowledge and skills through practice-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Enact evidence-based PBS processes guided by a person’s rights, values and preferences
Work in collaboration with key stakeholders to develop targeted intervention plans, including a plan for implementation, using professional language that is accessible to stakeholders
Critically evaluate behaviour support planning and guide reflective practices to inform practice improvements
Conduct, compile, and critically interpret individualised assessment data to develop formulation informed by a functional and contextual understanding of a person’s behaviour
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCPBS-Graduate Certificate in Positive Behaviour Support 1a Admission into MDPP-Master of Disability Policy and Practice 2 2 of DSRS8131, DSRS9057 3 ^ DSRS8130 Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a) and 2 and 3) ^ = may be enrolled concurrently

title: Disability, Rights and Embodiment
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop student's understanding of the complex interactions which contribute to the experience of disability: including lived body experience, social constructs of disability and the application of the biopsychosocial model in the Australian service system.

This topic helps students apply contemporary understandings of disability to practice. This includes how to apply an embodied approach to practice, activating human rights, and how to reconcile competing models of disability in service provision.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse how disability is conceptualised and measured at a national and international level
Examine the effect of the biopsychosocial model of disability and health on service systems
Define and outline an embodied approach to disability practice
Understand and examine the practice implications of international instruments such as the UNCRPD and the ICF

title: Leading Through Change
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to enhance practice informed leadership of students engaged in human service provision. Students will explore the interaction of practice, systems, policy, collaboration and co-design in the context of leadership in human services. Students will examine and reflect on their leadership style, flexibility, adaptability and innovation.

This topic focusses on leadership in human services. It will provide students with an understanding of the rapid and dynamic change to leadership approaches in disability services. It will explore the effect of funding models and workforce development on opportunities for leading meaningful service provision. You will develop new strategies for understanding leadership contexts, innovative solutions and how to thrive in continual change.
learning_outcomes: Reflect upon leadership style, approach and skills to develop a leadership action plan
Articulate the complex and dynamic nature of human service leadership and formulate innovative solutions
Demonstrate integration of collaboration, co-design and advocacy in approaches to leadership

title: Policy in the Lives of People with Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
The aim of this topic is to explore social policy theory and application, by understanding the purpose, influences and problems with policy. You will analyse the effectiveness of policy for people with disability and be challenged to understand and influence policy development and implementation to reduce structural disadvantage.

This topic will explore how policy influences people's daily lives, service provision and access to social systems and structures. We will consider major approaches to policy and key policy trends affecting the lives of people with disability. Practical policy skills will be applied, including adapting to change, influencing policy and applying policy within an organisational context.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the strengths and limitations of social policy in disability contexts
Identify and apply opportunities for contributing to constructive policy development
Evaluate the implementation of social policy and formulate implications and strategies for practice

title: Dissertation in Disability (9/18 units)
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with the opportunity to conduct a supervised research study in the broad area of disability/rehabilitation studies and/or its contributing discliplines. The findings of the study are to be presented in a dissertation of approximately 18,000 words, which shall be examined by two examiners.

Students will design and conduct research and submit a dissertation. Through the dissertation, students will demonstrate substantial analysis and research of a problem, mastery of the relevant literature, and thorough understanding of relevant research methodologies. Students will also apply their research findings to the development of disability scholarship.

Clearly describe the methods/procedures used in the study

title: Design and Evaluation of Disability Programs
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide students with an opportunity to explore and learn about: Fundamentals of service design Innovative and practical approaches to program evaluation Needs assessment and policy analysis Challenges related to designing, conducting and using evaluation as a means of enhancing the quality of life of people with disability

The topic is directed towards the design, development and evaluation of disability services. Each student will be required to design and implement an evaluation plan for an existing program, service or facility. Content emphasis will relate to student interest and activities.
learning_outcomes: Determine appropriate evaluation methodologies to respond to an evaluation's purpose and priorities
Examine ethical and procedural issues involved in designing, conducting, analysing and using evaluations
Appraise and review a range of evaluation methodologies for service contexts
Apply service design principles to the process of critiquing and designing inclusive service offerings

title: Advanced Practicum in Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to enable students to construct their professional identity, integrate knowledge, skills, values and disability practice in a human services placement project.

Within this topic students will apply and consolidate disability practice, policy and leadership knowledge and skills through a supervised placement project in the human service sector. Students will be expected to apply a critically reflective and reflexive approach to practice throughout their placement experience.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge, skills and professional values in a human services placement project
Apply and integrate professional practice and communication skills
Demonstrate critical reflection and reflexive approach to evaluating their practice
prerequisites: 1 36 units of study 2 Admission into MDPLA-Master of Disability Practice and Leadership 2a Admission into MDPLDE-Master of Disability Practice and Leadership (Developmental Education) 2b Admission into MDPP-Master of Disability Policy and Practice Must Satisfy: ((1) and (2 or 2a or 2b))

title: Directed Study in Disability
school: College of Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to equip students with an in depth understanding of a specific disability-related issue based on their independent research of that issue. Students will develop research skills, including critically appraising, analysing and communicating research.

In this topic students will independently research a current disability-related issue. Students will critically analyse literature and articulate research/ practice nexus.
learning_outcomes: Formulate a plan for conducting a literature review on a disability related issue, and reporting on the findings
Communicate the literature review findings, including in accessible ways
Critically review and appraise relevant literature
prerequisites: 36 units of study

title: Global Climate Change GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop: Detailed knowledge of processes that control and modify the Earth's climate globally, regionally, and locally An appreciation of the factors that modify climate, including extreme events triggered by geological processes and by climate itself Detailed understanding of the context of modern climates in relation to past ones A capacity to comprehend the contemporary debate about anthropogenic effects in climate change in the context of scientific evidence

This topic covers the definitions of climate, climate variability and climate change within geological, historical, and future time frames. It introduces students to climatic classifications, the composition and structure of the atmosphere, radiation balances and the Greenhouse effect, surface heat fluxes, the general circulation of the atmosphere, the hydrological cycle, carbon cycles, the role of the ocean in the climate system, inter-annual climate variability (e.g. El Nino events), extreme events, sea level rise, climate feedback mechanisms, climate proxies and dating, climate models and climate projections for the future.
learning_outcomes: Apply simple models of global climate changes for assessing the effects of changes to principal driving factors

Evaluate arguments about climate change through reference to earlier climate events in the history of the earth and comment in an informed and scientific way of the effects of human activity on climate
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the science relating to past and contemporary climate and climate change

title: Groundwater Modelling
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to introduce students to physical laws applied to describe, understand and predict the behaviour of fluids in motion in porous media.

This topic offers the basic knowledge needed to understand and to be able model fluids in motion in porous media (groundwater). Following an introduction to general theoretical aspects of earth fluid dynamics, students focus on flows in porous media with applications of Darcy's Law in several case studies.
learning_outcomes: Apply computational modelling of complex dynamical systems
Apply constitutive laws of porous media flow using numerical modelling to a wide range of settings
Outline the physical laws that describe fluids in motion in porous media
Demonstrate enhanced problem-solving, critical-thinking and reasoning abilities

title: Hydrochemistry
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide an appreciation of the nature and role of water chemistry in hydrological systems and develops skills in understanding and interpreting water composition in relation to hydrological and hydrochemical processes.

This topic covers those aspects of water chemistry relevant for an understanding of pollution, water quality and hydrogeochemistry, and includes the physical and chemical properties of natural waters and their classification, expressing concentrations and activity of dissolved chemical species, speciation, dissolution and precipitation, chemical interactions between water, sediments and soils, environmental tracers, nutrient cycles, and solute transport processes.
learning_outcomes: Discuss weathering as a transfer of geochemical constituents between surface and groundwaters and the biosphere
Discuss the relationship between management practices and water quality
Outline the principles of aqueous geochemistry
Outline the major types of water pollutants
Make simple approximations of the transport and fate of aqueous solutes and contaminants
Complete basic applications of chemical speciation modelling software
Explain applications and techniques of geochemical tracers in surface water and groundwater
prerequisites: 1 Admission into GCGH-Graduate Certificate in Science (Groundwater Hydrology) 1a Admission into GDPGH-Graduate Diploma in Science (Groundwater Hydrology) 1b Admission into MSCGH-Master of Science (Groundwater Hydrology) 1c Admission into MEMG-Master of Environmental Management 1d Admission into GDPSCWRM-Graduate Diploma in Science (Water Resources Management) 1e Admission into GCSCWRM-Graduate Certificate in Science (Water Resources Management) 1f Admission into MSCWRM-Master of Science (Water Resources Management) Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f))

title: NCGRT Australian Groundwater School GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to groundwater hydrology. It provides a breadth-first learning approach that covers a wide range of issues and is intended to present a "big picture" overview of groundwater hydrology and associated scientific, management and technology issues that relate directly to it. It is aimed at providing students with little or no background in groundwater hydrology with an overarching understanding of the greater discipline and presents both theoretical and practical aspects of the subject area and clearly articulates its relevance to society (and other less scientific factors such as political, economic, social and ethical considerations) and current pressing environmental issues. Furthermore this topic aims to foster higher level cognition (synthesis, application, critical thought etc) by way of enhanced student-directed learning on topics that are relevant and interesting to the students such that they can explore areas in greater detail by way of assessment that is designed to be flexible, yet comprehensive and fosters higher level cognitive skills (e.g., problem sets, well-designed essay topics, etc).

The NCGRT Short Course program is Australia's leading professional training agency for groundwater hydrology. NCGRT runs the Australian Groundwater School twice yearly. The School was first established in 1965 and has become Australia's leading short course for training groundwater professionals. It introduces students to a wide range of well balanced practical and theoretical concepts pertinent in the science, management and technology related to groundwater hydrology. Subjects covered include: hydrogeology, hydraulics, environmental isotopes in groundwater, recharge / discharge determination, dryland salinity and waterlogging, groundwater conceptual modelling, drilling methods, piezometer and bore design, an array of monitoring and sampling methods, groundwater microbiology, groundwater geophysics, groundwater pollution, groundwater and soil remediation, surface water groundwater interaction, ecosystem dependence on groundwater, groundwater management issues including resource allocation, quality protection and sustainability. This breadth of themes covered and the professional nature of this short course provide a comprehensive coverage of pressing issues in groundwater hydrology.
learning_outcomes: Identify a groundwater management or contemporary issue and write a review about it
Display a high-level vocabulary in groundwater hydrology
Detail the practical drivers for the study of groundwater hydrology, including societal and environmental issues that critically relate to groundwater phenomena
Apply basic and some of the more advanced scientific concepts and tools used by the groundwater hydrologist by way of problem solving

title: Field Methods in Hydrology
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Introduce students to a range of commonly used field and laboratory measurement techniques used in characterising natural systems Provide students with the principles of good professional practice relevant to field collection of data and samples Offer students practical experience in the application of relevant field equipment and collection of field data Extend student skills development in the interpretation of data Extend student skills development in the preparation of professional quality reports relevant to their discipline Broaden student perspectives on the nature of work within environmental disciplines Provide students with opportunities to participate in field work projects in a range of sites in the local region Introduce students to relevant workplace health and safety procedures

This topic will introduce and review a selection of techniques commonly used to monitor and characterise groundwater, surface water and the vadose zone. Students will be trained in the use of appropriate field methods and relevant health and safety procedures. Lectures and readings will provide theoretical background before demonstrating use of appropriate field equipment and collection and interpretation of field data via online lectures and/or face-to face at a local field site. The topic concentrates on teaching practical experiences of equipment use, data collection and interpretation and will therefore complement and built upon theoretical elements developed in other topics.
learning_outcomes: Specify the workplace health and safety issues that relate to working in the field
Analyse and synthesise results and prepare meaningful data reports
Demonstrate knowledge covering the 4 main topics presented in the quizzes
Be aware of policy, cultural and other issues that may impact on the conduct of a field investigation
Understand the strengths and limitations of field samples and data of different types and their impact on report conclusions
Be familiar with commonly used monitoring and measurement techniques in environmental disciplines

title: Physical Hydrogeology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to instil in students' knowledge and an appreciation of the storage and transport of groundwater, and its importance as a global water resource and integral part of the hydrologic cycle.

This topic offers the knowledge needed to investigate the dynamics of groundwater flow in aquifers. The topic is delivered in four parts: Part 1 includes groundwater and the hydrologic cycle - which covers the movement of water in the earth; Part 2 includes groundwater flow, including flow to wells, such as groundwater extraction situations and aquifer testing through pump tests; Part 3 covers the fundamentals of groundwater investigation techniques; and Part 4 covers groundwater management issues, particularly in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Estimate flows between aquifers and surface water systems
Explain the principles of radial flow associated with groundwater wells, and be able to use these concepts to undertake pump tests analysis
Describe in a professional report the application of hydrogeological theory and problem-solving skills through a case study application
Describe the governing equations for groundwater flow and solute transport and apply these to simple hydrogeological problems
Apply hydrogeology theory to real-world calculations of groundwater flow

title: Higher Degree Thesis (Master)
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire the appropriate research skills and training to enable them to work independently and complete a body of research at the level of a Masters by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Master's degree by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Masters by Research award. It is only available to students admitted to a Master's degree by research.
learning_outcomes: Explain their understanding of chosen methodological practices
Demonstrate their review and application of the literature in writing and orally (where appropriate)
Validate research through critical analysis of source material, results of experiments (where appropriate), and published works
Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work
Demonstrate their capacity to formulate a significant problem and synthesise a complex body of knowledge
prerequisites: Admission into Masters degree by research

title: Contaminant and Tracer Hydrology GE
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to instil in students knowledge and an appreciation of the issues relating to groundwater contamination, and the quantification of groundwater flow utilising advanced techniques.

This topic offers the advanced knowledge required to investigate the complex dynamics of unsaturated and saturated water flow and issues related to contaminant transport. The topic is delivered in four parts. Part 1 covers the physical flow and transport processes impacting the transport and spreading of pollutant plumes in soils and groundwater systems. Part 2 discusses the hydro(bio)geochemical processes affecting contaminant transport and the fate of pollutant plumes in the subsurface. Part 3 introduces the major groups of contaminants impacting Australian soils, surface- and groundwaters and discusses the available remediation technologies for different contaminant groups. Part 4 Tracer Hydrology: the last module in this topic concentrates on the use and application of environmental tracers to underpin the understanding of flow and transport processes, flow velocities, recharge and discharge processes and to estimate water residence times in the subsurface
learning_outcomes: Assess the severity of contamination issues, their impact on different receptors and determine suitable remediation technologies available for each contaminant group
Demonstrate high level problem solving, critical thinking and reasoning abilities in relation to soil and groundwater contamination problems
Describe and define processes involved in pollutant transport in the unsaturated zone and in groundwater
Have the ability to apply quantitative concepts to evaluate contaminant movement and fate in soils and in groundwater
Have an advanced understanding of current contamination issues affecting soils and groundwater

title: Higher Degree Thesis (PhD)
school: College of Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview:
The aims of this time-based thesis topic are to support students to develop specialised knowledge and research skills related to the area of their chosen research field. They will acquire high-level research skills and training, to enable them to work independently and complete a body of original research at the level of a Doctorate by research qualification.

This time-based thesis topic supports students to acquire the skills and knowledge to independently complete a Doctorate by research in their chosen field and develop the capacity to complete a body of work to meet the standards of a Doctorate by research award. Independently assess evidence of an original investigation or testing of ideas and competence in independent research or experimentation

Justify and disseminate acquired knowledge and skills through the presentation of well-written work

title: Microcredential: Applied Montessori Methods for Birth to Five
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview: In this practice-focused microcredential, learners examine Montessori materials, lesson design, observation techniques, and classroom management strategies across early years and primary contexts. Participants engage in applied tasks, demonstrations, and reflections to strengthen their capacity to implement Montessori methods in real learning environments.

title: Microcredential: Montessori Foundations for Early Childhood Practice
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview: This microcredential introduces participants to the core principles, philosophies, and practices underpinning Montessori education for young children. It explores Maria Montessori’s developmental theories, including the prepared environment, the role of the educator as a guide, and the significance of observation in supporting individualised learning. Participants will examine key Montessori materials and how they foster independence, sensory exploration, and holistic development. Through critical analysis and practical reflection, the topic connects foundational Montessori concepts with contemporary early childhood contexts.

title: Microcredential: Montessori Leadership and Pedagogical Practice
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview: This microcredential develops advanced capability in leading and sustaining Montessori pedagogy at the organisational level. Modules include mentoring and coaching, quality assurance, curriculum leadership, community engagement, and navigating contemporary challenges in Montessori education. Participants gain the skills to lead teams, shape pedagogical culture, and support continuous improvement in Montessori settings.

title: Montessori Foundations for Early Childhood Practice
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of the philosophical and theoretical foundations of Montessori education for early childhood. Develop participants' ability to interpret and analyse Montessori theory in relation to contemporary educational contexts, diverse learner needs, and current early childhood policies and frameworks. Enable participants to reflect on child‑centred pedagogies and to evaluate how Montessori principles inform holistic development, independence, and ethical teaching practice.

This topic introduces students to the core principles, philosophies, and practices underpinning Montessori education for young children. It explores Maria Montessori’s developmental theories, including the prepared environment, the role of the educator as a guide, and the significance of observation in supporting individualised learning. Students will examine key Montessori materials and how they foster independence, sensory exploration, and holistic development. Through critical analysis and practical reflection, the topic connects foundational Montessori concepts with contemporary early childhood contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on child‑centred and developmentally responsive pedagogies using Montessori frameworks
Evaluate Montessori concepts in relation to current research, policy directions, and contemporary early childhood education practices

title: Applied Montessori Methods for Birth to Five
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This Topic aims to develop learners’ practical skills in implementing Montessori pedagogical methods, using materials effectively, and facilitating purposeful, child‑centred learning

In this practice-focused microcredential, learners examine Montessori materials, lesson design, observation techniques, and classroom management strategies across early years and primary contexts. Participants engage in applied tasks, demonstrations, and reflections to strengthen their capacity to implement Montessori methods in real learning environments.
learning_outcomes: Design and deliver Montessori lessons that align with children’s developmental needs
Demonstrate practical understanding of key Montessori materials across learning domains
Apply Montessori classroom management strategies that support order, autonomy, and engagement

title: Montessori Leadership and Pedagogical Practice
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to strengthen learners’ leadership capability, pedagogical decision‑making, and capacity to support high‑quality Montessori practice at a team or organisational level.

This topic develops advanced capability in leading and sustaining Montessori pedagogy at the organisational level. Topics include mentoring and coaching, quality assurance, curriculum leadership, community engagement, and navigating contemporary challenges in Montessori education.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on contemporary challenges in Montessori education and develop strategies for improvement
Analyse leadership approaches that enhance Montessori pedagogy and organisational culture
Apply mentoring and coaching strategies to support educators’ professional growth

title: Approaches to Play and Learning (Professional Experience: Year 1A)
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Inquire into the relationship between practical experience, research and diverse theoretical perspectives regarding young children’s play, teaching and learning Demonstrate a sound understanding of the importance of play for young children’s learning Practice observational and analytic skills in relation to children’s learning Recognise the requirements of the Professional Experience program, including professional expectations and the legal and ethical responsibilities of a pre-service teacher Collaborate with children and practising early childhood educators to observe and support young children’s learning

This topic investigates the many benefits of play for young children’s learning whilst engaging and extending pre-service teachers’ thinking about the interrelationship between play, teaching and learning. Pre-service teachers reflect upon their experiences as learners as they critically engage with, analyse and reflect on research and theoretical perspectives regarding children’s learning. The topic enables pre-service teachers to develop the knowledge base necessary for engaging a diverse range of infants and young children in significant, meaningful and challenging play-based learning experiences. Concurrently, this topic prepares pre-service teachers for their Professional Experience placements at Flinders University. It introduces the expectations of professional behaviour for the teaching profession, including legal and ethical responsibilities. The lecture series is an essential pre-requisite for placement in school and centre settings. A 5-day community placement introduces pre-service teachers to an Early Childhood setting and allows them to make links between theory, practice and university learning.
learning_outcomes: Apply a theoretical knowledge base to analyse and reflect on the ways decisions about play, teaching and learning are made and implemented
Evaluate the educator’s role in supporting and encouraging children’s play and learning
Demonstrate sound knowledge of the requirements of the Professional Experience program, including professional expectations and the legal and ethical responsibilities of a pre-service teacher
Reflect upon the transition from the role of student to that of pre-service teaching professional through the investigation and implementation of learned theory and observation skills
Examine play; understanding its complexities, including cultural influences, diversity and inclusive perspectives
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BEDECBA-Bachelor of Education (Early Childhood), Bachelor of Arts 1a Admission into BEDECSEBDS-B Education (Early Childhood & Special Ed), B Disability Studies 1b Admission into BEDECBSE-Bachelor of Education (Early Childhood), Bachelor of Special Education 1c Admission into BECE-Bachelor of Early Childhood Education - Birth to 8 1d Admission into BISEEC-Bachelor of Inclusive and Specialised Education (Early Childhood) 1e Admission into BECEB Bachelor of Early Childhood - Birth to 5 Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e))

title: Teaching and Educational Contexts
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to develop: An awareness of the move from student to teacher in educational settings An awareness of different philosophies and aims of education An awareness of different educational contexts An awareness of the context of teaching demands in educational contexts Early skills in Critical thinking Foundational skills for university study An 'Educational Vocabulary' An awareness of social, cultural, and individual difference

In this topic students will be oriented to the concept of education and teaching and their role as a teacher. Education is considered in a broad sense, encompassing a range of settings from Early Childhood through Primary and Secondary to Tertiary educational contexts. The topic acknowledges the historical and political aspects of education and teaching. The topic provides an introduction to the education awards and acknowledges that education is differentiated across race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, ability, class and location. As the influences on educational contexts change across time, then so do teaching and learning contexts. The changing face of these contexts is explained through the process of globalisation. The issue of teacher identity and the teaching profession are explored through these key educational issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in critical thinking (cultural analysis) and foundational skills for university study
Describe theories of social, cultural, and individual difference
Demonstrate an awareness of different philosophies and aims of education
Demonstrate a developing 'Educational Vocabulary'
Articulate theories of globalisation and implications for education and teaching
Understand the role of teachers and systems in educational contexts
Describe different educational contexts that constitute the field of Australian Education
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BEDECBA-Bachelor of Education (Early Childhood), Bachelor of Arts 1a Admission into BEDMSSBSC-B Education (Middle & Secondary Schooling), B Science 1b Admission into BEDMSSBA-B Education (Middle & Secondary Schooling), B Arts 1c Admission into BEDECSEBDS-B Education (Early Childhood & Special Ed), B Disability Studies 1d Admission into BEDMSSEBDS-B Education (Middle & Secondary/Special Ed), B Disability Studies 1e Admission into BEDPRSEBDS-B Education (Primary R-7 & Special Ed), B Disability Studies 1f Admission into BEDSBA-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Arts 1g Admission into BEDSBHS-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Health Sciences 1h Admission into BEDSBSC-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Science 1i Admission into BEDSBSE-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Special Education 1j Admission into BEDSBLANG-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Languages 1k Admission into BAMTS-Bachelor of Arts, Master of Teaching (Secondary) 1l Admission into BSCMTS-Bachelor of Science, Master of Teaching (Secondary) 1m Admission into BEDECBSE-Bachelor of Education (Early Childhood), Bachelor of Special Education Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g or 1h or 1i or 1j or 1k or 1l or 1m))

title: Reading, Comprehending and Producing Texts
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to: Equip pre-service teachers’ to teach reading, writing, and comprehension effectively, focusing on vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension within the Australian Curriculum: English and Literacy (GC) Foster pre-service teachers’ ability to engage with contemporary literacy research, enhancing metalinguistic knowledge and pedagogical practices to plan and assess high-quality literacy learning sequences. Cultivate pre-service teachers knowledge and understanding of socially just teaching practices that engage children and young people from diverse backgrounds and build strong relationships with parents and carers to support children and young people's literacy learning.

This topic develops pre-service teachers’ comprehensive knowledge of literacy instruction within the framework of the Australian Curriculum: English and Literacy as a General Capability. It examines the knowledge and skills related to vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension, which are essential for fostering primary children and young peoples' literacy development. Through exploration of contemporary research, pre-service teachers will identify evidence-based teaching strategies for teaching reading, comprehending, and producing texts. The topic emphasises the importance of metalinguistic awareness, equipping pre-service teachers with the necessary pedagogical practices to support children and young peoples' language learning. The topic emphasises socially just approaches to teaching English and literacy, and the importance of engaging parents and carers in literacy learning.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-informed perspectives based on critical evaluation and synthesis of contemporary literacy research
Justify instructional decisions about literacy planning and sequencing based on evidence-based practices
Critically evaluate and select appropriate inclusive literacy practices that engage children and young people from diverse backgrounds and foster strong relationships with parents and carers

Evaluate written text samples at word and sentence levels using provided criteria and use the appropriate metalanguage associated with traditional and functional grammar to discuss students’ literacy learning with a range of audience

title: Middle Schooling Philosophy and Pedagogy
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
Students will be provided with the opportunity to: Consider the need for, and purpose of, middle schooling Examine the philosophy and pedagogy of middle schooling Investigate models of middle schooling Critically analyse middle schoolings claims regarding social justice

This topic introduces students to the foundational understandings regarding middle schooling philosophy and pedagogy. Theoretical and practical examples of models of middle schooling will be presented, and approaches to middle schooling will be examined and critiqued.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to demonstrate an understanding of how to plan for authentic learning through the application of middle schooling pedagogy
Articulate a personal philosophy of middle schooling
Demonstrate a clear understanding of the context and concept of middle schooling through critiquing and evaluating the claims of middle schooling philosophy, pedagogy and practice
prerequisites: 1 Admission into BEDMSSBA-B Education (Middle & Secondary Schooling), B Arts 1a Admission into BEDMSSBSC-B Education (Middle & Secondary Schooling), B Science 1b Admission into BEDMSSEBDS-B Education (Middle & Secondary/Special Ed), B Disability Studies 1c Admission into BEDSBA-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Arts 1d Admission into BEDSBHS-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Health Sciences 1e Admission into BEDSBSC-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Science 1f Admission into BEDSBLANG-Bachelor of Education (Secondary), Bachelor of Languages 1g Admission into BAMTS-Bachelor of Arts, Master of Teaching (Secondary) 1h Admission into BSCMTS-Bachelor of Science, Master of Teaching (Secondary) 2 EDUC1120 2a EDUC1101 Must Satisfy: ((1 or 1a or 1b or 1c or 1d or 1e or 1f or 1g or 1h) and (2 or 2a))

title: Foundations of Inclusive Education
school: College of Education, Psychology and Social Work
syllabus_overview:
This topic aims to introduce preservice teachers to the foundational philosophies, evidence-based principles and theories, relevant laws and policies, diverse and historical points of view, and human issues that inform an understanding of inclusive education. A core focus is placed on the treatment of students with diverse needs both in school and society and the ways in which Education can shape and apply inclusive approaches.

This topic establishes the importance of inclusion in diverse, contemporary classrooms. It examines the history of exclusion and segregation experienced by many students with disability and positions teachers to better explore inclusive pedagogical approaches, guided by current international commitments, legislation and policy.
learning_outcomes: Analyse research evidence and evaluate contemporary claims related to inclusive education
